docs.title: 1.4 A Short History of Databases
docs.text:
Databases began in the 1960s as navigational systems where programs followed pointers from record to record. In 1970 Edgar F. Codd proposed the relational model of simple tables, which led to SQL and to products such as Oracle, Db2 and later open-source MySQL and PostgreSQL. Since 2009 web-scale NoSQL systems, NewSQL, cloud databases and, most recently, vector databases for AI have joined them.

Six decades of databases. Each wave added options; none fully replaced relational databases.

Think of it like…

It is like the history of maps: first turn-by-turn directions you had to follow exactly (navigational), then a grid map where you can ask for any place by its coordinates (relational), then specialised maps for different journeys (NoSQL, vector).

Real-world example

A student, Tom, compares two ways to list all of a supplier's parts. In a 1970s CODASYL system he writes a loop that finds the supplier record then follows 'next part' pointers one by one. In SQL he writes one declarative line — SELECT part FROM supplies WHERE supplier = 'Acme' — and the DBMS decides how to find them. That shift is the heart of Codd's revolution.

docs.title: How it works
docs.text:
1. 1960s: hierarchical (IBM IMS) and network (CODASYL, Bachman's IDS) databases navigate pointers.
  2. 1970: Codd's paper proposes relations queried by what you want, not how to find it.
  3. 1974-1983: IBM System R invents SEQUEL/SQL; Oracle (1979) and Db2 (1983) commercialise it.
  4. 1986-1996: SQL becomes an ANSI then ISO standard; open-source MySQL (1995) and PostgreSQL (1996) appear.
  5. 2006-2012: Bigtable and Dynamo papers inspire NoSQL; the term spreads after a 2009 meetup; Spanner shows global SQL.
  6. 2010s-2020s: managed cloud databases, separated storage and compute, serverless, and vector search for AI.

Who uses it

Interviewers, lecturers and architects use this history to explain why today's systems look the way they do; it is a standard first-lecture topic in database courses.

Key takeaway

Remember three names and dates: Charles Bachman (navigational databases, Turing Award 1973), Edgar F. Codd (relational model, 1970; Turing Award 1981) and Michael Stonebraker (Ingres and Postgres; Turing Award 2014).

Going deeper

  • IBM built IMS (Information Management System) with North American Rockwell for the Apollo programme's bill of materials; first shipped around 1968, it still runs high-volume banking and insurance workloads on IBM mainframes today.
  • Codd's June 1970 paper in Communications of the ACM, 'A Relational Model of Data for Large Shared Data Banks', separated the logical view from physical storage; IBM was slow to adopt it because IMS was profitable.
  • System R's language was first called SEQUEL (Chamberlin and Boyce, 1974) and renamed SQL over a trademark conflict; Relational Software Inc., later renamed Oracle, shipped the first commercial SQL RDBMS, Oracle V2, in 1979.
  • Google's Bigtable (2006) and Amazon's Dynamo (2007) papers showed how to scale across thousands of cheap servers by relaxing relational features; 'NoSQL' was popularised by a June 2009 San Francisco meetup on non-relational databases.
  • Matthew Aslett of the 451 Group coined 'NewSQL' in 2011 for systems keeping SQL and ACID while scaling out; Google's Spanner paper (OSDI 2012) and later CockroachDB, TiDB and YugabyteDB followed that path.
  • The 2020s brought AI-driven change: vector search arrived as specialised databases and as features inside PostgreSQL (pgvector), Oracle, SQL Server 2025, MongoDB and others, so similarity search became a mainstream database capability.

Common mistakes & misconceptions

  • Thinking NoSQL replaced SQL: relational systems still top the DB-Engines ranking, and many NoSQL products have since added SQL-like languages and transactions.
  • Crediting Oracle with inventing SQL: SQL came from IBM's System R research; Oracle was first to sell a commercial SQL product.
  • Assuming 'legacy' means dead: IMS, mainframe Db2 and COBOL systems still process large shares of banking and airline transactions.

docs.title: 1.5 The Main Data Models at a Glance
docs.text:
A data model is the shape in which a database expects data and the way you ask questions about it. Relational databases use tables; document databases store JSON-like documents; key-value stores keep simple lookups; wide-column, graph, time-series, search and vector databases each specialise in one shape of data. Picking the right model makes the common questions easy and fast.

Eight data models. Same customer, eight shapes — each model optimises different questions.

Think of it like…

Data models are like storage furniture: a filing cabinet (relational), a box of labelled folders (document), a coat-check with numbered tickets (key-value), a corkboard with strings between pins (graph) — each suits different things.

Real-world example

The fictional streaming start-up Lumen stores subscribers and payments in PostgreSQL (relational), session data in Redis (key-value), its catalogue in MongoDB (document), 'people who watched this also watched' in Neo4j (graph), playback metrics in a time-series store, and film-description embeddings in a vector index for 'find something like this'.

docs.title: How it works
docs.text:
1. List the main things you store and the questions you ask most often.
  2. Notice the data's shape: tabular, nested, simple lookups, connections, time-stamped or similarity-based.
  3. Match the shape to a model: relational is the safe default; specialists fit specific patterns.
  4. Check consistency, transaction and scale needs before choosing a product.
  5. Accept that one system may use several models (polyglot persistence) or one multi-model engine.

Who uses it

Architects and senior engineers choose data models; every developer needs to recognise them when reading system designs or job descriptions.

Key takeaway

When unsure, start relational: PostgreSQL can also store JSON documents, key-value pairs, time series and vectors, so you only add a specialist database when a measured need appears.

Going deeper

  • Relational databases still dominate the October 2026 DB-Engines ranking: Oracle, MySQL, SQL Server and PostgreSQL occupy the top four places, with MongoDB, the leading document store, fifth.
  • Data models trade generality for speed: a key-value store can answer GET user:42 in well under a millisecond but cannot answer 'all users in Leeds' without a separate index you build and maintain.
  • Multi-model is now normal: PostgreSQL offers JSONB and vector extensions, Oracle and SQL Server 2025 add JSON and vector types, and MongoDB added multi-document ACID transactions in version 4.0 (2018).
  • Graph data has two main flavours — property graphs (Neo4j; queried with Cypher or ISO GQL) and RDF triples (queried with SPARQL) — and SQL:2023 added property-graph queries over ordinary tables.
  • The detailed products and trade-offs for each NoSQL model are covered in the NoSQL chapter; modelling techniques such as embedding versus referencing are covered in the data-modelling chapter.

Common mistakes & misconceptions

  • Choosing a database because it is fashionable rather than because its model fits your main queries.
  • Assuming 'schemaless' means no schema: the schema moves into application code, where it is harder to see and enforce.
  • Adding a new database per data model too early: every extra system needs backups, monitoring, security and skills.

docs.title: 1.6 Tables, Rows, Columns, Keys and Schemas
docs.text:
In a relational database data lives in tables. Each row is one thing (a customer, an order) and each column is one fact about it (name, email). A primary key uniquely identifies every row, a foreign key links a row to a row in another table, and the schema is the blueprint describing all tables, columns, types and rules.

Keys link the library's tables. Arrows point from a foreign key to the primary key it references.

Think of it like…

A table is like a class register: each line is one pupil, each column one detail, the pupil number is the primary key, and the 'form tutor' column pointing to the staff list is a foreign key.

Real-world example

The fictional Pine Valley Library has a members table (member_id, name, email) and a loans table (loan_id, member_id, book_id, due_date). Member 1047, Sara Khan, appears once in members; each of her three loans stores only 1047 in its member_id foreign-key column. Changing Sara's email updates one row, and the database refuses a loan for member 9999 because no such member exists.

docs.title: How it works
docs.text:
1. Decide which things (entities) you store; each becomes a table.
  2. Give each table columns with names and data types.
  3. Choose a primary key that uniquely identifies every row.
  4. Link related tables with foreign keys that reference primary keys.
  5. Add constraints (NOT NULL, UNIQUE, CHECK) and record it all in the schema.

Who uses it

Every developer, analyst and DBA reads and writes table definitions; designing them well is the job of data modellers and backend engineers.

Key takeaway

A primary key must be unique and never NULL; a foreign key may repeat and (unless declared NOT NULL) may be NULL — a favourite beginner interview question.

Going deeper

  • Tables are formally unordered: without ORDER BY a database may return rows in any order, and that order can change after an update, a VACUUM or a new query plan.
  • Primary keys are almost always backed by a unique index, so looking up one row among 100 million typically costs only three or four page reads in a B-tree.
  • Surrogate keys (an auto-generated number or UUID) are usually preferred over natural keys like email addresses, which change and can be reused; the modelling chapter compares bigint identity, UUIDv4 and UUIDv7.
  • Cardinality describes relationships: one-to-many (one member, many loans) uses a foreign key on the 'many' side; many-to-many (books and authors) needs a junction table holding two foreign keys.
  • The word 'schema' has two meanings: the overall design of a database, and a named namespace inside it (PostgreSQL's 'public' schema, SQL Server's 'dbo').

Common mistakes & misconceptions

  • Relying on the order rows were inserted: always use ORDER BY when order matters.
  • Using a person's name or email as the primary key — names repeat and emails change; use a surrogate key and a UNIQUE constraint instead.
  • Forgetting that SQLite enforces foreign keys only after PRAGMA foreign_keys = ON on each connection.

docs.title: Try it: Create two linked tables and watch a foreign key protect them (PostgreSQL or SQLite)
docs.text:
CREATE TABLE members (
  member_id INTEGER PRIMARY KEY,
  name      TEXT NOT NULL,
  email     TEXT UNIQUE
);
CREATE TABLE loans (
  loan_id   INTEGER PRIMARY KEY,
  member_id INTEGER NOT NULL REFERENCES members(member_id),
  due_date  DATE NOT NULL
);
INSERT INTO members VALUES (1047, 'Sara Khan', 'sara@example.org');
INSERT INTO loans VALUES (1, 1047, '2026-10-22');   -- works
INSERT INTO loans VALUES (2, 9999, '2026-10-22');   -- fails: no member 9999
-- (SQLite: run PRAGMA foreign_keys = ON; first)

docs.title: 1.7 Transactions and ACID in Plain English
docs.text:
A transaction is a group of database changes that must succeed or fail together. ACID names four promises a database makes about transactions: Atomicity (all or nothing), Consistency (rules are never broken), Isolation (simultaneous transactions don't see each other's half-done work) and Durability (once confirmed, it survives crashes).

Life of a bank-transfer transaction. Nothing is permanent until the commit record reaches durable storage.

Think of it like…

A transaction is like a vending machine purchase: either you get the snack and the machine keeps your coin, or you get your coin back — never a lost coin and no snack.

Real-world example

Jo transfers £200 from her current account to savings at the fictional Northgate Bank. The database must subtract £200 from one row and add £200 to another. If the server crashes after the first change, atomicity rolls it back so no money vanishes; a CHECK rule keeps balances from going negative; isolation stops a statement run halfway from seeing the money in neither account; durability means that after 'Transfer complete' appears, the change survives a power cut.

docs.title: How it works
docs.text:
1. BEGIN starts the transaction.
  2. Each change is applied in memory and described in the write-ahead log.
  3. The DBMS checks constraints and isolates the changes from other sessions.
  4. COMMIT forces the log to durable storage, then reports success.
  5. If anything fails before commit, ROLLBACK undoes every change.

Who uses it

Banking, payments, booking, stock control and any system handling money or scarce items depends on ACID; backend developers must understand it to write correct code.

Key takeaway

Know who coined it: Theo Härder and Andreas Reuter named ACID in 1983, building on Jim Gray's transaction work; and know that the 'C' is partly the application's job — the database enforces only the rules you declare.

Going deeper

  • Atomicity and durability are implemented with a write-ahead log: changes are recorded in the log before data pages, so after a crash the DBMS redoes committed work and undoes uncommitted work (the ARIES recovery method, 1992, is the classic design).
  • Isolation is a dial, not a switch: the SQL standard defines READ UNCOMMITTED, READ COMMITTED, REPEATABLE READ and SERIALIZABLE; PostgreSQL and SQL Server default to READ COMMITTED and MySQL InnoDB to REPEATABLE READ.
  • Durability costs time because a commit waits for the log to reach stable storage; on a cloud SSD this fsync often takes 0.5-2 ms, which is why databases batch commits together (group commit).
  • The CAP-era alternative BASE (Basically Available, Soft state, Eventual consistency) describes many NoSQL systems that relax isolation or consistency for availability and scale.
  • Many operations are transactions even without BEGIN: in autocommit mode (the default in most drivers) each statement is its own transaction, committed immediately.
  • How isolation is implemented — locking, MVCC, snapshot isolation and the anomalies each level allows — is covered in depth in the internals chapter.

Common mistakes & misconceptions

  • Believing the 'C' in ACID means the database magically knows business rules: it enforces only declared constraints, triggers and the logic your transaction runs.
  • Holding a transaction open while waiting for a user or a slow API call — it blocks others and bloats the database; keep transactions short.
  • Assuming ACID means SERIALIZABLE: most databases default to weaker isolation that allows some anomalies.

docs.title: Try it: Watch ROLLBACK undo a transfer (psql or sqlite3)
docs.text:
CREATE TABLE accounts(id INT PRIMARY KEY, owner TEXT, balance NUMERIC CHECK (balance >= 0));
INSERT INTO accounts VALUES (1,'Jo current',500),(2,'Jo savings',100);
BEGIN;
UPDATE accounts SET balance = balance - 200 WHERE id = 1;
UPDATE accounts SET balance = balance + 200 WHERE id = 2;
SELECT * FROM accounts;   -- 300 and 300 inside the transaction
ROLLBACK;
SELECT * FROM accounts;   -- back to 500 and 100

docs.title: 1.8 OLTP vs OLAP: Running the Business vs Understanding It
docs.text:
Databases serve two very different jobs. OLTP (online transaction processing) handles many small, fast reads and writes as the business runs — placing orders, booking seats. OLAP (online analytical processing) runs fewer but huge read-only queries that scan millions of rows to answer questions like 'sales by region by month'. Because the workloads differ, they usually run on differently built systems.

Two workloads, two designs

OLTP OLAP Typical query Fetch/update one order Sum sales by month Rows touched 1-100 Millions to billions Writes Constant small inserts Bulk loads, appends Storage layout Row-oriented Column-oriented, compressed Key metric Latency, transactions/s Scan throughput, GB/s Schema style Normalised Star schema, wide tables Examples PostgreSQL, MySQL Snowflake, BigQuery, ClickHouse

HTAP systems try to serve both columns at once.

Think of it like…

OLTP is the shop till — quick, constant, one customer at a time; OLAP is the accountant at year-end — few questions, but each one needs every receipt.

Real-world example

The fictional Tidewater Hotels group's booking database handles about 400 small transactions per second: check availability, insert a booking, update a room. Every night its data is copied to a cloud warehouse, where the revenue team runs a query scanning 900 million historical bookings to compare occupancy by city and season. Running that scan on the booking database would slow guests' bookings, so the two workloads are kept apart.

docs.title: How it works
docs.text:
1. Applications write business events to an OLTP database in small transactions.
  2. A pipeline copies or streams changes out (ETL/ELT or change data capture).
  3. Data is reshaped for analysis — often into fact and dimension tables.
  4. An OLAP engine stores it column by column, compressed, for fast scans.
  5. Analysts and dashboards run large aggregate queries without touching OLTP.

Who uses it

Backend developers and DBAs own OLTP systems; data engineers, analytics engineers and analysts work on the OLAP side — knowing which side you are on shapes every design choice.

Key takeaway

In interviews contrast them on four axes: query shape (point lookups vs big scans), writes (constant vs batch loads), storage (row vs column) and users (applications vs analysts).

Going deeper

  • Row stores keep each row's columns together, ideal for fetching one whole order; column stores keep each column together, so a query summing one column of a 50-column table reads roughly 2% of the data and compresses it far better.
  • Benchmarks formalise the split: TPC-C (1992) models an order-entry OLTP workload measured in transactions per minute, while TPC-H and TPC-DS model decision-support queries over large data sets.
  • Codd and colleagues coined 'OLAP' in a 1993 white paper; earlier analytical systems used multidimensional 'cubes' that pre-computed totals along dimensions such as time, product and region.
  • HTAP (hybrid transactional/analytical processing) engines keep a row store for transactions plus a column replica for analytics — examples include TiDB with TiFlash, SQL Server columnstore indexes and Oracle Database In-Memory.
  • Many teams send analytics to a read replica of the OLTP database before adopting a warehouse; this protects the primary but still uses a row store poorly suited to big scans.
  • Warehouses, lakehouses, columnar formats and pipelines are covered in depth in the analytics and data-engineering chapter.

Common mistakes & misconceptions

  • Running heavy reports on the production OLTP primary at peak hours — they compete for CPU, memory and I/O with customers' transactions.
  • Assuming a warehouse can replace the OLTP database: most are not built for thousands of small concurrent updates with strict latency.
  • Thinking OLAP data is always out of date: streaming and CDC pipelines can keep analytical copies seconds behind.

docs.title: 1.9 Database Architectures: Embedded to Cloud-Native
docs.text:
Databases are deployed in a few basic shapes. Embedded databases run inside your application as a library; client-server databases run as a separate server that many applications connect to over a network; distributed databases spread data across many machines; and cloud services add serverless billing and a split between storage and compute so each can grow on its own.

Cloud-native: compute separated from storage. Compute nodes can be added or paused without copying the data.

Think of it like…

Embedded is a notebook in your pocket, client-server is a shared office filing room, distributed is a chain of branch offices sharing records, and serverless cloud is a self-storage company that charges only for the space and the minutes you use.

Real-world example

The fictional fitness app PulsePath keeps each user's workouts in SQLite on the phone (embedded) so it works offline. Phones sync to a PostgreSQL server (client-server) behind the company API. As users grow to 20 million, PulsePath moves to a managed cloud database where storage is replicated across three data centres and compute scales down to almost nothing overnight.

docs.title: How it works
docs.text:
1. Embedded: the app links the engine library and reads a local file directly.
  2. Client-server: apps send queries over TCP to a database server process.
  3. Replicated: one primary server streams changes to read replicas.
  4. Distributed: data is partitioned and replicated across many nodes that cooperate.
  5. Cloud-native: compute nodes run queries while a shared storage service keeps data; serverless adds scale-to-zero.

Who uses it

Solution architects, cloud engineers and DBAs choose deployment architecture; mobile and desktop developers meet embedded databases; most backend developers work with client-server or managed cloud databases.

Key takeaway

Remember the three classic parallel architectures — shared-memory, shared-disk (e.g. Oracle RAC) and shared-nothing (e.g. most distributed SQL and NoSQL) — and that cloud-native designs often share storage but not compute.

Going deeper

  • Embedded engines avoid network round trips entirely: a SQLite point lookup can complete in microseconds, while even a same-data-centre client-server query usually costs a few hundred microseconds of network latency.
  • Client-server databases listen on well-known TCP ports — PostgreSQL 5432, MySQL 3306, SQL Server 1433, Oracle 1521, MongoDB 27017, Redis 6379 — and each connection consumes server memory, which is why connection pools exist.
  • Amazon Aurora (announced 2014) pioneered pushing the log to a distributed storage layer that keeps six copies across three Availability Zones, so writer and readers share one volume instead of each holding a full copy.
  • Separating storage from compute lets warehouses such as Snowflake and BigQuery run many independent compute clusters over one data set, and lets serverless Postgres services pause compute when idle and resume in under a second or so.
  • Shared-nothing systems scale by partitioning data across nodes that own their own disks; the price is distributed coordination — cross-node transactions, rebalancing and consensus — covered in the distributed-data chapter.
  • In-process analytics engines such as DuckDB bring the embedded idea to OLAP: a laptop can scan multi-gigabyte Parquet files with SQL without any server.

Common mistakes & misconceptions

  • Putting a SQLite file on a network drive for many writers: SQLite allows one writer at a time and network file locking is unreliable — use a client-server database.
  • Assuming serverless means free or limitless: you pay per request or capacity unit, cold starts add latency, and limits still apply.
  • Going distributed too early: a single well-tuned server with replicas handles far more load than most applications ever reach.

docs.title: Try it: Compare embedded and client-server in Python
docs.text:
import sqlite3                     # embedded: no server, just a file
con = sqlite3.connect('local.db')
print(con.execute('select sqlite_version()').fetchone())

# client-server: needs a running PostgreSQL server (pip install psycopg)
import psycopg
with psycopg.connect('host=localhost port=5432 dbname=postgres user=postgres') as c:
    print(c.execute('select version()').fetchone())

Shared-nothing architectureMichael Stonebraker, 1986 paper · Concept · Current · Advanced · General Each node has its own CPU, memory and disk; data is partitioned across nodes, which coordinate over the network. A Cassandra cluster spreads customer data across 12 independent nodes. Shared-disk architecturee.g. Oracle Real Application Clusters (RAC) · Concept · Current · Advanced · Relational Several database servers share the same storage and coordinate access to it, so any node can read any data. A bank's Oracle RAC cluster keeps working when one of its four servers fails. Distributed databaseGeneral term · Concept · Current · Intermediate · General A database whose data is stored and processed across multiple machines but appears to users as one database. CockroachDB keeps three replicas of each data range on different servers. Separation of storage and computeCloud-native design (Snowflake, Aurora, BigQuery, Neon, AlloyDB) · Concept · Current · Intermediate · General Keeping data in a shared storage service while independent compute nodes run queries, so each scales separately. A warehouse spins up a second compute cluster for month-end reporting over the same data. Serverless databasee.g. Aurora Serverless v2, DynamoDB on-demand, Neon, Cloud Firestore · Concept · Current · Intermediate · General A managed database that scales capacity automatically, sometimes to zero, and bills by usage instead of fixed servers. A hobby project's serverless Postgres pauses overnight and costs pennies a month. Database as a service (DBaaS)e.g. Amazon RDS (2009), Azure SQL Database, Google Cloud SQL · Concept · Current · Beginner · General A cloud provider runs the database for you, handling installation, patching, backups and failover. A start-up uses Amazon RDS for PostgreSQL instead of hiring a full-time DBA. Primary-replica topologyReplication pattern · Concept · Current · Intermediate · General One primary accepts writes and streams changes to read-only replicas that share the read load. An app sends writes to the primary and product-page reads to two replicas. Amazon AuroraAmazon Web Services (announced 2014, generally available 2015) · Service · Current · Intermediate · Relational A MySQL- and PostgreSQL-compatible cloud database whose distributed storage keeps six copies across three Availability Zones. An e-commerce site adds Aurora readers in minutes because they share one storage volume. In-process OLAPe.g. DuckDB, chDB, Polars SQL · Concept · Current · Intermediate · Analytical Running an analytical column engine inside the application or notebook process, with no server. An analyst queries 3 GB of Parquet in a Jupyter notebook with DuckDB. Edge databasee.g. Cloudflare D1, Turso (libSQL) · Concept · Emerging · Intermediate · Relational Databases replicated to many locations close to users so reads have low latency worldwide. A blog's comments are read from a SQLite-based replica in the nearest city.

docs.title: 1.10 The 2026 Database Landscape
docs.text:
Hundreds of database products exist, but a handful dominate. Two public yardsticks are widely quoted: the monthly DB-Engines ranking, which measures popularity from web searches, job ads and discussions, and the Stack Overflow Developer Survey, which asks developers what they actually use. In 2026 both show relational databases on top, with PostgreSQL the developers' favourite.

Most used databases — Stack Overflow 2026 survey. Share of respondents to the database question; people may tick several.

Think of it like…

Rankings are like football league tables built from different statistics — one counts how often a team is talked about, the other how many people play for it — so the order differs but the big clubs are the same.

Real-world example

Priya, a computing student, wants to pick one database to learn first. She checks the October 2026 DB-Engines ranking (Oracle first, then MySQL, SQL Server and PostgreSQL) and the 2026 Stack Overflow survey (PostgreSQL used by 57.9% of respondents who answered the database question). She chooses PostgreSQL for skills that transfer everywhere, then adds SQLite and MongoDB basics.

docs.title: How it works
docs.text:
1. Read DB-Engines for overall industry popularity and trends over time.
  2. Read the Stack Overflow survey for what working developers use and want.
  3. Check job adverts in your region — enterprises still hire heavily for Oracle and SQL Server.
  4. Note fast risers: cloud warehouses, lakehouses, and vector-capable databases.
  5. Pick one relational database to master, then sample one NoSQL and one analytical system.

Who uses it

Students choosing what to learn, architects choosing a platform and recruiters writing job ads all consult these rankings.

Key takeaway

Quote rankings with their method: DB-Engines measures popularity (mentions, searches, jobs), not market share or quality; survey percentages count respondents who answered that question.

Going deeper

  • October 2026 DB-Engines top ten: Oracle (about 1,120 points), MySQL (838), Microsoft SQL Server (694), PostgreSQL (689), MongoDB (375), Snowflake (221), Databricks (171), Redis (156), IBM Db2 (106) and Apache Cassandra (99).
  • DB-Engines scores combine website mentions, Google Trends, Stack Overflow and DBA Stack Exchange questions, job offers, LinkedIn profiles and social media; scores are relative, so twice the points means roughly twice the measured popularity.
  • In the Stack Overflow survey PostgreSQL has been the most used database since 2023; in 2025 it reached 55.6% of all respondents (58.2% of professional developers), and the 2026 edition shows 57.9%.
  • Analytics platforms have climbed fastest: Snowflake and Databricks both entered the DB-Engines top ten, reflecting the move of reporting workloads to cloud warehouses and lakehouses.
  • Versions current in October 2026 include PostgreSQL 18 (19 in beta), MySQL 9.7 LTS and 8.4 LTS, SQL Server 2025, SQLite 3.53 and Oracle AI Database 26ai; check vendors' sites, as releases are frequent.
  • Ownership changes reshape the market: Databricks bought serverless-Postgres company Neon and Snowflake bought Crunchy Data in 2025, showing data platforms racing to add operational Postgres.

Common mistakes & misconceptions

  • Treating DB-Engines points as market share: they measure online popularity signals, not revenue or installed base.
  • Concluding Oracle is unused because it ranks low among survey developers: it remains first on DB-Engines and dominant in large enterprises.
  • Adding survey percentages to 100%: respondents can select several databases.

docs.title: 1.11 How an Application Talks to a Database
docs.text:
Applications never read database files directly when using a database server. They use a driver — a library that speaks the database's network protocol — to open a connection, send SQL, and receive rows back. On top of drivers sit connection pools that reuse connections and, often, ORMs that map rows to objects in your programming language.

One query from app to PostgreSQL. The pool hides connection set-up, which can cost several network round trips.

Think of it like…

The driver is a phone line and interpreter: your program dials the database (connection), speaks through the interpreter (protocol), and the pool is a switchboard that keeps a few lines open so nobody waits for a dial tone.

Real-world example

Marco builds a booking API for the fictional Harbour Kayaks. His Python code borrows a connection from a pool of 10, sends 'SELECT * FROM slots WHERE day = %s' with the date as a separate parameter, and the psycopg driver turns the reply into Python tuples. Using parameters rather than pasting the date into the string keeps the query safe from SQL injection.

docs.title: How it works
docs.text:
1. The app reads a connection string: host, port, database, user, TLS settings.
  2. The driver opens a TCP connection, negotiates TLS and authenticates.
  3. The app sends SQL text plus separate parameter values (a prepared or parameterised statement).
  4. The server parses, plans and executes, then streams rows back in the wire protocol.
  5. The driver converts rows to language types; the connection returns to the pool.

Who uses it

Backend and full-stack developers write this code daily; DBAs and SREs tune pools and connection limits; security teams check credentials and parameterisation.

Key takeaway

Never build SQL by gluing user input into strings — always use parameters (placeholders like ?, %s or $1); it is the single most important database security habit and a near-certain interview question.

Going deeper

  • Each database has its own wire protocol: PostgreSQL's frontend/backend protocol (version 3 since 2003), MySQL's client/server protocol, Microsoft's TDS (Tabular Data Stream) for SQL Server and Oracle's TNS/Net8 — drivers hide these details.
  • Standard driver APIs let code stay similar across databases: ODBC (1992) for C and many tools, JDBC (1997) for Java, ADO.NET for .NET, Python's DB-API 2.0 (PEP 249) and Go's database/sql.
  • Opening a connection can cost several round trips plus authentication and, in PostgreSQL, forking a new server process, so apps keep pools of open connections; external poolers such as PgBouncer multiplex thousands of clients onto a few dozen server connections.
  • Prepared statements send SQL once and parameters separately: the server can reuse the parsed plan, and because values are never interpreted as SQL text, injection attacks fail.
  • ORMs (Object-Relational Mappers) such as SQLAlchemy, Hibernate, Entity Framework Core and Prisma generate SQL from code; they speed development but can hide inefficient queries — the operations chapter covers their pitfalls, such as N+1 queries.
  • Some services expose databases over HTTP instead of a driver protocol — for example PostgREST and Supabase for PostgreSQL, or Microsoft's Data API builder — useful for serverless and edge functions that cannot hold long-lived connections.

Common mistakes & misconceptions

  • Opening a new connection per web request without a pool: latency rises and the server can run out of connection slots (PostgreSQL's default max_connections is 100).
  • Concatenating user input into SQL strings — this causes SQL injection; use parameters every time.
  • Hard-coding passwords in source code: load credentials from environment variables or a secrets manager.

docs.title: Try it: A safe parameterised query in Python with the built-in sqlite3 driver
docs.text:
import sqlite3
con = sqlite3.connect(':memory:')
con.execute('CREATE TABLE slots(day TEXT, time TEXT, free INT)')
con.executemany('INSERT INTO slots VALUES (?,?,?)',
                [('2026-10-10','09:00',4), ('2026-10-10','11:00',0)])
day = '2026-10-10'            # imagine this came from a web form
for row in con.execute('SELECT time, free FROM slots WHERE day = ? AND free > 0', (day,)):
    print(row)

docs.title: 1.12 Follow a 'Buy' Click Through the Database
docs.text:
When you press 'Buy', a small chain of database work happens in about a tenth of a second: stock is checked and reserved, an order is written, payment is recorded, and the whole thing is committed atomically. Afterwards the change ripples out to replicas, caches, search indexes and the analytics warehouse.

A checkout, step by step. Only the commit makes the order real; everything downstream follows from it.

Think of it like…

It is like a restaurant order: the waiter checks the kitchen still has the dish, writes the ticket, takes payment, and only then shouts 'order in!' — and later the day's tickets are added up in the back office.

Real-world example

Ana buys the last pair of size-6 boots from the fictional shop TrailNest. Her click reaches an API server, which starts a transaction, locks the stock row, finds quantity 1, sets it to 0, inserts an order and three order lines, stores the payment reference and commits. A second shopper clicking a millisecond later waits on the lock, then sees quantity 0 and gets 'sold out' instead of a double sale.

docs.title: How it works
docs.text:
1. The browser sends POST /checkout with an idempotency key; the API borrows a pooled connection.
  2. BEGIN; SELECT … FOR UPDATE locks the product's stock row and checks quantity.
  3. UPDATE decrements stock; INSERT … RETURNING creates the order and its lines.
  4. The payment is authorised (ideally outside or before the long part of the transaction) and its reference stored.
  5. COMMIT writes the WAL to disk; replicas, caches and CDC streams pick up the change.

Who uses it

Backend engineers design this flow; DBAs tune it; SREs watch its latency; data engineers consume its change stream for analytics.

Key takeaway

Interviewers love 'how do you stop overselling the last item?' — answer with a transaction plus a row lock (SELECT … FOR UPDATE) or a conditional UPDATE … WHERE quantity > 0, and an idempotency key for retries.

Going deeper

  • A typical checkout transaction touches five to twenty rows and should finish in a few milliseconds; most of the user-visible 100-300 ms is network, application code and the external payment call, not the database.
  • SELECT … FOR UPDATE takes a row lock that blocks other writers until commit; alternatives are optimistic concurrency (a version column checked in the UPDATE) and the single-statement conditional UPDATE shown in the snippet.
  • Idempotency keys stop double orders when a nervous user clicks twice or a mobile network retries: the API stores the key with a UNIQUE constraint, and a repeat request returns the original order instead of creating another.
  • Calling a payment provider inside an open transaction holds locks for hundreds of milliseconds or more; many designs reserve stock, commit, call the provider, then record the result in a second short transaction.
  • After commit, change data capture tools such as Debezium read the write-ahead log and publish an 'order created' event to Kafka, feeding search indexes, email services and the warehouse without slowing checkout.
  • Read replicas are typically milliseconds to seconds behind; showing Ana her order from a lagging replica could display 'no orders yet', so 'read-your-own-writes' pages read from the primary.

Common mistakes & misconceptions

  • Checking stock with a plain SELECT and updating later in separate steps — two shoppers can both see quantity 1 and both buy it.
  • Holding the transaction open during slow external calls, which blocks other buyers of popular items.
  • Retrying a failed request without an idempotency key, creating duplicate orders and double charges.

docs.title: Try it: Oversell-proof stock decrement (PostgreSQL)
docs.text:
BEGIN;
UPDATE stock SET quantity = quantity - 1
 WHERE sku = 'BOOT-6' AND quantity > 0
 RETURNING quantity;          -- 0 rows returned = sold out
INSERT INTO orders(customer_id, sku, total_pence)
VALUES (42, 'BOOT-6', 8999)
RETURNING order_id;
COMMIT;

docs.title: 1.13 Who Works With the Database?
docs.text:
Many different people touch a company's databases, each in a different way. Some design them, some keep them running, some write the code that reads and writes them, and others copy data out to analyse it. Knowing who does what helps you understand job adverts and who to ask when something breaks.

Roles along the data's journey. Data flows down; questions and requirements flow back up.

Think of it like…

A database is like a city's water system: engineers design it, operators keep it flowing, plumbers connect each building, inspectors test the water, and planners study usage to decide what to build next.

Real-world example

At the fictional delivery company SwiftCart, backend developer Ravi adds a 'delivery slot' column through a migration; DBA Helen reviews it and schedules it for low-traffic hours; data engineer Kofi updates the pipeline copying orders to the warehouse; analytics engineer Mei models a 'slot usage' table; analyst Dan builds the dashboard; and the data protection officer checks that customer addresses are deleted after the retention period.

docs.title: How it works
docs.text:
1. Architects and data modellers design schemas and choose platforms.
  2. Backend developers write application queries and schema migrations.
  3. DBAs and database reliability engineers keep databases fast, secure, backed up and available.
  4. Data engineers move data into warehouses and lakehouses; analytics engineers model it.
  5. Analysts, data scientists and ML engineers query it for insight and models; governance roles police its use.

Who uses it

This map is for students choosing a direction; detailed career paths, skills and certifications are in the careers chapter.

Key takeaway

Whatever role you target, SQL is the shared language — it appears in job adverts for developers, analysts, data scientists and engineers alike.

Going deeper

  • Database administrators traditionally own installation, upgrades, backups, security and tuning; in cloud-managed environments routine tasks shrink and the role shifts toward performance, cost, architecture and automation.
  • Database reliability engineering, described in the 2017 O'Reilly book of that name, applies SRE practices — service-level objectives, automation, infrastructure as code, blameless post-mortems — to databases.
  • The analytics engineer role emerged around 2018-2020 with dbt: they write tested, version-controlled SQL transformations so analysts can trust warehouse tables.
  • Under GDPR Article 37, public authorities and organisations whose core activities involve large-scale monitoring or special-category data must appoint a data protection officer, who advises on lawful processing of personal data in databases.
  • Small companies merge roles: a single 'full-stack' developer may design the schema, write migrations, run the managed database and build the dashboards.

Common mistakes & misconceptions

  • Assuming only DBAs need deep database skills: developers' queries and schema choices cause most performance problems.
  • Thinking data scientists mostly do machine learning: much of their time goes on finding, querying and cleaning data with SQL.
  • Ignoring governance roles: privacy and retention rules can force schema and pipeline changes late in a project.

docs.title: Chapter 7: Distributed Data, Scaling & Reliability
docs.text: One database server eventually runs out of room, and every server eventually fails. This chapter explains how databases grow beyond one machine and keep running through failures: scaling up and out, replication and its lag, sharding, the CAP and PACELC trade-offs, consistency models, consensus with Paxos and Raft, and distributed transactions. It then covers the everyday reliability toolkit — caching, connection pooling, failover, backups and disaster recovery, change data capture and event streaming — and finishes with databases that span the globe.

docs.title: 7.1 Scaling Up vs Scaling Out
docs.text:
When a database gets too busy you have two choices. Scaling up (vertical scaling) means moving to one bigger machine with more CPU, memory and faster disks. Scaling out (horizontal scaling) means spreading the work across many machines, either by copying the data (replicas) or splitting it (shards).

Scale up vs scale out

Scale up (vertical) Scale out (horizontal) How Bigger machine More machines App changes Usually none Routing, replicas or shards Ceiling Largest server available Practically very high Failure impact One box = whole service Partial failures possible Cost curve Steep at the top end Roughly linear per node Consistency Easy (one copy) Harder (many copies)

Scaling up is simpler; scaling out has no single-machine ceiling but adds coordination.

Think of it like…

A busy café can buy a bigger espresso machine (scale up) or open more counters with more baristas (scale out) — the second handles more customers but now the counters must coordinate who has which order.

Real-world example

ShopNest, a fictional online store, runs PostgreSQL on an 8-core server that hits 90% CPU every Black Friday. First they scale up to 64 cores — quick, no code changes. A year later they add three read replicas for product browsing. Only when writes outgrow the biggest machine do they consider sharding, because it changes how the app queries data.

docs.title: How it works
docs.text:
1. Measure first: find whether the bottleneck is CPU, memory, disk I/O, connections or locks.
  2. Tune queries and indexes — often the cheapest 10× win before any hardware change.
  3. Scale up: move to a larger instance; simple, but has a ceiling and a price curve that rises steeply.
  4. Scale reads out: add read replicas and send read-only queries to them.
  5. Split by function: move search, analytics or sessions to separate systems.
  6. Scale writes out: shard the data across many primaries (the hardest step).

Who uses it

Backend engineers, DBAs, site reliability engineers and solution architects make scaling decisions; capacity planning is a classic system-design interview topic.

Key takeaway

Interview rule of thumb: optimise, then scale up, then add read replicas, then shard — and always say what metric tells you it is time for the next step.

Going deeper

  • Cloud servers are now enormous: the largest general-purpose instances offer hundreds of vCPUs and multiple terabytes of RAM, and specialised memory-optimised machines reach tens of terabytes, so scaling up goes further than most people expect.
  • Amdahl's law says speed-up is limited by the serial part of the work: if 5% of each transaction must run serially (for example a hot row lock), no number of extra nodes can exceed a 20× speed-up.
  • Neil Gunther's Universal Scalability Law adds a coherency penalty: past a point, adding nodes makes throughput fall because nodes spend time keeping each other in sync — a common shape in real database benchmarks.
  • Little's Law (L = λ × W) links concurrency, throughput and latency: 2,000 queries per second at 5 ms each means about 10 queries in flight on average, which guides connection-pool and CPU sizing.
  • Read-heavy apps (often 90%+ reads) scale well with replicas; write-heavy apps do not, because every replica must still apply every write — only sharding divides write load.
  • Large services have run surprisingly far on one primary: OpenAI has described serving ChatGPT's core PostgreSQL workload from a single primary with dozens of read replicas, offloading write-heavy data elsewhere.

Common mistakes & misconceptions

  • Sharding too early: it adds cross-shard queries, resharding and operational pain; most apps never outgrow a well-tuned large instance plus replicas.
  • Adding hardware to fix a missing index: a full table scan is still slow on a bigger machine — check EXPLAIN plans first.
  • Measuring only averages: users feel p99 latency, so a change that improves the mean but doubles the tail can make things worse.

docs.title: Try it: Benchmark a local PostgreSQL with pgbench (scale factor 50 ≈ 5 million rows)
docs.text:
createdb benchdb
pgbench -i -s 50 benchdb          # create and load test tables
pgbench -c 10 -j 4 -T 60 benchdb  # 10 clients, 4 threads, 60 seconds
pgbench -c 50 -j 4 -T 60 benchdb  # does TPS grow, or does latency just rise?

docs.title: 7.2 Replication: Single-Leader, Multi-Leader & Leaderless
docs.text:
Replication means keeping copies of the same data on several machines, so you survive failures and can serve more reads. The big design question is who is allowed to accept writes: one leader, several leaders, or any node. A second question is whether the leader waits for copies to confirm (synchronous) or not (asynchronous).

Three replication topologies

Single-leader Multi-leader Leaderless Who accepts writes One primary Several primaries Any replica Conflicts None Must be resolved Must be resolved Failover Promote a replica Other leaders continue No failover needed Typical use Most SQL databases Multi-region, offline apps High-write, always-on Examples PostgreSQL, MySQL Galera, CouchDB, global tables Cassandra, ScyllaDB, Riak

The more nodes that can accept writes, the better the availability — and the more conflicts you must resolve.

Think of it like…

Single-leader is a teacher writing on the board while students copy; multi-leader is several teachers each with a board who swap notes later; leaderless is a group chat where you ask several friends and trust the majority answer.

Real-world example

Kestrel Bank, a fictional bank, uses single-leader PostgreSQL with one synchronous standby so no committed payment is lost. Its mobile notes app uses multi-leader sync so phones work offline. Its fraud-signal store uses leaderless Cassandra with replication factor 3, writing and reading at QUORUM so any one node can fail without errors.

docs.title: How it works
docs.text:
1. A client sends a write to a node allowed to accept it (the leader, any leader, or several nodes).
  2. That node records the change in its log (for example the write-ahead log or binlog).
  3. The change is shipped to the other replicas, in commit order.
  4. Synchronous mode: the client gets 'OK' only after one or more replicas confirm; asynchronous: immediately.
  5. Replicas apply the change; reads can be served from replicas, possibly slightly behind.
  6. If copies disagree (multi-leader, leaderless), a conflict-resolution rule decides the winner.

Who uses it

Every production database team configures replication; it is central to DBA, SRE and backend system-design interviews.

Key takeaway

Memorise the quorum rule: with N copies, choosing write quorum W and read quorum R such that R + W > N means every read overlaps at least one up-to-date copy.

Going deeper

  • Amazon's 2007 Dynamo paper popularised leaderless design: consistent hashing, sloppy quorums, hinted handoff, vector clocks and Merkle-tree anti-entropy — ideas inherited by Cassandra, Riak and Voldemort.
  • Quorum arithmetic: N = 3 with W = R = 2 tolerates one node down for reads and writes; N = 5 with W = R = 3 tolerates two, at the cost of more network traffic.
  • Synchronous replication to every replica makes availability worse, not better: one slow follower stalls all writes. Practical systems use one synchronous standby or a quorum (PostgreSQL ANY 2 of 3).
  • Asynchronous replication keeps writes fast but has a non-zero recovery point objective: commits not yet shipped are lost if the leader dies, typically milliseconds to seconds of data.
  • Last-writer-wins resolves conflicts by timestamp but silently drops one of two concurrent updates; CRDTs (Shapiro et al., 2011) merge concurrent updates mathematically so no write is lost.
  • Even with R + W > N, leaderless systems can return stale data during sloppy quorums, concurrent writes or after a failed write that partially succeeded — quorums are not linearizability.

Common mistakes & misconceptions

  • Thinking replicas are backups: a DROP TABLE or bad UPDATE replicates to every copy within milliseconds. You still need point-in-time backups.
  • Using multi-leader to 'scale writes' for one dataset: every leader still applies every write, and you inherit conflict resolution.
  • Assuming asynchronous replication loses nothing on failover: unshipped transactions vanish, so measure and alert on replication lag.

docs.title: Try it: Tunable quorum in Cassandra's cqlsh (local single-node test cluster)
docs.text:
CREATE KEYSPACE shop WITH replication =
  {'class': 'SimpleStrategy', 'replication_factor': 1};
CONSISTENCY QUORUM;   -- R/W must reach a majority of replicas
CONSISTENCY ONE;      -- fastest, weakest
CONSISTENCY;          -- show current level

docs.title: 7.3 Replication in Practice: Lag, Read-Your-Writes & Real Systems
docs.text:
Real databases replicate by shipping their change log — PostgreSQL's write-ahead log or MySQL's binary log — to replicas, which replay it. Because shipping takes time, replicas are often a little behind: this is replication lag. Apps must cope, for example by reading a user's own recent changes from the primary.

How a stale read happens. The write is committed, but the replica has not replayed it yet when the read arrives.

Think of it like…

Replication lag is like a live TV broadcast with a few seconds' delay: viewers see the same show, just slightly behind the studio.

Real-world example

Priya updates her profile photo on a fictional social app. The write goes to the primary, but the next page load reads from a replica 2 seconds behind, so her old photo appears and she uploads it again. The team fixes it by routing each user's reads to the primary for 5 seconds after they write — a read-your-writes guarantee.

docs.title: How it works
docs.text:
1. The primary writes each change to its log (WAL, binlog, oplog) before committing.
  2. A sender process streams log records to each replica over the network.
  3. The replica writes them to its own log, then a replay process applies them to its data files.
  4. The replica reports positions back (received, flushed, replayed), so lag can be measured.
  5. The application or a proxy decides which reads may go to replicas and which must hit the primary.
  6. Monitoring alerts when lag exceeds a threshold, such as 10 seconds or 100 MB of WAL.

Who uses it

DBAs and SREs monitor lag daily; backend developers must design around it; it is a favourite interview question ('why did my user not see their own update?').

Key takeaway

Know the three lag-related guarantees by name — read-your-writes, monotonic reads and consistent prefix reads — and one technique for each.

Going deeper

  • PostgreSQL's synchronous_commit controls the wait: off, local, remote_write, on (standby flushed WAL) or remote_apply (standby replayed it) — only remote_apply makes a replica read immediately see the commit.
  • Physical (streaming) replication copies WAL byte-for-byte, so replicas are identical and must run the same major version; logical replication, built in since PostgreSQL 10 (2017), ships row changes per table and works across versions.
  • A replication slot makes the primary keep WAL until a consumer has received it; an abandoned slot can fill the disk, which is why PostgreSQL 13 added max_slot_wal_keep_size and PostgreSQL 18 added an idle-slot timeout.
  • MySQL replicates through the binary log; row-based format has been the default since 5.7.7, and GTIDs (5.6+) give every transaction a global ID so a replica can switch sources without file-and-position bookkeeping.
  • Amazon Aurora writes six copies of each log record across three Availability Zones, needing 4 of 6 for writes and 3 of 6 for reads; its replicas share storage, so replica lag is usually tens of milliseconds.
  • Common read-your-writes techniques: read from the primary for N seconds after a write; pass the commit's log position and wait until the replica reaches it; or pin a user's session to one replica.

Common mistakes & misconceptions

  • Long queries on a hot-standby replica can be cancelled by replication conflicts, or (with hot_standby_feedback) cause bloat on the primary — choose consciously.
  • Load balancers that spread reads across replicas randomly break monotonic reads; a user can see a comment appear and then disappear.
  • Forgetting to drop unused replication slots: the primary keeps WAL forever and eventually runs out of disk.

docs.title: Try it: Measure replication lag in PostgreSQL
docs.text:
-- on the primary
SELECT application_name, state, sync_state,
       write_lag, flush_lag, replay_lag
FROM pg_stat_replication;

-- on a replica
SELECT now() - pg_last_xact_replay_timestamp() AS replay_delay;

docs.title: 7.4 Partitioning & Sharding
docs.text:
Partitioning splits one big table into smaller pieces. When those pieces live on different servers it is called sharding, and each server (shard) holds only part of the data. A shard key, such as customer ID, decides where each row goes. Sharding is the main way to scale writes beyond one machine.

A query router in front of shards. The router hashes the shard key and sends each query to the one shard that owns it.

Think of it like…

A phone book split into volumes A-F, G-M and N-Z is range partitioning; giving each volume to a different librarian is sharding.

Real-world example

PlayLoop, a fictional gaming company, stores 6 billion match records. They hash player_id into 256 logical shards spread over 16 PostgreSQL servers. A query for one player touches one server; a 'top scores worldwide' query must ask all 16 and merge the results. When a famous streamer's player row becomes a hot spot, they cache it.

docs.title: How it works
docs.text:
1. Choose a shard key that appears in most queries and spreads load evenly (for example tenant_id or user_id).
  2. Pick a strategy: ranges of key values, a hash of the key, or a lookup directory.
  3. Create many more logical shards than servers so they can be moved later.
  4. Route each query: a proxy or library computes the shard and sends the query there.
  5. Queries without the shard key fan out to all shards (scatter-gather) and merge results.
  6. Rebalance by moving logical shards to new servers as data grows (resharding).

Who uses it

Backend and platform engineers at high-growth SaaS, social, gaming and fintech companies; sharding is a staple of system-design interviews.

Key takeaway

In interviews, say the shard key out loud and justify it: even distribution, present in the hottest queries, and keeps related data (one tenant's rows) together.

Going deeper

  • Hash sharding spreads keys evenly but destroys range scans; range sharding keeps ranges together but timestamps or auto-increment IDs send all new writes to the last shard.
  • Naive hash mod N moves almost every key when N changes; consistent hashing (Karger et al., 1997) moves only about 1/N of keys, and virtual nodes smooth out uneven ranges.
  • Notion split its PostgreSQL database in 2021 into 480 logical shards (schemas) over 32 physical machines, choosing 480 because it divides evenly by many machine counts.
  • DynamoDB splits tables into partitions that each serve up to 3,000 read units and 1,000 write units per second and about 10 GB, so a single hot key cannot exceed those limits.
  • MongoDB shards collections into ranges (default 128 MB since 6.0), moved by a balancer; since version 5.0 reshardCollection can change the shard key online.
  • Vitess, born at YouTube in 2010 and a CNCF graduated project since 2019, routes MySQL queries through VTGate using 'vindexes' and reshards online with VReplication; Slack, GitHub and Shopify have used it.

Common mistakes & misconceptions

  • Choosing a low-cardinality or skewed shard key (country, status): one shard takes most traffic and you cannot split it further.
  • Forgetting cross-shard operations: joins, unique constraints and transactions across shards become slow, distributed or impossible.
  • Creating exactly as many shards as servers: later growth forces rehashing everything instead of simply moving logical shards.

docs.title: Try it: Declarative partitioning in PostgreSQL (single node)
docs.text:
CREATE TABLE events (id bigint, user_id bigint, created date)
  PARTITION BY HASH (user_id);
CREATE TABLE events_p0 PARTITION OF events FOR VALUES WITH (MODULUS 4, REMAINDER 0);
CREATE TABLE events_p1 PARTITION OF events FOR VALUES WITH (MODULUS 4, REMAINDER 1);
CREATE TABLE events_p2 PARTITION OF events FOR VALUES WITH (MODULUS 4, REMAINDER 2);
CREATE TABLE events_p3 PARTITION OF events FOR VALUES WITH (MODULUS 4, REMAINDER 3);
EXPLAIN SELECT * FROM events WHERE user_id = 42;  -- only one partition scanned

docs.title: 7.5 CAP & PACELC, Explained Honestly
docs.text:
The CAP theorem says that when the network splits a distributed database into groups that cannot talk (a partition), each group must choose: refuse some requests to stay consistent, or answer everything and risk returning stale or conflicting data. PACELC adds that even when the network is fine, you trade latency against consistency.

PACELC classifications (Abadi's framing)

PA/EL PC/EC PA/EC During partition Stay available Stay consistent Stay available Normal operation Favour latency Favour consistency Favour consistency Examples Dynamo, Cassandra, Riak Spanner, VoltDB, HBase MongoDB (default config) Good for Carts, feeds, telemetry Money, inventory, IDs General apps

Most systems are tunable, so labels describe defaults, not fixed laws.

Think of it like…

Two bank branches lose their phone line: either they stop allowing withdrawals until it is fixed (consistent) or they keep serving customers and risk the same money being withdrawn twice (available).

Real-world example

Mia's fictional ticketing start-up sells concert seats from two data centres. During a 3-minute fibre cut, a CP design makes the smaller site reject seat purchases, so no seat is sold twice. An AP design keeps selling in both sites and later finds 14 double-booked seats to refund. For a 'likes' counter, the AP choice would be perfectly fine.

docs.title: How it works
docs.text:
1. Assume partitions will happen: cables are cut, switches fail, long garbage-collection pauses look like failures.
  2. During a partition (P), choose availability (A) or consistency (C) for each operation.
  3. Else (E), in normal operation, choose lower latency (L) or stronger consistency (C).
  4. Classify the operation's business need: money and inventory usually need C; feeds and counters tolerate A/L.
  5. Pick a database or setting whose default trade-off matches, or tune per query (quorums, consistency levels).

Who uses it

Architects, backend engineers and anyone in a system-design interview; it frames choices between Spanner, Cassandra, DynamoDB, MongoDB and others.

Key takeaway

Say 'CAP only applies during a partition; PACELC covers the everyday latency-versus-consistency trade-off' — interviewers love that nuance.

Going deeper

  • Eric Brewer presented the CAP conjecture at the PODC 2000 keynote; Seth Gilbert and Nancy Lynch proved a formal version in 2002, defining C as linearizability and A as every non-failing node answering.
  • Brewer's 2012 article 'CAP Twelve Years Later' stressed that 'pick two of three' misleads: partitions are rare, and systems can make fine-grained, per-operation choices and recover afterwards.
  • Daniel Abadi's PACELC (2010 blog, 2012 IEEE Computer paper) points out that the latency-consistency trade-off exists all the time, because waiting for remote replicas costs round trips even without failures.
  • Martin Kleppmann's 2015 critique argues that most real databases are neither CAP-consistent nor CAP-available under the theorem's strict definitions, so labels like 'CP database' oversimplify.
  • Google Spanner is technically CP but advertises 99.999% availability for multi-region instances because Google's private network makes partitions extremely rare — engineering can shrink the cost of choosing C.
  • Fox and Brewer's 1999 'harvest and yield' idea offers a gentler view: under failure, answer with partial data (lower harvest) rather than refuse (lower yield).

Common mistakes & misconceptions

  • Treating 'CA' as an option: in a distributed system you cannot opt out of partitions, so the real choice is what to do when one happens.
  • Confusing CAP's C (linearizability across replicas) with ACID's C (integrity constraints inside a transaction) — they are unrelated ideas.
  • Labelling a whole product AP or CP: settings like Cassandra's QUORUM or MongoDB's read and write concerns change the behaviour per query.

docs.text: Name What it does Example CAP theoremBrewer 2000; Gilbert & Lynch 2002 · Concept · Current · Intermediate · General A distributed system cannot be both linearizable and fully available while a network partition separates its nodes. During a datacentre link failure, a CP store rejects writes in the minority site to avoid divergence. Consistency (CAP sense)Gilbert & Lynch, 2002 · Concept · Current · Intermediate · General Every read returns the most recent completed write, as if there were one copy — formally linearizability. After a seat is booked in London, a read in New York must show it as taken. Availability (CAP sense)Gilbert & Lynch, 2002 · Concept · Current · Intermediate · General Every request to a non-failed node gets a non-error response, even if the data might be stale. A Cassandra node cut off from peers still accepts writes at consistency ONE. Partition toleranceCAP theorem · Concept · Current · Intermediate · General The system keeps operating despite messages between nodes being lost or delayed indefinitely. A switch failure isolates two of five nodes; the remaining three must still behave correctly. Network partitionDistributed systems · Concept · Current · Beginner · General A failure where groups of nodes are up but cannot communicate; includes long pauses that look like failures. A 40-second garbage-collection pause makes a leader appear dead, and a new leader is elected. CP systemse.g. Spanner, etcd, HBase, ZooKeeper · Concept · Current · Intermediate · General Systems that refuse or delay some requests during a partition rather than risk inconsistent answers. etcd's minority side rejects writes during a split, so Kubernetes never sees two conflicting configs. AP systemse.g. Cassandra (at ONE), Riak, CouchDB · Concept · Current · Intermediate · General Systems that keep answering on every side of a partition and reconcile differences afterwards. A shopping-cart service accepts adds in both regions and merges carts once the link returns. PACELCDaniel Abadi, 2010/2012 · Concept · Current · Intermediate · General If Partitioned choose Availability or Consistency; Else choose Latency or Consistency. DynamoDB's default eventually consistent reads are an 'EL' choice: faster and half the read cost. Latency-consistency trade-offPACELC · Concept · Current · Intermediate · General Stronger consistency requires waiting for more replicas, which adds round trips even when nothing has failed. A strongly consistent cross-region write waits about 70 ms for a transatlantic acknowledgement. Split-brainDistributed systems · Concept · Current · Intermediate · General Two parts of a cluster both believe they are in charge and accept conflicting writes. Two MySQL servers both promote themselves after a heartbeat failure and both accept orders. Harvest and yieldFox & Brewer, 1999 · Concept · Current · Advanced · General Yield is the share of requests answered; harvest is the completeness of each answer. Degrade harvest to keep yield. A search engine returns results from 9 of 10 index shards rather than an error page.

docs.title: 7.6 Consistency Models: From Linearizable to Eventual
docs.text:
A consistency model is a promise about what reads can return when data is copied across machines. The strongest promise (linearizability) makes many copies behave like one. Weaker promises, such as causal or eventual consistency, are faster and more available but allow you to see old or out-of-order data for a while.

The consistency ladder (strongest at the top). Moving down trades freshness and ordering for speed and availability.

Think of it like…

Linearizable is a single scoreboard everyone watches; eventual consistency is many scoreboards updated by runners, which will all match once the runners stop running.

Real-world example

On a fictional Q&A site, Omar posts a question and Lena answers it. With only eventual consistency, a reader in another region briefly sees Lena's answer without Omar's question. Causal consistency prevents that: because the answer depends on the question, nobody can see the answer first. Neither needs full linearizability, which would slow every post.

docs.title: How it works
docs.text:
1. Identify which operations users would notice if they were stale or reordered.
  2. Map each need to a model: linearizable (locks, counters, uniqueness), causal (comments, chats), eventual (likes, views).
  3. Add session guarantees where users interact with their own data (read-your-writes, monotonic reads).
  4. Configure the database: quorum levels, read concerns, consistency levels or leader-only reads.
  5. Test under failure with tools like Jepsen-style fault injection, not just in a quiet lab.

Who uses it

Distributed-systems engineers, database developers and backend engineers working with replicated or multi-region data; frequent in senior interviews.

Key takeaway

Memorise the ladder: strict serializable > linearizable > sequential > causal > eventual, plus the four session guarantees from the Bayou paper.

Going deeper

  • Linearizability (Herlihy and Wing, 1990) requires every operation to appear to take effect at one instant between its start and finish; it is what you need for leader election, locks and unique-username checks.
  • Serializability is a transaction (ACID isolation) property, linearizability a single-object recency property; strict serializability combines both and is offered by Spanner, CockroachDB and FoundationDB.
  • The 1994 Bayou paper by Terry and colleagues defined four session guarantees: read-your-writes, monotonic reads, monotonic writes and writes-follow-reads — practical middle ground for user-facing apps.
  • Azure Cosmos DB exposes five named levels — strong, bounded staleness, session (the default), consistent prefix and eventual — making it a handy real-world map of the spectrum.
  • Werner Vogels' 2008 ACM Queue article 'Eventually Consistent' explained Amazon's choice; strong eventual consistency (with CRDTs) adds that replicas receiving the same updates are immediately identical.
  • Jepsen (since 2013) and its Elle checker (2020) have found anomalies in many databases' advertised guarantees, which is why vendors now publish formal models and test suites.

Common mistakes & misconceptions

  • Assuming 'strong consistency' means the same thing everywhere — vendors use it loosely; ask whether they mean linearizable, serializable or just leader reads.
  • Believing eventual consistency means 'consistent within a second': there is no bound unless the system documents bounded staleness.
  • Using read replicas for uniqueness checks ('is this username free?'): a stale replica can approve a duplicate.

docs.title: Try it: Choose consistency per query in MongoDB (mongosh)
docs.text:
db.orders.insertOne({_id: 1, total: 42}, {writeConcern: {w: 'majority'}})
db.orders.find({_id: 1}).readConcern('majority')      // only majority-committed data
db.orders.find({_id: 1}).readConcern('linearizable')  // strongest, slower; single-document reads
