docs.text: Name What it does Example Strict serializabilitySpanner, CockroachDB, FoundationDB · Concept · Current · Advanced · General Transactions behave as if run one at a time, in an order matching real time — the strongest common guarantee. A transfer committed at 10:00:01 is visible to every transaction starting after that, in any region. LinearizabilityHerlihy & Wing, 1990 · Concept · Current · Advanced · General Each operation appears to happen atomically at one moment, so all clients see a single, up-to-date copy. Once etcd returns success for a lock key, no client anywhere can read the old value. Sequential consistencyLeslie Lamport, 1979 · Concept · Current · Advanced · General All clients see operations in the same single order that respects each client's own order, but not necessarily real time. Two users see posts A then B in the same order, even if B was actually written slightly earlier. Causal consistencyAhamad et al., 1995; MongoDB causal sessions · Concept · Current · Advanced · General Operations that depend on each other are seen in cause-before-effect order; unrelated ones may be seen in any order. Nobody sees a reply 'Congrats!' before the 'I got the job' message it answers. Eventual consistencyWerner Vogels, 2008 · Concept · Current · Beginner · General If writes stop, all replicas eventually return the same value; meanwhile reads may be stale. A video's view count differs by a few hundred between regions but converges within seconds. Strong eventual consistencyShapiro et al., 2011 (CRDTs) · Concept · Current · Advanced · General Replicas that have received the same set of updates are identical, with no conflict-resolution step needed. Two offline phones' shopping lists merge into the same list as soon as both sync. Monotonic readsTerry et al. (Bayou), 1994 · Concept · Current · Intermediate · General Once you have seen a value, later reads never show you an older one. Pinning a user to one replica stops their new message vanishing on refresh. Monotonic writesTerry et al. (Bayou), 1994 · Concept · Current · Advanced · General A client's writes are applied everywhere in the order the client issued them. 'Create album' always replicates before 'add photo to album' from the same user. Consistent prefix readsBayou; Azure Cosmos DB · Concept · Current · Intermediate · General Readers see writes in an order without gaps: some prefix of the history, never later writes without earlier ones. A chat never shows message 5 before message 4, even if both arrive late. Bounded stalenessAzure Cosmos DB, Spanner stale reads · Concept · Current · Intermediate · General Reads may lag, but by no more than a set time or number of versions. A dashboard accepts data at most 10 seconds old, letting Spanner serve it from a nearby replica. Cosmos DB consistency levelsMicrosoft Azure · Feature · Current · Intermediate · Multi-model Five selectable levels: strong, bounded staleness, session, consistent prefix and eventual, with session as default. A retailer uses session consistency for carts and strong consistency for its single-region inventory account. MongoDB read and write concernsMongoDB Inc. · Feature · Current · Intermediate · Document Per-operation settings (w: majority, readConcern majority/linearizable/snapshot) controlling durability and visibility. Payments use w: 'majority' so an acknowledged write survives the primary failing. ElleKingsbury & Alvaro, VLDB 2020 · Tool · Current · Advanced · General A checker that infers transaction dependency graphs from test histories to detect isolation anomalies efficiently. Elle reports a G2 anti-dependency cycle, proving a database's 'serializable' mode allowed write skew.

docs.title: 7.7 Consensus: Paxos, Raft & Where Databases Use Them
docs.text:
Consensus algorithms let a group of machines agree on one value — such as who the leader is or the next entry in a log — even if some machines crash or messages are lost. As long as a majority is alive and connected, they keep working. Paxos was the first practical one; Raft was designed to be easier to understand.

Raft commits one log entry. The entry is committed once a majority (2 of 3) has it — the slow follower does not block the write.

Think of it like…

A jury of five must agree on a verdict; as long as three jurors are present and talking, a decision can be made and recorded, and two absent jurors cannot overturn it later.

Real-world example

A fictional logistics firm runs a 3-node CockroachDB cluster. Each data range has a Raft group with a leaseholder. When the server holding the leader for the 'shipments' range loses power, the remaining two nodes elect a new leader within seconds; no committed shipment is lost because every commit had already reached two of three nodes.

docs.title: How it works
docs.text:
1. Nodes start as followers; if one hears no heartbeat before its election timeout, it becomes a candidate.
  2. The candidate increments its term and asks for votes; a majority makes it leader for that term.
  3. Clients send writes to the leader, which appends them to its log and sends AppendEntries to followers.
  4. When a majority has stored an entry, the leader marks it committed and applies it.
  5. Followers apply committed entries in the same order, so every node's state machine ends up identical.
  6. If the leader fails, a new election starts; only candidates with up-to-date logs can win.

Who uses it

Database engineers, Kubernetes and platform operators (etcd), and anyone running distributed SQL, Kafka or ZooKeeper; Raft is a common senior interview topic.

Key takeaway

Remember the sizing rule: 2f + 1 nodes tolerate f crash failures — 3 nodes survive 1 failure, 5 survive 2 — and even numbers add cost without extra tolerance.

Going deeper

  • The FLP result (Fischer, Lynch and Paterson, 1985) proves no deterministic algorithm can guarantee consensus in a fully asynchronous network with even one crash, so real algorithms use timeouts to make progress.
  • Leslie Lamport's Paxos ('The Part-Time Parliament', published 1998; 'Paxos Made Simple', 2001) uses prepare/promise and accept/accepted phases; Multi-Paxos keeps a stable leader to skip the first phase.
  • Raft (Ongaro and Ousterhout, USENIX ATC 2014) splits consensus into leader election, log replication and safety; its paper suggests randomised election timeouts of 150-300 ms to avoid split votes.
  • Databases rarely run one giant Raft group: CockroachDB, TiKV and YugabyteDB run a separate group per range or tablet (thousands per cluster) so leadership and load spread across nodes.
  • Apache Kafka 4.0 (March 2025) removed ZooKeeper entirely; its metadata now lives in KRaft, a Raft-based quorum of controller nodes. ZooKeeper itself uses the ZAB protocol.
  • These algorithms tolerate crashes, not lies. Byzantine fault tolerance (PBFT, Castro and Liskov 1999) needs 3f + 1 nodes and is used in blockchains rather than ordinary databases.

Common mistakes & misconceptions

  • Running a two-node 'cluster': losing either node loses the majority, so availability is worse than one node. Use 3 or 5.
  • Spreading a 3-node Raft group across only two data centres: losing the site with two nodes stops all writes.
  • Trusting a lease or lock without fencing tokens: a paused old leader can wake up and write after a new leader exists.

docs.title: Try it: Run a single etcd node with Docker and inspect its Raft status
docs.text:
docker run -d --name etcd -p 2379:2379 quay.io/coreos/etcd:v3.5.17 \
  etcd --listen-client-urls http://0.0.0.0:2379 --advertise-client-urls http://localhost:2379
docker exec etcd etcdctl put /config/leader-demo hello
docker exec etcd etcdctl get /config/leader-demo
docker exec etcd etcdctl endpoint status -w table   # shows RAFT TERM and RAFT INDEX

docs.title: Key databases, concepts, languages, tools & standards
docs.text: Name What it does Example ConsensusDistributed systems theory · Concept · Current · Intermediate · General Getting several machines to agree irrevocably on a value or sequence of values despite failures. Five nodes agree that node 3 is the new leader, and no two nodes ever believe different leaders in the same term. FLP impossibilityFischer, Lynch & Paterson, 1985 · Concept · Current · Advanced · General Proof that no deterministic algorithm can always reach consensus in a purely asynchronous system with one faulty process. Raft works around FLP by using timeouts, accepting that elections may occasionally take several rounds. PaxosLeslie Lamport (1989 draft, 1998 paper) · Algorithm · Current · Advanced · General The classic consensus algorithm: proposers get promises then acceptances from a majority of acceptors. Google's Chubby lock service and Spanner's replication groups are built on Paxos variants. Multi-PaxosPaxos family · Algorithm · Current · Advanced · General Runs Paxos for a whole log with a stable leader, so each new entry needs only one round trip. Spanner keeps one long-lived Paxos leader per split, making normal writes a single majority round. RaftDiego Ongaro & John Ousterhout, 2014 · Algorithm · Current · Intermediate · General A consensus algorithm designed for understandability: strong leader, terms, elections and replicated logs. etcd, Consul, CockroachDB, TiKV and Redpanda all replicate their state with Raft. Leader electionRaft, Paxos, ZAB · Concept · Current · Intermediate · General Choosing one node to coordinate writes; a new election starts when the leader stops sending heartbeats. A follower hears nothing for 250 ms, becomes a candidate in term 8 and wins three of five votes. Replicated logState machine replication · Data structure · Current · Intermediate · General An ordered list of commands copied to every node; applying it in order makes all nodes' states identical. Every node applies 'debit 50' then 'credit 50' in the same order, so all balances match. Term / epochRaft (term), ZAB (epoch), Paxos (ballot) · Concept · Current · Advanced · General A monotonically increasing number identifying each leadership period, used to reject messages from stale leaders. A returning old leader with term 6 is ignored because followers have already accepted term 7. Majority quorumConsensus algorithms · Concept · Current · Beginner · General More than half of the voting members; any two majorities overlap, which prevents conflicting decisions. In a 5-node cluster, 3 is a majority, so the cluster tolerates 2 failed nodes. Apache ZooKeeper & ZABApache Software Foundation (from Yahoo!) · Tool · Legacy · Intermediate · Key-value A coordination service using the ZAB atomic broadcast protocol, long used by Hadoop, HBase and older Kafka. An HBase cluster stores which RegionServer owns each region in ZooKeeper. etcdCNCF graduated (originally CoreOS) · Database · Current · Intermediate · Key-value A Raft-based, strongly consistent key-value store; Kubernetes keeps all cluster state in it. A Kubernetes control plane runs a 3-member etcd cluster, surviving one member failure. KRaftApache Kafka (KIP-500; only mode since Kafka 4.0) · Protocol · Current · Intermediate · General Kafka's built-in Raft-based metadata quorum that replaced ZooKeeper for storing cluster metadata. A Kafka 4.x cluster runs three controller nodes in KRaft mode and no ZooKeeper at all. Raft groups per rangeCockroachDB, TiKV, YugabyteDB · Pattern · Current · Advanced · Relational Splitting data into many ranges, each with its own Raft group, so leaders and load spread across the cluster. A 9-node CockroachDB cluster holds 40,000 ranges, each replicated three ways with its own leader. Fencing tokenKleppmann, 'How to do distributed locking', 2016 · Pattern · Current · Advanced · General A number that increases with each lock grant; storage rejects writes carrying an older token. A paused worker wakes with token 33, but storage already accepted token 34 and rejects it. Byzantine fault toleranceLamport et al. 1982; PBFT 1999 · Concept · Current · Advanced · General Consensus that tolerates nodes that lie or misbehave, needing 3f + 1 nodes to tolerate f bad ones. A permissioned ledger uses BFT consensus because participating banks do not fully trust each other.

docs.title: 7.8 Distributed Transactions: 2PC, Percolator, TrueTime, Sagas & the Outbox
docs.text:
A distributed transaction changes data on several machines or services and must succeed or fail as a whole. Inside one distributed database this is done with protocols like two-phase commit plus clever timestamps. Across separate microservices, teams usually use sagas: a sequence of local steps with 'undo' actions if a later step fails.

Two-phase commit. Between 'YES' and the final decision, participants hold locks and cannot decide alone.

Think of it like…

Two-phase commit is a wedding: the officiant asks each person 'do you?', and only if both say yes is the marriage declared; a saga is booking a trip step by step and cancelling the hotel if the flight falls through.

Real-world example

TripNest, a fictional travel site, books a flight, hotel and car through three services. A single 2PC across all three would lock rooms while waiting on a slow airline. Instead, an orchestrated saga books each in turn; when the car rental fails, it runs compensations: cancel hotel, refund flight. An outbox table ensures every 'booking created' event is published exactly when the booking commits.

docs.title: How it works
docs.text:
1. Phase 1 (prepare): the coordinator asks every participant to prepare; each writes its changes durably and votes yes or no.
  2. Phase 2 (commit): if all voted yes, the coordinator logs 'commit' and tells everyone to commit; otherwise it aborts.
  3. Distributed SQL databases add a timestamp scheme (TrueTime, hybrid logical clocks or a timestamp oracle) to order transactions.
  4. Across microservices, a saga runs local transactions in sequence, each with a compensating action.
  5. The outbox pattern writes the business row and the event row in one local transaction; a relay publishes the event.
  6. Consumers deduplicate with idempotency keys because events may be delivered more than once.

Who uses it

Backend and microservice architects, distributed-database engineers and payment engineers; sagas and the outbox pattern are favourite system-design interview answers.

Key takeaway

Know why 2PC 'blocks': a participant that voted yes cannot decide on its own if the coordinator disappears, so it holds locks until the coordinator returns.

Going deeper

  • Jim Gray described two-phase commit in 1978; the X/Open XA standard (1991) lets a transaction manager such as a Java JTA server coordinate several databases and message brokers.
  • Google's Percolator (OSDI 2010) added snapshot-isolated transactions on Bigtable using a timestamp oracle and a 'primary lock' per transaction; TiDB's storage layer TiKV uses the same model with its Placement Driver as the oracle.
  • Spanner's TrueTime API returns an interval [earliest, latest] using GPS and atomic clocks; a committing transaction waits out the uncertainty (commit wait, historically a few milliseconds) so timestamps match real time.
  • Without atomic clocks, CockroachDB and YugabyteDB use hybrid logical clocks (Kulkarni et al., 2014) with a maximum clock-offset setting; reads hitting the uncertainty window may restart.
  • Sagas come from Garcia-Molina and Salem (1987). Orchestrated sagas use a coordinator such as Temporal or AWS Step Functions; choreographed sagas react to each other's events.
  • The transactional outbox avoids the 'dual write' bug (database commits but message publish fails); Debezium's outbox event router can stream the outbox table into Kafka via change data capture.

Common mistakes & misconceptions

  • Writing to the database and then calling Kafka or an API in application code (dual write): a crash between the two leaves them inconsistent — use an outbox.
  • Forgetting that saga compensations are not rollbacks: other users may already have seen the intermediate state, so design semantic undo actions.
  • Leaving prepared transactions orphaned in PostgreSQL: they hold locks and block VACUUM until committed or rolled back.

docs.title: Try it: Two-phase commit by hand in PostgreSQL (set max_prepared_transactions = 10 and restart first)
docs.text:
BEGIN;
UPDATE accounts SET balance = balance - 50 WHERE id = 1;
PREPARE TRANSACTION 'transfer-778';   -- phase 1: durable, survives a crash

SELECT gid, prepared FROM pg_prepared_xacts;
COMMIT PREPARED 'transfer-778';       -- phase 2 (or ROLLBACK PREPARED)

docs.title: Key databases, concepts, languages, tools & standards
docs.text: Name What it does Example Distributed transactionGeneral · Concept · Current · Intermediate · General A transaction whose changes span several nodes or systems but must commit or abort atomically. Moving money between accounts stored on two different shards must debit and credit together. Two-phase commit (2PC)Jim Gray, 1978 · Protocol · Current · Intermediate · General A coordinator asks all participants to prepare, then commits only if every one voted yes. CockroachDB commits a transaction touching three ranges using a 2PC-style protocol with a transaction record. Blocking problem of 2PCDistributed systems theory · Concept · Current · Advanced · General Prepared participants cannot safely decide alone if the coordinator fails, so they wait while holding locks. A coordinator crashes after PREPARE; inventory rows stay locked until it restarts 20 minutes later. XA transactionsX/Open XA (1991); JTA · Standard · Legacy · Advanced · Relational Standard interface letting a transaction manager run 2PC across different databases and queues. A Java EE app server commits a message dequeue and an Oracle update in one XA transaction. PREPARE TRANSACTIONPostgreSQL · Command · Current · Advanced · Relational PostgreSQL command that durably prepares a transaction for later COMMIT PREPARED or ROLLBACK PREPARED. An external coordinator issues PREPARE TRANSACTION 'tx42' on two servers, then commits both. Textbooks teach 3PC to show why non-blocking commit is hard; production systems rarely use it. PercolatorGoogle, OSDI 2010 · Algorithm · Current · Advanced · Key-value Snapshot-isolation transactions on a key-value store using a timestamp oracle and primary/secondary locks. TiDB writes a primary lock on one key, secondary locks on others, then commits the primary first. Spanner TrueTimeGoogle · Feature · Current · Advanced · Relational Clock API returning a bounded time interval from GPS and atomic clocks, enabling globally ordered commits. TT.now() returns [10:00:00.000, 10:00:00.004]; Spanner waits until 'earliest' passes the commit timestamp. Commit waitGoogle Spanner · Concept · Current · Advanced · Relational Delaying a commit's acknowledgement until clock uncertainty has passed, guaranteeing external consistency. A Spanner write waits a few extra milliseconds so later transactions anywhere get larger timestamps. An e-commerce saga: reserve stock, charge card, create shipment; if shipping fails, refund and release stock. Orchestration vs choreographyMicroservices practice · Concept · Current · Intermediate · General Orchestration uses a central coordinator; choreography lets services react to each other's events. TripNest uses Temporal to orchestrate bookings, while its notification services simply react to events. A shipping service stores each OrderPlaced event ID in an inbox table and ignores the duplicate delivery. A sequencer batches transactions every 10 ms; all partitions run the batch in the same order.

docs.title: 7.9 Caching Strategies: Cache-Aside, Write-Through, TTLs & Invalidation
docs.text:
A cache keeps copies of frequently read data in fast memory so the database is asked less often. The hard parts are deciding when to fill the cache, how long entries live (TTL), and how to remove or update entries when the real data changes (invalidation).

Cache-aside read and invalidation. The application, not the cache, talks to the database and keeps the two in step.

Think of it like…

A cache is the sticky note on your monitor with the Wi-Fi password: much faster than finding the router manual, but useless if someone changed the password and nobody updated the note.

Real-world example

Ravi's fictional recipe site gets 5,000 page views per second, mostly for 200 popular recipes. With cache-aside in Valkey and a 10-minute TTL, 97% of reads never reach PostgreSQL. When an editor fixes a recipe, the app deletes that key so the next reader reloads it. On a TV mention, request coalescing stops 3,000 simultaneous misses hammering the database.

docs.title: How it works
docs.text:
1. The app asks the cache for a key such as recipe:812.
  2. Hit: return the cached value in well under a millisecond.
  3. Miss: read from the database, store the result in the cache with a TTL, then return it.
  4. On update: write the database, then delete (or update) the cache key.
  5. Protect hot keys from stampedes with locks, request coalescing or early refresh.
  6. Watch hit ratio, memory use and evictions to size the cache.

Who uses it

Backend engineers, SREs and performance engineers; caching questions appear in almost every system-design interview.

Key takeaway

Prefer deleting a cache key after a database write over updating it — it avoids races where an older value overwrites a newer one.

Going deeper

  • Facebook's 2013 NSDI paper 'Scaling Memcache at Facebook' described leases to stop stale sets and thundering herds, and serving billions of requests per second from memcached clusters in front of MySQL.
  • Probabilistic early expiration (Vattani et al., VLDB 2015, 'XFetch') lets a random request refresh a hot key slightly before its TTL ends, avoiding a synchronised stampede at expiry.
  • Redis and Valkey default to maxmemory-policy noeviction; caches usually set allkeys-lru or allkeys-lfu, which use sampled approximations (maxmemory-samples, default 5) rather than exact LRU lists.
  • HTTP caching is standardised in RFC 9111 (2022); Cache-Control: max-age, s-maxage and stale-while-revalidate (RFC 5861) let CDNs serve slightly old content while fetching a fresh copy.
  • MySQL removed its built-in query cache in 8.0 because global invalidation on every write caused contention; modern designs cache at the application, proxy (for example ReadySet) or CDN layer instead.
  • Hit ratio drives payoff: at 99% hits, the database sees 1 in 100 reads; dropping to 90% multiplies database load tenfold, which is why cold caches after restarts can cause outages.

Common mistakes & misconceptions

  • Caching without a TTL or invalidation plan: users see stale prices or permissions indefinitely.
  • Restarting or flushing a large cache at peak time: the cold cache sends every request to the database at once.
  • Caching personalised or permission-filtered data under a shared key, leaking one user's data to another.

docs.text:

docs.text: Name What it does Example Cache-aside (lazy loading)Common practice · Pattern · Current · Beginner · Key-value The application checks the cache, loads from the database on a miss and stores the result itself. A product page reads product:55 from Valkey; on a miss it queries PostgreSQL and caches for 5 minutes. Read-through cacheCache libraries, DAX · Pattern · Current · Intermediate · Key-value The cache itself loads missing data from the database, so the app only ever talks to the cache. A Java app uses a Caffeine LoadingCache whose loader function queries the database on misses. Write-through cacheCommon practice; DAX · Pattern · Current · Intermediate · Key-value Every write goes to the cache and the database synchronously, keeping the cache fresh at the cost of write latency. Amazon DAX updates its item cache as writes pass through to DynamoDB. Write-behind (write-back)Common practice · Pattern · Current · Advanced · Key-value Writes go to the cache first and are flushed to the database later in batches; fast but risks loss. A game server buffers score updates in memory and writes them to the database every 5 seconds. Write-aroundCommon practice · Pattern · Current · Intermediate · Key-value Writes skip the cache and go straight to the database; the cache fills only on later reads. Bulk-imported archive records bypass the cache so they do not evict popular items. Refresh-aheadCommon practice · Pattern · Current · Advanced · Key-value Hot entries are reloaded shortly before they expire so readers rarely see a miss. Exchange-rate keys with a 60-second TTL are refreshed in the background at 50 seconds. TTL (time to live)Caches, DNS, CDNs · Concept · Current · Beginner · General How long a cached entry is valid before it expires and must be reloaded. Session tokens use a 30-minute TTL; static logos use a one-year TTL with versioned filenames. Cache invalidation strategiesGeneral · Concept · Current · Intermediate · General Ways to keep caches correct: delete-on-write, TTL expiry, event-driven purges from CDC, and versioned keys. Bumping a key prefix from v41 to v42 instantly retires every cached price after a bulk update. Cache stampede (thundering herd)General · Concept · Current · Intermediate · General Many requests miss the same expired key at once and all hit the database together. A homepage key expires at 9:00 and 4,000 requests run the same 200 ms query simultaneously. Request coalescingGo singleflight, CDN collapsed forwarding · Pattern · Current · Advanced · General Only one request recomputes a missing key while others wait for and share its result. With singleflight, 4,000 concurrent misses produce exactly one database query. Cache hit ratioGeneral · Metric · Current · Beginner · General The share of reads served from the cache; the key number for judging a cache's value. Hits rise from 82% to 98% after increasing cache memory from 4 GB to 16 GB. Eviction policies (LRU, LFU)Redis/Valkey maxmemory-policy, Memcached · Algorithm · Current · Intermediate · Key-value Rules for which entries to drop when memory is full: least recently used, least frequently used, or by TTL. Switching to allkeys-lfu keeps steady favourites cached even after a one-off crawler touches many keys. Redis / Valkey as a cacheRedis Ltd.; Valkey (Linux Foundation) · Database · Current · Beginner · Key-value In-memory key-value stores with TTLs, rich data types and sub-millisecond reads, the default choice for app caching. An API caches user profiles in a three-node Valkey cluster with replicas for failover. MemcachedBrad Fitzpatrick, 2003 (LiveJournal) · Database · Current · Intermediate · Key-value A simple, multithreaded in-memory key-value cache with no persistence; items up to 1 MB by default. A forum caches rendered thread pages in a 64 GB Memcached pool spread by consistent hashing. Amazon DynamoDB Accelerator (DAX)Amazon Web Services · Service · Current · Intermediate · Key-value A managed write-through cache for DynamoDB delivering microsecond reads with the same API. A bidding platform adds DAX so repeated item lookups drop from milliseconds to microseconds. CDN & HTTP cachingRFC 9111; Cloudflare, Fastly, CloudFront, Akamai · Concept · Current · Beginner · General Edge servers worldwide cache responses using Cache-Control headers, removing traffic before it reaches the database. Product images and public API responses with max-age=300 are served from 300+ edge locations.

docs.title: 7.10 Connection Pooling: PgBouncer, ProxySQL & RDS Proxy
docs.text:
Opening a database connection is slow and each open connection uses server memory. A connection pool keeps a small set of connections open and lends them to requests. Poolers can live inside the app (a library) or as a separate proxy that many app servers share.

Many clients, few server connections. Thousands of client connections are multiplexed onto a pool sized for the database's CPUs.

Think of it like…

A pool is like a taxi rank: instead of building a new taxi for every passenger, a few taxis wait, take one passenger each and come back for the next.

Real-world example

Sunita's fictional delivery app runs 300 serverless functions, each opening its own PostgreSQL connection. At lunchtime the database hits max_connections = 100 and errors flood in. Adding PgBouncer in transaction mode lets 3,000 client connections share 40 server connections; CPU drops and errors vanish.

docs.title: How it works
docs.text:
1. The pooler opens a fixed number of real connections to the database.
  2. Clients connect to the pooler instead of the database (often on port 6432 for PgBouncer).
  3. When a client starts a transaction, the pooler assigns it a free server connection.
  4. In transaction mode, the connection returns to the pool as soon as the transaction ends.
  5. If all connections are busy, new requests wait in a queue rather than overloading the database.
  6. Monitor pool usage, wait times and errors; size the pool to the database's cores, not the number of clients.

Who uses it

Backend developers, platform engineers and DBAs, especially with PostgreSQL, serverless functions and Kubernetes autoscaling.

Key takeaway

A smaller pool is often faster: HikariCP's guide suggests starting near (CPU cores × 2) + effective disks, then measuring.

Going deeper

  • PostgreSQL forks one operating-system process per connection, each using several megabytes plus per-query work_mem; the default max_connections is 100, and thousands of idle connections waste memory and slow snapshots.
  • PgBouncer offers session, transaction and statement pooling; transaction mode gives the biggest win but breaks session state such as SET, advisory locks and LISTEN unless the app avoids them.
  • PgBouncer 1.21 (2023) added protocol-level prepared statement support in transaction mode via max_prepared_statements, removing a long-standing reason teams avoided transaction pooling with ORMs.
  • ProxySQL, a C++ proxy for MySQL, adds query rules, read/write splitting, query caching and failover awareness; recent 3.x releases also began adding PostgreSQL support.
  • Amazon RDS Proxy (GA 2020) pools connections for RDS and Aurora, integrates with IAM and Secrets Manager, and is aimed at serverless functions that would otherwise create connection storms.
  • Other poolers include PgCat (Rust, with sharding and load balancing), Supavisor (Elixir, built by Supabase for millions of connections), Odyssey (Yandex) and PgDog; Cloudflare Hyperdrive pools for edge Workers.

Common mistakes & misconceptions

  • Setting the pool size equal to the number of app threads or users: it overloads the database; size by database cores and measure.
  • Using session-level features (SET search_path, temp tables, advisory locks) behind a transaction-mode pooler — state leaks between clients.
  • Stacking pools without thinking: 50 pods × a 20-connection app pool = 1,000 connections, even if a central pooler exists.

docs.title: Try it: Minimal pgbouncer.ini for transaction pooling
docs.text:
[databases]
shop = host=127.0.0.1 port=5432 dbname=shop

[pgbouncer]
listen_port = 6432
auth_type = scram-sha-256
auth_file = /etc/pgbouncer/userlist.txt
pool_mode = transaction
max_client_conn = 2000
default_pool_size = 40
max_prepared_statements = 100   ; PgBouncer 1.21+

# then: psql -p 6432 -d pgbouncer -c 'SHOW POOLS;'

docs.title: 7.11 High Availability & Failover: Patroni, Orchestrator, Always On
docs.text:
High availability (HA) means the database keeps working when a server fails. A standby copy is kept in sync, and when the primary dies, a tool detects it and promotes the standby — a failover. Good HA needs reliable failure detection, a way to stop the old primary (fencing), and a way for apps to find the new one.

Allowed downtime per year by availability target. Each extra nine cuts allowed downtime tenfold — and usually multiplies cost.

Think of it like…

HA is a co-pilot ready to take the controls: they follow every move, and if the pilot faints the co-pilot takes over and tells air traffic control.

Real-world example

Kestrel Bank runs PostgreSQL with Patroni on three servers in three zones, using etcd to agree on the leader. At 02:14 the primary's disk controller fails. Patroni's leader key expires after 30 seconds, the most up-to-date replica is promoted, and HAProxy routes connections to it. Customers see about 40 seconds of errors and no lost payments.

docs.title: How it works
docs.text:
1. Run at least one standby, ideally in another availability zone, receiving changes continuously.
  2. Monitor the primary with health checks and a distributed lock or consensus store.
  3. On failure, pick the most up-to-date healthy standby and promote it.
  4. Fence the old primary (shut it down, revoke its lease or block its traffic) to prevent split-brain.
  5. Redirect clients via a virtual IP, DNS change, proxy or smart driver.
  6. Rebuild the failed node as a new standby and rehearse the whole process regularly.

Who uses it

DBAs, SREs and platform engineers own HA; architects set availability targets (SLAs/SLOs) with the business.

Key takeaway

Know the nines: 99.9% allows about 8.8 hours of downtime a year, 99.99% about 53 minutes, and 99.999% about 5 minutes.

Going deeper

  • Patroni (Zalando, Python) stores a leader key with a TTL (default 30 s) in etcd, Consul, ZooKeeper or the Kubernetes API; the primary renews it every loop_wait (10 s), and a replica takes over if it expires.
  • On Kubernetes, operators such as CloudNativePG, Crunchy PGO and Zalando's postgres-operator automate PostgreSQL failover, backups and rolling upgrades using native Kubernetes resources.
  • SQL Server Always On availability groups (since 2012) replicate databases to secondary replicas in synchronous or asynchronous commit mode; a Windows Server Failover Cluster or Pacemaker on Linux decides failover.
  • Amazon RDS Multi-AZ instance failover typically takes 60-120 seconds, while Multi-AZ DB clusters with two readable standbys typically fail over in under 35 seconds, according to AWS documentation.
  • MongoDB replica sets elect a new primary automatically; with default settings the median election should not exceed about 12 seconds, and retryable writes let drivers resend interrupted writes.
  • Failover time = detection + promotion + client redirection. DNS-based redirection is limited by TTLs and client caching, so proxies or topology-aware drivers usually recover faster.

Common mistakes & misconceptions

  • Never testing failover: untested automation fails at 3 a.m. Schedule regular switchovers and game days.
  • Failing over with asynchronous replicas without checking lag: the promoted node may silently miss recent commits.
  • Missing fencing: the old primary comes back and accepts writes, causing split-brain and divergent data.

docs.title: Try it: Check and rehearse a Patroni cluster
docs.text:
patronictl -c /etc/patroni.yml list            # members, roles, lag, timeline
patronictl -c /etc/patroni.yml switchover --leader pg1 --candidate pg2   # planned, safe
# SQL Server: SELECT replica_server_name, role_desc, synchronization_health_desc
#             FROM sys.dm_hadr_availability_replica_states s
#             JOIN sys.availability_replicas r ON s.replica_id = r.replica_id;

Raising the timeout from 5 to 30 seconds stops network blips triggering needless promotions.

docs.title: 7.12 Backups, Point-in-Time Recovery & Disaster Recovery
docs.text:
Backups protect against what replication cannot: mistakes, bugs, ransomware and disasters. A full backup plus the stream of changes since (the transaction log) lets you restore the database to any moment — point-in-time recovery. Disaster recovery plans say how much data you may lose (RPO) and how quickly you must be back (RTO).

Point-in-time recovery. Base backup + archived WAL lets you stop replay one second before the mistake.

Think of it like…

A full backup is a photo of your room each Sunday; the transaction log is a video of every change since — together you can rebuild the room exactly as it was at 3:42 p.m. on Wednesday.

Real-world example

At 14:05 on a Wednesday, an engineer at a fictional charity runs DELETE FROM donors without a WHERE clause. Replicas delete the rows within milliseconds. The DBA restores Sunday's pgBackRest backup to a new server, replays archived WAL up to 14:04:59, and copies the donors table back. Total loss: zero rows; total time: 50 minutes.

docs.title: How it works
docs.text:
1. Decide RPO and RTO with the business for each database.
  2. Take regular full (and optionally incremental) physical backups.
  3. Archive the transaction log (WAL, binlog, redo) continuously to separate, durable storage.
  4. Keep copies off-site and immutable, following the 3-2-1 rule.
  5. To recover, restore the base backup and replay logs to the chosen time or transaction.
  6. Test restores regularly and time them — an untested backup is only a hope.

Who uses it

DBAs, SREs, cloud and infrastructure engineers, and security teams planning ransomware resilience; auditors ask for restore-test evidence.

Key takeaway

RPO = how much data you can lose (look backwards); RTO = how long you can be down (look forwards). Interviewers often check you do not swap them.

Going deeper

  • PostgreSQL 17 added native incremental backups: pg_basebackup --incremental uses WAL summaries (summarize_wal = on), and pg_combinebackup merges a full backup with incrementals into a restorable data directory.
  • Logical backups (pg_dump, mysqldump, mongodump) are portable across versions but slow to restore at terabyte scale; physical backups (pg_basebackup, Percona XtraBackup, Oracle RMAN) copy data files and restore far faster.
  • SQL Server's full recovery model supports full, differential and transaction-log backups for point-in-time restore; the simple model truncates the log and cannot restore between full or differential backups.
  • Amazon RDS automated backups can be retained for up to 35 days and typically allow restores to within the last five minutes; manual snapshots persist until deleted.
  • On 31 January 2017 GitLab accidentally deleted about 300 GB of production PostgreSQL data and lost around six hours of changes, partly because several backup methods were silently failing — a famous lesson in restore testing.
  • AWS's disaster-recovery guidance names four strategies in rising cost and falling RTO/RPO: backup and restore, pilot light, warm standby, and multi-site active/active.

Common mistakes & misconceptions

  • Treating replicas or RAID as backups: they faithfully copy deletions, corruption and ransomware encryption.
  • Storing backups with the same credentials and account as production — attackers who own production delete the backups too. Use immutable, separate storage.
  • Never measuring restore time: a 10 TB logical dump may take days to reload, blowing the RTO.

docs.title: Try it: Logical backup and restore, plus a PITR target (PostgreSQL)
docs.text:
pg_dump -Fc -d shop -f shop.dump          # logical, compressed custom format
createdb shop_restore
pg_restore -d shop_restore -j 4 shop.dump  # parallel restore

# PITR (postgresql.conf on the restored server, plus an empty recovery.signal file)
# restore_command = 'cp /archive/%f %p'
# recovery_target_time = '2026-10-07 14:04:59+00'

docs.title: 7.13 Change Data Capture, Event Streaming, Event Sourcing & CQRS
docs.text:
Change data capture (CDC) watches a database's transaction log and turns every insert, update and delete into an event that other systems can consume. Event streaming platforms like Kafka store and deliver those events. Event sourcing goes further: the list of events is the source of truth, and CQRS keeps separate models for writing and reading.

Log-based CDC pipeline. One change in PostgreSQL fans out to many systems without touching application code.

Think of it like…

CDC is a court stenographer recording every change as it happens; event sourcing is keeping only the stenographer's transcript and replaying it whenever you need to know the current state.

Real-world example

ShopNest needs its search index, cache and warehouse to reflect product changes within seconds. Debezium reads PostgreSQL's WAL through a replication slot and publishes each change to a Kafka topic. Three consumers update OpenSearch, delete stale cache keys and load the data warehouse — with no extra code in the main application.

docs.title: How it works
docs.text:
1. Enable logical change output in the database (for example wal_level = logical or row-based binlog).
  2. A CDC connector such as Debezium reads the log from a saved position and converts changes into events.
  3. Events are written to topics in Kafka or a compatible platform, keyed by primary key to preserve order.
  4. Consumers update search indexes, caches, warehouses or other services at their own pace.
  5. Schemas are tracked in a schema registry so producers and consumers can evolve safely.
  6. With event sourcing, services rebuild state by replaying events; CQRS read models are projections of them.

Who uses it

Data engineers, platform and integration engineers, and microservice architects; Kafka skills are in high demand across finance, retail and tech.

Key takeaway

Remember: CDC derives events from database changes; event sourcing stores events as the primary data — related, but not the same.

Going deeper

  • Log-based CDC is preferred over triggers or polling because it captures deletes, adds almost no load and preserves commit order; sources include PostgreSQL logical decoding, MySQL row binlogs, SQL Server CDC and MongoDB change streams.
  • Apache Kafka (LinkedIn, open-sourced 2011) stores events in partitioned, replicated logs; Kafka 4.0 (2025) runs only in KRaft mode, and Kafka 4.2 (2026) made share groups — queue-style consumption — production-ready.
  • Exactly-once processing in Kafka, added in version 0.11 (2017), combines idempotent producers and transactions; end-to-end exactly-once still requires idempotent or transactional sinks.
  • Log compaction keeps at least the latest record for each key, so a compacted topic can act as a changelog from which consumers rebuild current state.
  • The streaming market consolidated: Confluent bought WarpStream in 2024, and IBM completed its roughly $11 billion acquisition of Confluent in March 2026; Redpanda offers a Kafka-API-compatible C++ alternative.
  • Event sourcing (popularised by Martin Fowler's 2005 article) needs snapshots for long streams and 'upcasting' to read old event versions; CQRS, named by Greg Young around 2010, extends Bertrand Meyer's command-query separation.

Common mistakes & misconceptions

  • Leaving a CDC replication slot active while the connector is down: the database keeps all WAL and can fill its disk.
  • Assuming exactly-once delivery everywhere: most pipelines are at-least-once, so consumers must be idempotent.
  • Adopting event sourcing for simple CRUD apps: it adds versioning, replay and projection complexity that pays off only for audit-heavy domains.

docs.title: Try it: See raw CDC with PostgreSQL logical decoding (requires wal_level = logical)
docs.text:
SELECT pg_create_logical_replication_slot('demo_slot', 'test_decoding');
CREATE TABLE items (id int PRIMARY KEY, name text);
INSERT INTO items VALUES (1, 'kettle');
UPDATE items SET name = 'steel kettle' WHERE id = 1;
SELECT lsn, data FROM pg_logical_slot_get_changes('demo_slot', NULL, NULL);
SELECT pg_drop_replication_slot('demo_slot');   -- always clean up slots!

docs.title: 7.14 Multi-Region & Global Databases
docs.text:
A multi-region database keeps data in several geographic regions so it survives a whole region failing and serves users with lower latency. The catch is physics: light takes tens of milliseconds to cross continents, so every design chooses between waiting for other regions (consistency) and answering locally (speed).

Typical round-trip times (approximate). Every synchronous cross-region step adds a round trip; physics sets the floor.

Think of it like…

A global company with offices in London, New York and Tokyo can keep one master ledger (accurate, but everyone phones London) or a ledger in each office reconciled nightly (fast, but sometimes briefly out of step).

Real-world example

GlobeFit, a fictional fitness app with users in the EU, US and Australia, uses CockroachDB with REGIONAL BY ROW tables: each user's row lives in their home region, so profile reads take 2 ms instead of 250 ms. The exercise catalogue is a GLOBAL table, readable quickly everywhere. EU personal data stays in EU regions to meet residency rules.

docs.title: How it works
docs.text:
1. Decide goals: survive a region outage, lower latency, data residency — or all three.
  2. Choose active-passive (one writing region) or active-active (writes in several regions).
  3. Place data: replicate everything everywhere, or pin rows to their users' home regions.
  4. Choose consistency per table: synchronous cross-region writes, or asynchronous with conflict resolution.
  5. Route users to the nearest healthy region with global load balancing or DNS.
  6. Rehearse region evacuation and measure real RPO and RTO.

Who uses it

Cloud architects, SREs and database engineers at global SaaS, gaming, finance and e-commerce companies.

Key takeaway

Rule of thumb: light in fibre covers about 200 km per millisecond, so a London–New York round trip can never be much under 60 ms.

Going deeper

  • Google Spanner offers 99.999% availability for multi-region configurations (99.99% regional), using Paxos replicas across regions plus TrueTime to keep strict serializability worldwide.
  • CockroachDB's multi-region SQL offers REGIONAL BY TABLE, REGIONAL BY ROW and GLOBAL localities, with survival goals of ZONE (default) or REGION, which needs at least three regions.
  • Amazon Aurora DSQL, generally available since May 2025, provides PostgreSQL-compatible active-active multi-region clusters with strong consistency, using two regional clusters plus a witness region.
  • DynamoDB global tables originally offered multi-region eventual consistency with last-writer-wins; in 2025 AWS added a multi-region strong consistency mode spanning three Regions.
  • Aurora Global Database replicates at the storage layer to secondary Regions with lag typically under a second, supporting managed switchover and fast cross-region failover.
  • Cassandra's NetworkTopologyStrategy sets a replication factor per data centre; LOCAL_QUORUM keeps latency local while EACH_QUORUM waits for a majority in every data centre.

Common mistakes & misconceptions

  • Making every write synchronous across continents by default: each commit pays 100+ ms. Use it only for data that truly needs it.
  • Running active-active with last-writer-wins on data like balances or inventory: concurrent updates are silently lost.
  • Forgetting that the control plane, DNS, secrets and app servers must also be multi-region, or the database survives while the service does not.

docs.title: Try it: Multi-region table localities in CockroachDB (local demo: cockroach demo --nodes 9 --demo-locality ...)
docs.text:
ALTER DATABASE globefit SET PRIMARY REGION "europe-west1";
ALTER DATABASE globefit ADD REGION "us-east1";
ALTER DATABASE globefit ADD REGION "australia-southeast1";
ALTER TABLE users SET LOCALITY REGIONAL BY ROW;   -- rows live near their users
ALTER TABLE exercises SET LOCALITY GLOBAL;       -- fast reads everywhere
ALTER DATABASE globefit SURVIVE REGION FAILURE;

docs.title: Glossary of Terms
A
docs.text: ACID Atomicity, Consistency, Isolation, Durability: the four guarantees of a reliable transaction — all or nothing, rules hold, no interference, and committed data survives crashes.

docs.title: B
docs.text: BASE Basically Available, Soft state, Eventually consistent — the looser guarantees many NoSQL systems accept in exchange for availability and scale. Bloom filter A compact probabilistic structure that answers 'definitely not present' or 'maybe present'; LSM-tree engines use it to skip files that cannot hold a key. B+tree The balanced tree structure behind most database indexes; all values sit in linked leaf pages, so lookups and range scans need only a few page reads. Buffer pool The database's own memory cache of disk pages; reads and writes go through it, and its hit ratio strongly affects performance.

docs.title: C
docs.text: CAP theorem During a network partition a distributed system must choose between consistency and availability; PACELC adds the latency-versus-consistency trade-off when there is no partition. Change data capture (CDC) Streaming every insert, update and delete from a database's log to other systems, for example with Debezium into Kafka. Columnar storage Storing each column's values together instead of whole rows, so analytical queries read only the columns they need and compress very well. Common table expression (CTE) A named temporary result defined with WITH at the start of a query; recursive CTEs can walk hierarchies and graphs. Connection pool A set of open database connections shared by many application requests, avoiding the cost of reconnecting; examples are HikariCP and PgBouncer. Consensus Agreement among replicated servers on a single order of decisions despite failures; Raft and Paxos are the best-known algorithms. Constraint A rule the database enforces on data — primary key, foreign key, UNIQUE, CHECK, NOT NULL — rejecting changes that would break it.

docs.title: D
docs.text: Data lake Cheap object storage holding raw files of any format (often Parquet) for later processing and analytics. Data warehouse A database optimised for analytical queries over large, integrated, historical data, such as Snowflake, BigQuery or Redshift. DBMS Database management system: the software that stores, queries, secures and recovers data, such as PostgreSQL, Oracle or MongoDB. Deadlock Two or more transactions each waiting for a lock the other holds; the database detects it and aborts one of them. Denormalisation Deliberately duplicating data to make reads faster or simpler, at the cost of extra storage and harder updates. Document database A NoSQL database storing self-contained JSON-like documents, such as MongoDB or Firestore.

docs.title: E
docs.text: Embedding A vector of numbers produced by a machine-learning model so that similar meanings lie close together; the basis of vector search. Entity-relationship (ER) diagram A drawing of entities, their attributes and the relationships between them, used to design a database before building it. ETL / ELT Extract, transform, load — or load first and transform inside the warehouse (ELT) — the two main patterns for moving data into analytics systems. Eventual consistency A guarantee that replicas converge to the same value if no new writes arrive, though reads may briefly return stale data. EXPLAIN A command that shows the execution plan the optimiser chose for a query; EXPLAIN ANALYZE also runs it and reports real timings.

docs.title: F
docs.text: Foreign key A column whose values must match a key in another table, enforcing referential integrity between related rows.

docs.title: G
docs.text: Graph database A database storing nodes and relationships as first-class data, queried with languages like Cypher or GQL; Neo4j is the best known.

docs.title: H
docs.text: HNSW Hierarchical Navigable Small World: a layered graph index for fast approximate nearest-neighbour vector search.

docs.title: I
docs.text: Index An extra data structure that lets the database find rows without scanning the whole table, at the cost of storage and slower writes. Isolation level How strongly concurrent transactions are separated: read uncommitted, read committed, repeatable read or serializable.

docs.title: J
docs.text: Join Combining rows from two tables based on a related column; inner, left, right, full outer, cross and self joins are the main kinds.

docs.title: K
docs.text: Key-value store A database that stores values under unique keys with very fast lookups, such as Redis, Valkey or DynamoDB.

docs.title: L
docs.text: Lakehouse An architecture combining data-lake storage with warehouse features such as ACID tables and SQL, using open table formats like Iceberg or Delta Lake. Least privilege Giving every user and application only the permissions it needs, limiting the damage from mistakes or stolen credentials. LSM-tree Log-structured merge-tree: a write-optimised storage structure that buffers writes in memory and merges sorted files in the background.

docs.title: M
docs.text: Materialized view A stored result of a query that can be refreshed, trading freshness for much faster reads. Model Context Protocol (MCP) An open protocol that lets AI applications call external tools and data sources, including databases, through standard servers. MVCC Multi-version concurrency control: keeping several versions of rows so readers see a consistent snapshot without blocking writers.

docs.title: N
docs.text: Normalisation Organising tables to remove redundancy and update anomalies, following normal forms such as 1NF, 2NF, 3NF and BCNF. NoSQL A broad family of non-relational databases — key-value, document, wide-column and graph — built for particular data shapes and scale. NULL A marker for a missing or unknown value; comparisons with NULL yield 'unknown', which is why SQL uses three-valued logic.

docs.title: O
docs.text: OLAP Online analytical processing: complex queries scanning large volumes of historical data for reporting and analysis. OLTP Online transaction processing: many small, fast reads and writes from applications, such as orders and payments. Open table format A specification such as Apache Iceberg, Delta Lake or Hudi that adds tables, transactions and schema evolution on top of files in object storage. ORM Object-relational mapper: a library that maps programming-language objects to database rows and generates SQL, such as Hibernate or SQLAlchemy.

docs.title: P
docs.text: Parameterised query A query sent with placeholders and separate values, so user input can never change the SQL — the main defence against SQL injection. Parquet An open columnar file format with compression and statistics, the standard storage format for data lakes and lakehouses. Partitioning Splitting a large table into smaller pieces by range, list or hash, within one server or across servers. Point-in-time recovery (PITR) Restoring a database to any chosen moment by replaying archived transaction logs on top of a base backup. Primary key The column or columns that uniquely identify each row in a table; it cannot be NULL or duplicated.

docs.title: Q
docs.text: Query optimiser The DBMS component that estimates the cost of alternative plans using statistics and picks the cheapest way to run a query. Quorum The minimum number of replicas that must acknowledge a read or write; with W + R > N, reads overlap the latest write.

docs.title: R
docs.text: Relational model E. F. Codd's 1970 model representing data as relations (tables) of tuples (rows) with attributes (columns), manipulated declaratively. Replication Keeping copies of the same data on several servers for availability, durability and read scaling; it can be synchronous or asynchronous. Retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) Retrieving relevant data, often by vector search, and passing it to a language model so its answer uses current, private facts. Row-level security (RLS) Database policies that automatically filter which rows each user may see or change. RPO / RTO Recovery point objective (how much data you can afford to lose) and recovery time objective (how long you can afford to be down).

docs.title: S
docs.text: Schema The defined structure of a database — tables, columns, types, constraints and relationships — or a named namespace grouping such objects. Sharding Splitting data horizontally across several servers, each holding a subset of rows chosen by a shard key. Snapshot isolation An isolation level in which each transaction reads a consistent snapshot as of its start; it prevents most anomalies but allows write skew. SQL Structured Query Language: the standard declarative language for defining, querying and changing relational data, standardised by ISO/IEC 9075. SQL injection An attack in which untrusted input concatenated into SQL text changes the query's meaning; prevented by parameterised queries. Star schema A dimensional model with a central fact table of measurements surrounded by dimension tables describing who, what, where and when. Stored procedure Named code stored and run inside the database, written in languages such as PL/pgSQL, T-SQL or PL/SQL. Surrogate key An artificial identifier, such as an identity integer or UUID, used as a primary key instead of a natural business value.

docs.title: T
docs.text: Transaction A group of database operations treated as one unit that either commits completely or rolls back completely. Transparent data encryption (TDE) Engine-level encryption of data and log files at rest, invisible to applications. Two-phase commit (2PC) A protocol in which a coordinator first asks all participants to prepare, then tells them all to commit, keeping a distributed transaction atomic.

docs.title: V
docs.text: Vector database A database specialised in storing embeddings and finding nearest neighbours quickly; many general databases now offer vector search too.

docs.title: W
docs.text: Window function A function such as ROW_NUMBER, RANK or SUM OVER that computes across related rows without collapsing them into groups. Write-ahead log (WAL) A log to which every change is written before the data pages, so committed transactions can be recovered after a crash.

docs.title: Chapter 4: How Databases Work Inside
docs.text: This chapter opens the bonnet. It follows a query through the parser, optimiser and executor; shows how rows sit in pages and how the buffer pool caches them; explains B+trees, specialised indexes and LSM-trees; reads EXPLAIN plans and compares join algorithms; covers locking, MVCC, isolation levels and their anomalies; shows how write-ahead logging makes commits survive crashes; and ends with columnar, vectorized analytics engines and the vector indexes behind AI search.

docs.title: 4.1 Inside a DBMS: Parser, Optimiser, Executor and Storage Engine
docs.text:
A database server is a pipeline of cooperating parts. The parser checks your SQL and turns it into a tree; the optimiser (planner) picks the fastest way to run it; the executor runs that plan; and the storage engine reads and writes pages on disk through a memory cache called the buffer pool. Side managers handle locks, transactions and the recovery log.

The layers of a relational DBMS. A query travels down the stack; rows travel back up.

Think of it like…

It is like a restaurant: the waiter checks your order makes sense (parser), the head chef decides the cooking order (optimiser), line cooks do the work (executor), and the pantry staff fetch ingredients from the cold store into the kitchen (storage engine and buffer pool).

Real-world example

When Lucía's app at the fictional BookNest store sends SELECT title FROM book WHERE isbn = '978…', PostgreSQL's backend process parses it, resolves book in the system catalog, rewrites any views, and the planner chooses an index scan costing 8.3 units over a sequential scan costing 2,150. The executor walks the B-tree, fetches one heap page via the buffer manager, checks the row is visible to her transaction, and returns one row in 0.1 ms.

docs.title: How it works
docs.text:
1. Connection: the client connects; PostgreSQL forks a backend process, MySQL assigns a thread, and authentication runs.
  2. Parse and analyse: the SQL text becomes a parse tree; names are resolved against the system catalog and types are checked.
  3. Rewrite and optimise: views and rules are expanded, then the cost-based optimiser builds and costs alternative plans and keeps the cheapest.
  4. Execute: the executor runs the plan tree, pulling rows from operators such as scans, joins and sorts.
  5. Access storage: access methods ask the buffer manager for pages; the lock, transaction and log managers keep concurrent changes safe and durable.

Who uses it

Database engineers, DBAs diagnosing performance, backend developers reading query plans, and students in database-systems courses.

Key takeaway

Be able to draw the stack from memory — connection manager, parser, rewriter, optimiser, executor, access methods, buffer manager, disk — with the lock and log managers alongside; it anchors every internals interview question.

Going deeper

  • Hellerstein, Stonebraker and Hamilton's "Architecture of a Database System" (2007) describes the same five parts in almost every engine: process manager, query processor, transactional storage manager, shared utilities and the catalog.
  • PostgreSQL uses a process per connection, so thousands of idle connections cost memory and need a pooler; MySQL and SQL Server use threads, and SQL Server schedules them with its own SQLOS layer.
  • Most executors follow the Volcano iterator model (Graefe, 1994): each operator exposes open, next and close, and a parent pulls one row at a time from its children; analytic engines pull batches instead.
  • MySQL separates the SQL layer from pluggable storage engines (InnoDB has been the default since 5.5 in 2010), and PostgreSQL 12 added a table access method API so alternative storage formats can plug in.
  • SQLite compiles each statement into bytecode for its virtual machine (the VDBE), a design you can inspect with EXPLAIN, which prints the bytecode program rather than a plan tree.
  • The system catalog is itself a set of tables (pg_class, pg_attribute, information_schema) that the parser and planner query constantly, so catalog bloat from thousands of temporary tables slows every query.

Common mistakes & misconceptions

  • Thinking SQL runs top to bottom as written: the optimiser freely reorders joins and filters, so the plan, not the text, decides performance.
  • Opening a new connection per request: connection setup and PostgreSQL's process fork cost milliseconds and memory; use a connection pool.
  • Assuming every database has the same architecture: MySQL's storage-engine split and SQLite's in-process library behave very differently from PostgreSQL.

docs.title: Try it: Peek at the stages in PostgreSQL
docs.text:
-- print parse, rewritten and plan trees to the server log
SET debug_print_parse = on;  SET debug_print_plan = on;
SET client_min_messages = log;
SELECT 1;

-- see one backend process per connection
SELECT pid, backend_type, state, query FROM pg_stat_activity;

docs.title: Key databases, concepts, languages, tools & standards
docs.text: Name What it does Example Connection managerDBMS architecture · Concept · Current · Intermediate · General Accepts client connections, authenticates them and assigns a process or thread to run each session's queries. PostgreSQL's postmaster forks a new backend for each connection; max_connections defaults to 100. ParserDBMS architecture · Concept · Current · Beginner · Relational Checks SQL syntax and builds a parse tree; PostgreSQL's grammar is generated with Bison from gram.y. SELEC * FROM book fails at parse time with "syntax error at or near SELEC" before touching any data. Semantic analyser (binder)DBMS architecture · Concept · Current · Intermediate · Relational Resolves table and column names against the catalog, checks types and permissions, and produces a query tree. SELECT titel FROM book parses fine but fails analysis with "column titel does not exist". Query rewriterDBMS architecture · Concept · Current · Intermediate · Relational Transforms the query tree before planning, expanding views, applying rules and row-level security policies. A query on the view active_customers is rewritten into a query on customer WHERE deleted_at IS NULL. Query optimiser (planner)DBMS architecture · Concept · Current · Intermediate · Relational Generates alternative execution plans, estimates their costs using statistics and picks the cheapest. For a 3-table join the planner compares orders, join methods and index choices before running anything. ExecutorDBMS architecture · Concept · Current · Intermediate · Relational Runs the chosen plan tree, passing rows or batches between operators such as scans, joins, sorts and aggregates. A Hash Join node pulls all rows from its inner child to build a table, then streams the outer child through it. Volcano iterator modelGoetz Graefe (1994) · Algorithm · Current · Advanced · Relational Execution design where every operator implements open(), next() and close(), and rows are pulled through the plan one at a time. A Limit 10 node stops calling next() after ten rows, so the scan beneath it stops early. Storage engineDBMS architecture · Concept · Current · Beginner · General The component that stores, retrieves and updates data on disk, including page formats, indexes and transactional guarantees. MySQL can use InnoDB for transactional tables and MyRocks for compressed, write-heavy tables in the same server. Access methodDBMS architecture · Concept · Current · Intermediate · Relational Code that implements a specific way to store or find rows, such as a heap, B-tree, hash or GIN index. PostgreSQL lists available index access methods in the pg_am catalog: btree, hash, gist, gin, spgist, brin. Lock managerDBMS architecture · Concept · Current · Intermediate · General Grants, queues and releases locks on rows, pages and tables, and detects deadlocks between transactions. pg_locks shows which backend holds a RowExclusiveLock and who is waiting for it. Log managerDBMS architecture · Concept · Current · Intermediate · General Writes the write-ahead log, assigns log sequence numbers and flushes records so committed changes survive crashes. PostgreSQL's WAL writer process flushes WAL buffers to pg_wal segment files. System catalogDBMS architecture; SQL information_schema · Concept · Current · Beginner · Relational Tables describing the database itself — tables, columns, types, indexes, users — read by the parser and planner. SELECT relname, reltuples FROM pg_class WHERE relkind = 'r' lists tables with their estimated row counts. MySQL pluggable storage enginesOracle MySQL · Feature · Current · Intermediate · Relational MySQL's split between a common SQL layer and interchangeable engines such as InnoDB, MyISAM, MEMORY and NDB. SHOW ENGINES lists available engines; CREATE TABLE ... ENGINE=InnoDB is the default choice since 5.5. SQLite VDBESQLite · Feature · Current · Advanced · Relational SQLite's virtual machine that executes statements compiled to bytecode inside the application's own process. EXPLAIN SELECT * FROM t in the sqlite3 shell prints opcodes like OpenRead, Rewind, Column and ResultRow. Architecture of a Database SystemHellerstein, Stonebraker and Hamilton (2007) · Resource · Current · Advanced · General Free survey paper explaining how real DBMSs are structured, from process models to storage managers. Students read it alongside CMU 15-445 lectures to connect theory with PostgreSQL and SQL Server internals.

docs.title: 4.2 Storage Layout: Pages, Slotted Pages and Heap Files
docs.text:
Databases do not read single rows from disk; they read fixed-size blocks called pages, typically 8 KB or 16 KB. Each page holds a header, a small directory of pointers (slots) and the rows themselves. A table stored as an unordered collection of pages is a heap file; some engines instead store the table inside its primary-key index.

Inside an 8 KB slotted page (PostgreSQL). Slots grow down from the top and tuples grow up from the bottom until they meet.

Think of it like…

A page is like a page in a ring binder: a contents list at the top says where each entry starts, entries fill up from the bottom, and you can move an entry within the page by just updating the contents list.

Real-world example

Ahmed, a DBA at the fictional TideWater Shipping, checks why the 12 GB shipments table is slow. PostgreSQL stores it as 1.5 million 8 KB heap pages. pgstattuple shows 35% dead tuples after heavy updates, so each page holds fewer live rows and scans read more pages. After VACUUM and lowering fillfactor to 85 for HOT updates, the table stops growing and scans read 30% fewer pages.

docs.title: How it works
docs.text:
1. The table file is divided into fixed-size pages, each addressed by its block number.
  2. Each page starts with a header (LSN, checksum, free-space pointers) followed by an array of slot pointers.
  3. Rows (tuples) are written from the end of the page backwards; each slot records a row's offset and length.
  4. A row is identified by (page number, slot number) — PostgreSQL's ctid — so it can move within a page without changing its address.
  5. Values too large for a page are compressed or moved to overflow storage (TOAST in PostgreSQL, off-page columns in InnoDB).

Who uses it

DBAs sizing storage and diagnosing bloat, database engine developers, and performance engineers estimating I/O.

Key takeaway

Memorise default page sizes: PostgreSQL 8 KB, SQL Server 8 KB, Oracle 8 KB by default, MySQL InnoDB 16 KB, SQLite 4 KB.

Going deeper

  • A PostgreSQL heap tuple has a 23-byte header holding xmin, xmax, ctid and flags before any user data, so a row of three small integers still costs around 40 bytes including its 4-byte line pointer.
  • TOAST compresses or moves field values out of line when a row exceeds about 2 KB, storing chunks in a side table; a single field can hold up to 1 GB.
  • InnoDB stores each table as a clustered B+tree ordered by primary key, so secondary indexes store the primary-key value rather than a physical address and lookups traverse two trees.
  • Fillfactor leaves space free on each page (PostgreSQL tables default to 100, B-tree indexes to 90) so updates can stay on the same page; PostgreSQL's heap-only tuple (HOT) updates then avoid touching indexes.
  • Free-space maps track which pages have room for inserts, and PostgreSQL's visibility map marks all-visible pages so VACUUM can skip them and index-only scans can avoid heap visits.
  • Page checksums detect silent disk corruption; PostgreSQL 18 enables them by default for new clusters created with initdb, and SQL Server and InnoDB have long used page checksums.

Common mistakes & misconceptions

  • Thinking the database reads one row at a time from disk: it always reads whole pages, so row width and packing drive I/O cost.
  • Ignoring bloat after mass updates or deletes: dead space stays in pages until vacuumed or rebuilt, inflating scans and backups.
  • Assuming SELECT * order equals insert order: heap files are unordered, and rows move after updates; only ORDER BY guarantees order.

docs.title: Try it: See physical row addresses and page contents in PostgreSQL
docs.text:
CREATE TABLE t (id int, note text);
INSERT INTO t SELECT g, 'row ' || g FROM generate_series(1, 1000) g;
SELECT ctid, id FROM t LIMIT 5;          -- (page, slot)
SELECT pg_relation_size('t') / 8192 AS pages;

CREATE EXTENSION IF NOT EXISTS pageinspect;
SELECT lp, lp_off, lp_len, t_xmin, t_xmax
FROM heap_page_items(get_raw_page('t', 0)) LIMIT 5;

docs.title: 4.3 Buffer Pool Management
docs.text:
Reading from memory is thousands of times faster than reading from disk, so a database keeps recently used pages in a large shared memory area called the buffer pool. When a page is needed, the buffer manager returns it from memory if possible; otherwise it reads it from disk, evicting a less useful page to make room. Changed (dirty) pages are written back later, safely, thanks to the log.

What happens on a page request. The write-ahead rule — log before data — applies whenever a dirty page is evicted.

Think of it like…

The buffer pool is a desk next to a huge filing room: you keep the folders you use most on the desk, and when the desk is full you return the folder you have not touched for longest — after copying any notes you scribbled in it.

Real-world example

At the fictional Kestrel Insurance, the claims database is 200 GB but the server has 64 GB RAM. The DBA sets InnoDB's buffer pool to 48 GB; the hot working set of the last 90 days of claims fits, and the hit ratio rises from 91% to 99.6%. A nightly full-table report no longer evicts daytime pages because InnoDB inserts newly read pages at the midpoint of its LRU list.

docs.title: How it works
docs.text:
1. The executor asks the buffer manager for page N; the manager looks it up in a hash table of cached pages.
  2. On a hit, the page is pinned (marked in use) and returned; its usage information is updated.
  3. On a miss, a victim frame is chosen by the replacement policy; if it is dirty, its log records must be flushed before writing it out.
  4. The requested page is read from disk into the frame, pinned and returned.
  5. Background writers and checkpoints flush dirty pages gradually so evictions rarely have to wait for writes.

Who uses it

DBAs tuning memory settings, performance engineers, and engine developers; buffer pools are a core topic in database-systems courses.

Key takeaway

Know the typical starting points: PostgreSQL shared_buffers about 25% of RAM (the OS cache does the rest) and InnoDB buffer pool 50-75% of RAM on a dedicated server.

Going deeper

  • PostgreSQL uses a clock-sweep algorithm: each buffer has a usage count up to 5 that is bumped on access and decremented as the clock hand passes; a buffer at zero that is unpinned becomes the victim.
  • InnoDB splits its LRU list into young and old sublists, inserting new pages at the midpoint (innodb_old_blocks_pct defaults to 37%) so one large scan cannot flush the hot working set.
  • PostgreSQL relies on both shared_buffers and the operating system's page cache (double buffering), which is why shared_buffers is usually only about 25% of RAM; InnoDB commonly bypasses the OS cache with O_DIRECT.
  • Large sequential scans and VACUUM in PostgreSQL use small ring buffers (256 KB for bulk reads) instead of the whole pool, protecting cached pages from one-off scans.
  • Replacement policies studied in research include LRU-K (O'Neil, 1993), 2Q and ARC; SQL Server documents an LRU-K variant for its buffer pool.
  • PostgreSQL 18 added asynchronous I/O (io_method = worker by default, or io_uring on Linux), letting sequential scans, bitmap heap scans and vacuum issue several reads at once.

Common mistakes & misconceptions

  • Giving the buffer pool all the RAM: the OS, connections, sorts and hash tables also need memory, and swapping is far worse than cache misses.
  • Trusting the hit ratio alone: 99% hits can still mean millions of misses per minute on a busy server; look at absolute reads too.
  • Benchmarking on a cold cache once: the first run measures disk, later runs measure memory; warm up and repeat measurements.

docs.title: Try it: Check cache hit ratio and buffer contents in PostgreSQL
docs.text:
SELECT datname,
       round(100.0 * blks_hit / nullif(blks_hit + blks_read, 0), 2) AS hit_pct
FROM pg_stat_database WHERE datname = current_database();

SHOW shared_buffers;
CREATE EXTENSION IF NOT EXISTS pg_buffercache;
SELECT c.relname, count(*) AS buffers
FROM pg_buffercache b JOIN pg_class c ON b.relfilenode = c.relfilenode
GROUP BY c.relname ORDER BY buffers DESC LIMIT 10;

docs.title: 4.4 B+Tree Indexes in Depth
docs.text:
A B+tree is the standard index structure in relational databases. It is a short, wide tree of pages: the root and inner pages hold sorted keys that act as signposts, and the leaf pages hold every key with a pointer to its row, linked left-to-right for range scans. Because each page holds hundreds of keys, finding one row among billions takes only three or four page reads.

A three-level B+tree. Inner pages only guide the search; all keys and row pointers live in linked leaves.

Think of it like…

It is like a large dictionary with thumb tabs: the tabs (root) send you to the right section, the running heads at the top of each page (inner nodes) narrow it down, and on the final page the words are in order, so you can also read on to the next ones.

Real-world example

The fictional CityBike scheme has 900 million ride rows. Its B+tree on ride_id has a fan-out of about 400 keys per 8 KB page, so the tree is four levels deep: root, two inner levels and leaves. Looking up ride 712,004,511 reads four pages — usually three are already cached — and a range query for the next 1,000 rides walks along neighbouring leaf pages.

docs.title: How it works
docs.text:
1. Search: start at the root, binary-search the keys in the page, follow the child pointer, and repeat until reaching a leaf.
  2. Range scan: find the first matching key in a leaf, then follow sibling links to read keys in order.
  3. Insert: place the key in the correct leaf; if full, split it into two half-full pages and push a separator key up to the parent.
  4. Splits may propagate up to the root; a root split is the only way the tree grows taller, so all leaves stay at the same depth.
  5. Delete: remove the key; engines often leave under-full pages alone or merge them lazily, and VACUUM or rebuilds reclaim space.

Who uses it

Every developer who creates an index, DBAs tuning queries, and engine developers; B+trees are among the most-asked internals interview topics.

Key takeaway

Know why height matters: with fan-out f, a tree of height h indexes about f^h keys, so 400^4 is 25.6 billion — four page reads cover almost any table.

Going deeper

  • Bayer and McCreight introduced the B-tree in 1970-72 at Boeing; Douglas Comer's 1979 survey "The Ubiquitous B-Tree" popularised the B+tree variant, where only leaves hold records and leaves are chained.
  • PostgreSQL's nbtree implements Lehman and Yao's 1981 B-link tree: each page has a right-link and high key, so readers can recover from concurrent splits without locking the whole path.
  • Monotonically increasing keys (identity, UUIDv7, timestamps) always insert at the rightmost leaf, and engines optimise this case; random keys such as UUIDv4 split pages all over the tree and leave them about half full.
  • PostgreSQL 13 added B-tree deduplication, storing a repeated key once with a list of row pointers, which can shrink indexes on low-cardinality columns several-fold; suffix truncation keeps inner pages compact.
  • An index on (a, b) is sorted by a then b, so it serves filters on a, or on a plus b; PostgreSQL 18's skip scan can also serve filters on b alone when a has few distinct values.
  • An index-only scan answers a query entirely from the index when all needed columns are in it; PostgreSQL must still check the visibility map, so recently modified pages force heap visits.

Common mistakes & misconceptions

  • Expecting an index on (a, b) to help a query that filters only on b: column order matters, and leading columns must normally be constrained.
  • Wrapping indexed columns in functions: WHERE lower(email) = ? cannot use a plain index on email; create an expression index instead.
  • Assuming indexes always help: fetching 30% of a table through an index is usually slower than a sequential scan, and the planner knows it.

docs.title: Try it: Inspect a B-tree's height and size in PostgreSQL
docs.text:
CREATE TABLE ride AS SELECT g AS ride_id FROM generate_series(1, 5000000) g;
CREATE INDEX ride_pk ON ride (ride_id);

CREATE EXTENSION IF NOT EXISTS pageinspect;
SELECT level AS height_minus_1, fastroot, root
FROM bt_metap('ride_pk');
SELECT pg_size_pretty(pg_relation_size('ride_pk')) AS index_size;

EXPLAIN (ANALYZE, BUFFERS) SELECT * FROM ride WHERE ride_id = 4242424;
