docs.title: 4.5 Beyond B-trees: Hash, Bitmap, GiST, GIN, BRIN and the Cost of Indexes
docs.text:
B-trees are the default, but other index types suit other questions. Hash indexes do fast equality lookups; bitmap indexes suit low-cardinality columns in warehouses; GIN and inverted indexes find rows containing a word or JSON key; GiST handles geometry and ranges; BRIN summarises huge, naturally ordered tables in a few kilobytes. Every index also has a cost: it slows writes and uses space.

Which index for which question?

Best for Typical example B-tree Equality, ranges, sorting WHERE created_at > now() - '1 day' Hash Equality only WHERE session_token = ? Bitmap Low-cardinality warehouse filters Oracle: gender, region, status GIN / inverted Contains word, key or element tags @> '["vip"]', full-text GiST / SP-GiST Geometry, ranges, nearest Shops within 2 km (PostGIS) BRIN Huge, naturally ordered tables Append-only sensor time series

Match the index to the operator in your WHERE clause.

Think of it like…

Indexes are like the different finding aids in a library: the alphabetical catalogue (B-tree), the back-of-book index of words (inverted/GIN), a map of shelves by area (GiST) and a sign saying "aisles 1-10: books from 1900-1950" (BRIN).

Real-world example

The fictional GeoFleet logistics company stores 5 billion GPS pings. A BRIN index on recorded_at is just 2 MB yet lets time-range queries skip 99% of blocks; a GiST index on the PostGIS location column finds trucks within 5 km of a depot; a GIN index on the tags JSONB column finds pings tagged 'refrigerated'. A rarely used B-tree on driver_note was dropped, speeding up inserts by 8%.

docs.title: How it works
docs.text:
1. Start from the query: equality, range, containment, full-text, nearest-neighbour or spatial overlap.
  2. Pick the matching index type and operator class (B-tree for ranges, GIN for containment, GiST for geometry, BRIN for ordered append-only data).
  3. Narrow it: add INCLUDE columns for index-only scans, a WHERE clause for a partial index, or an expression for computed lookups.
  4. Create it without blocking writes (CREATE INDEX CONCURRENTLY or ONLINE options) and confirm with EXPLAIN that it is used.
  5. Monitor usage and drop indexes that are never scanned, because each one costs write time, storage and vacuum work.

Who uses it

Backend developers, DBAs and data engineers tuning PostgreSQL, Oracle, SQL Server, Elasticsearch or warehouse workloads.

Key takeaway

Interviewers like the trade-off answer: indexes speed reads but slow every INSERT, UPDATE and DELETE, so index for your actual queries and remove unused ones.

Going deeper

  • PostgreSQL hash indexes became crash-safe and replicated only in version 10 (2017); before that they were not WAL-logged, which is why older advice says never to use them.
  • Oracle bitmap indexes store one bitmap per distinct value and combine them with fast AND/OR operations, but a single-row update can lock many rows, so they suit warehouses, not OLTP.
  • GiST (Hellerstein, Naughton and Pfeffer, 1995) is a framework for balanced search trees over any data type that defines consistency and union functions; PostGIS R-tree-style spatial indexes are built on it.
  • GIN maps each element — word, array value or JSON key — to a posting list of rows, making containment searches fast; pending-list updates (fastupdate) buffer inserts at the cost of slower later reads.
  • A BRIN index stores the minimum and maximum value per range of 128 pages by default, so it is tiny but only effective when values correlate with physical row order.
  • Each extra index adds work to every insert and most updates, can prevent PostgreSQL HOT updates, and must be vacuumed and backed up; write-heavy tables often perform best with only a handful of indexes.

Common mistakes & misconceptions

  • Indexing every column "just in case": write throughput drops and the planner still uses only a few of them.
  • Using BRIN on randomly ordered data: block ranges overlap completely, so the index excludes nothing and every block is read.
  • Forgetting operator classes: a default B-tree on text may not help LIKE 'abc%' under non-C collations; use text_pattern_ops or a trigram GIN index.

docs.title: Try it: Several index types on one PostgreSQL table
docs.text:
CREATE TABLE ping (id bigint, truck_id int, recorded_at timestamptz,
                   tags jsonb, status text);
CREATE INDEX ping_time_brin ON ping USING brin (recorded_at);
CREATE INDEX ping_tags_gin  ON ping USING gin (tags jsonb_path_ops);
CREATE INDEX ping_open      ON ping (truck_id) WHERE status = 'open';   -- partial
CREATE INDEX ping_cover     ON ping (truck_id) INCLUDE (recorded_at);  -- covering

-- which indexes are never used?
SELECT indexrelname, idx_scan FROM pg_stat_user_indexes ORDER BY idx_scan;

Index maintenance costDatabase performance · Concept · Current · Beginner · General Every index adds write work, storage, cache pressure and vacuum time, so unused indexes are pure overhead. Dropping four unused indexes cut a ledger table's insert latency from 3.1 ms to 1.4 ms. pg_stat_user_indexesPostgreSQL statistics views · Tool · Current · Intermediate · Relational View reporting how often each index has been scanned, used to find unused or rarely used indexes. idx_scan = 0 after a month of production traffic flags an index as a candidate to drop.

docs.title: 4.6 LSM-Trees vs B-Trees
docs.text:
A log-structured merge-tree (LSM-tree) is built for fast writes. New writes go into a sorted in-memory table and a log; when it fills, it is written to disk as an immutable sorted file (an SSTable). Background compaction merges these files over time. Reads may need to check several files, so LSM engines use bloom filters to skip files that cannot contain the key.

The write and read path of an LSM-tree. Writes are sequential; compaction pays the sorting cost later, in the background.

Think of it like…

An LSM-tree is like handling post by dropping letters into a tray and filing whole trays at the end of the day, then occasionally merging old files; a B-tree is like filing each letter into the right folder the moment it arrives.

Real-world example

The fictional PulseWear fitness company ingests 400,000 heart-rate readings per second. On a B-tree engine, random inserts cause constant page rewrites; on RocksDB, writes hit the memtable and WAL, are flushed as 64 MB SSTables, and leveled compaction keeps reads to a few files. Bloom filters at 10 bits per key mean only about 1% of lookups read an SSTable needlessly.

docs.title: How it works
docs.text:
1. Append each write to a write-ahead log for durability, then insert it into the in-memory sorted memtable.
  2. When the memtable fills, freeze it and flush it to disk as an immutable, sorted SSTable file.
  3. Reads check the memtable, then SSTables from newest to oldest, using bloom filters and fence pointers to skip files.
  4. Updates and deletes are new entries (deletes write tombstones); the newest version wins.
  5. Background compaction merges SSTables, discarding overwritten values and expired tombstones, in leveled or size-tiered fashion.

Who uses it

Engineers working with Cassandra, ScyllaDB, HBase, RocksDB-based systems (TiKV, MyRocks, Kafka Streams state), CockroachDB's Pebble and time-series databases.

Key takeaway

Summarise the trade-off with the RUM conjecture: you can optimise two of Read, Update and Memory overheads at the expense of the third — B-trees favour reads, LSM-trees favour writes.

Going deeper

  • The LSM-tree was described by O'Neil, Cheng, Gawlick and O'Neil in 1996; Google's Bigtable (2006) and LevelDB (2011) made it mainstream, and Facebook forked LevelDB into RocksDB in 2012.
  • Leveled compaction keeps each level about 10 times larger than the previous one with non-overlapping files, giving good read and space efficiency but higher write amplification; size-tiered compaction writes less but uses more space.
  • A bloom filter with about 10 bits per key gives roughly a 1% false-positive rate, so a point lookup for a missing key usually touches no SSTable data blocks at all.
  • Write amplification, read amplification and space amplification are the three metrics engineers tune; compaction can rewrite each byte many times, which matters for SSD wear.
  • Tombstones from deletes must survive until compaction reaches the oldest data they shadow; Cassandra keeps them for gc_grace_seconds (10 days by default) so replicas do not resurrect deleted rows.
  • Cassandra 5.0 introduced the Unified Compaction Strategy, while CockroachDB uses Pebble, a Go key-value engine inspired by RocksDB; MongoDB's WiredTiger, by contrast, uses B-trees by default.

Common mistakes & misconceptions

  • Assuming LSM engines are always faster: range scans and point reads over many levels can be slower than a well-cached B-tree.
  • Ignoring compaction debt: if writes outpace compaction, files pile up, reads slow and engines throttle or stall writes.
  • Mass deletes in Cassandra: millions of tombstones make reads scan dead data and can trigger query failures until compaction removes them.

docs.title: Try it: Write to an LSM engine (RocksDB) from Python and inspect its files
docs.text:
# pip install rocksdict   (Python bindings for RocksDB)
from rocksdict import Rdict
db = Rdict("./lsm_demo")
for i in range(200_000):
    db[f"user:{i:07d}"] = f"steps={i % 9000}"
db.flush()                    # memtable -> SSTable on disk
print(db["user:0012345"])
db.close()
# Inspect ./lsm_demo: *.sst files, a WAL (*.log) and the MANIFEST

docs.title: 4.7 Query Processing and Cost-Based Optimisation (EXPLAIN Explained)
docs.text:
SQL says what you want, not how to get it. The optimiser considers many possible plans — which indexes, which join order, which join method — and estimates the cost of each from statistics about your data, mainly how many rows each step will produce. EXPLAIN shows the plan it chose; EXPLAIN ANALYZE runs the query and shows actual row counts and times next to the estimates.

From SQL to an executed plan. Bad cardinality estimates early in the pipeline produce bad plans later.

Think of it like…

It is like a satnav choosing a route: it uses a map and traffic statistics to estimate each route's time and picks the fastest; if its traffic data is out of date, it confidently sends you into a jam.

Real-world example

At the fictional Harbourview Hotels, a booking report took 40 seconds. EXPLAIN ANALYZE showed the planner estimated 12 rows from a filter that really returned 480,000, so it chose a nested loop that ran 480,000 index lookups. The columns city and country were correlated; after CREATE STATISTICS on (city, country) and ANALYZE, the estimate became 470,000, the planner switched to a hash join, and the report ran in 1.2 seconds.

docs.title: How it works
docs.text:
1. Collect statistics with ANALYZE: row counts, null fractions, distinct values, most-common values and histograms per column.
  2. Estimate selectivity of each filter and the cardinality (row count) of each intermediate result.
  3. Enumerate plans: access paths for each table, join orders and join algorithms, pruning expensive options.
  4. Cost each plan using a model of page reads and CPU work, then choose the cheapest.
  5. Use EXPLAIN (ANALYZE, BUFFERS) to compare estimated and actual rows; large mismatches point to stale or missing statistics.

Who uses it

Backend developers fixing slow queries, DBAs and performance engineers, and data engineers tuning warehouse SQL.

Key takeaway

When reading a plan, compare estimated rows with actual rows at each node: the first big mismatch, read bottom-up, is usually the cause of a bad plan.

Going deeper

  • Selinger and colleagues' 1979 System R paper introduced cost-based optimisation with dynamic programming over join orders; most optimisers still follow its bottom-up design or the Volcano/Cascades top-down framework used by SQL Server.
  • The number of join orders grows factorially, so PostgreSQL searches exhaustively only up to geqo_threshold (12 FROM items by default) and switches to a genetic algorithm beyond that.
  • PostgreSQL's ANALYZE samples 300 × default_statistics_target rows (30,000 by default) and keeps up to 100 most-common values and histogram buckets per column; raising the target helps skewed columns.
  • Optimisers assume columns are independent unless told otherwise, so correlated filters (city and country) multiply selectivities and underestimate rows; extended statistics (PostgreSQL 10+) fix this.
  • Leis et al.'s 2015 VLDB study "How Good Are Query Optimizers, Really?" found cardinality estimation errors, often by orders of magnitude, matter far more than the cost model itself.
  • PostgreSQL's cost units are arbitrary: seq_page_cost = 1.0 and random_page_cost = 4.0 by default; on SSDs many DBAs lower random_page_cost to about 1.1 so index scans are costed realistically.

Common mistakes & misconceptions

  • Running EXPLAIN ANALYZE on a DELETE or UPDATE in production: it actually executes the statement; wrap it in BEGIN ... ROLLBACK.
  • Reading costs as milliseconds: costs are abstract units for comparing plans, not times; use ANALYZE timings for real durations.
  • Fixing plans with hints before checking statistics: stale or missing statistics cause most bad plans, and ANALYZE is the first fix.

docs.title: Try it: Read an execution plan in PostgreSQL
docs.text:
EXPLAIN (ANALYZE, BUFFERS, FORMAT TEXT)
SELECT b.booking_id, h.name
FROM booking b JOIN hotel h ON h.hotel_id = b.hotel_id
WHERE h.city = 'Lisbon' AND b.check_in >= DATE '2026-10-01';

-- inspect the statistics the planner uses
SELECT attname, n_distinct, most_common_vals, histogram_bounds
FROM pg_stats WHERE tablename = 'hotel' AND attname = 'city';

-- teach it about correlated columns
CREATE STATISTICS hotel_city_country (dependencies) ON city, country FROM hotel;
ANALYZE hotel;

docs.title: 4.8 Join Algorithms: Nested Loop, Hash and Sort-Merge
docs.text:
A join combines rows from two tables that match on some condition. Databases have three main ways to do it. A nested loop checks each outer row against the inner table (fast when one side is tiny or indexed). A hash join builds a hash table from the smaller input and probes it with the larger one (best for big equality joins). A sort-merge join sorts both inputs and walks them together (good when inputs are already sorted).

Choosing a join algorithm

Nested loop Hash join Sort-merge join Best when Outer tiny, inner indexed Large inputs, equality Inputs already sorted Join conditions Any (=, <, LIKE ...) Equality only Equality (and some ranges) Memory Minimal Hash table of smaller side Sort buffers Rough cost M × index probe M + N Sort + M + N First row returned Immediately After build phase After sorting

No method always wins; sizes, indexes, order and memory decide.

Think of it like…

Matching guests to name badges: you can search the whole badge table for each guest (nested loop), sort badges into pigeonholes by surname first (hash join), or line up both guests and badges alphabetically and walk down both lines together (merge join).

Real-world example

The fictional StreamBox video service joins 2 billion play events with 40 million accounts. For one user's history, the planner uses a nested loop: an index lookup per play row. For a monthly revenue report on all plays, it uses a hash join, building a 2.5 GB hash table on accounts and streaming plays through it. When both sides come from indexes sorted by account_id, it picks a merge join with no extra memory.

docs.title: How it works
docs.text:
1. Nested loop: for each row of the outer input, scan or index-probe the inner input for matches.
  2. Hash join (build): read the smaller input and insert each row into an in-memory hash table keyed on the join column.
  3. Hash join (probe): stream the larger input, hash each join key and look up matches; spill partitions to disk if memory runs out.
  4. Sort-merge join: sort both inputs on the join key (or use existing order), then advance two cursors, emitting matches.
  5. The optimiser picks a method per join from estimated sizes, available indexes, sort orders and memory limits such as work_mem.

Who uses it

Anyone reading query plans — backend developers, DBAs, data engineers — and students in database-systems courses, where join costs are classic exam questions.

Key takeaway

Remember the costs: nested loop O(M × N) without an index, hash join about O(M + N) for equality joins, sort-merge O(M log M + N log N) unless inputs are pre-sorted.

Going deeper

  • Block nested loop reads the outer input in chunks to cut inner scans; MySQL replaced its block nested loop with hash join in 8.0.20, after adding hash join in 8.0.18 (2019).
  • When the build side exceeds memory (work_mem in PostgreSQL, multiplied by hash_mem_multiplier), the hash join partitions both inputs to disk in batches — the Grace hash join technique from the 1980s.
  • Semi-joins (EXISTS, IN) stop at the first match and anti-joins (NOT EXISTS) emit rows with no match; optimisers implement both with variants of the same three algorithms.
  • PostgreSQL 14 added a Memoize node that caches inner-side results of a parameterised nested loop, making repeated lookups of the same key nearly free.
  • SQL Server 2017 introduced adaptive joins that choose between hash join and nested loop at run time once the actual row count of the build input is known.
  • Distributed engines add strategies such as broadcast joins (copy the small table to every node) and shuffle joins (repartition both sides by join key), which dominate cost in Spark and cloud warehouses.

Common mistakes & misconceptions

  • Blaming nested loops in general: they are ideal for small, indexed lookups; the problem is a nested loop chosen because of a bad row estimate.
  • Starving hash joins of memory: a too-small work_mem makes them spill to disk in many batches; check EXPLAIN ANALYZE for Batches > 1.
  • Joining on mismatched types: comparing int to text or applying functions to join keys blocks index use and hash join efficiency.

docs.title: Try it: Make PostgreSQL show each join method
docs.text:
CREATE TABLE a AS SELECT g AS id, g % 1000 AS k FROM generate_series(1,200000) g;
CREATE TABLE b AS SELECT g AS k, md5(g::text) AS v FROM generate_series(1,1000) g;
ANALYZE a; ANALYZE b;
EXPLAIN SELECT * FROM a JOIN b USING (k);          -- likely Hash Join
SET enable_hashjoin = off;
EXPLAIN SELECT * FROM a JOIN b USING (k);          -- Merge Join
SET enable_mergejoin = off;
EXPLAIN SELECT * FROM a JOIN b USING (k);          -- Nested Loop
RESET ALL;

docs.title: 4.9 Locking, Two-Phase Locking and Deadlocks
docs.text:
When many transactions run at once, the database must stop them corrupting each other's work. Locking is the classic approach: a transaction takes shared locks to read and exclusive locks to write, and others wait. Two-phase locking (2PL) — acquire locks, then release them only at the end — guarantees transactions behave as if run one after another. The price is waiting and, occasionally, deadlocks.

A deadlock between two transfers. Each transaction holds what the other needs; the detector breaks the cycle by aborting one.

Think of it like…

Locks are like booking meeting rooms: many people can look through a window at once (shared), only one team can use the room (exclusive), and if two teams each hold one room while waiting for the other's, nobody moves until someone gives up — a deadlock.

Real-world example

At the fictional Brightwater Bank, transfer A moves £50 from account 1 to 2 while transfer B moves £20 from 2 to 1. A locks account 1, B locks account 2, then each waits for the other's lock. After PostgreSQL's 1-second deadlock_timeout, the deadlock detector finds the cycle and aborts B, which the app retries. The team then updates accounts in ascending ID order, and deadlocks stop.

docs.title: How it works
docs.text:
1. Before reading, a transaction requests a shared (S) lock; before writing, an exclusive (X) lock on the row, page or table.
  2. The lock manager grants the lock if compatible with locks others hold; otherwise the request waits in a queue.
  3. Growing phase: the transaction keeps acquiring locks; under strict 2PL it releases none until it commits or aborts.
  4. If a wait-for cycle forms, the deadlock detector picks a victim transaction and aborts it, releasing its locks.
  5. On commit or rollback, all locks are released and waiting transactions are woken up.

Who uses it

Backend developers writing concurrent code, DBAs investigating blocking and deadlocks, and students studying concurrency control.

Key takeaway

To avoid deadlocks, always lock resources in a consistent order and keep transactions short; and always be ready to retry a transaction aborted as a deadlock victim.

Going deeper

  • Two-phase locking was proved to guarantee conflict-serializable schedules by Eswaran, Gray, Lorie and Traiger at IBM in 1976; strict 2PL, holding write locks to commit, also prevents cascading aborts.
  • Multiple-granularity locking adds intention locks (IS, IX, SIX) on tables and pages so a transaction can lock a whole table without checking every row lock inside it.
  • Deadlocks are detected by finding cycles in a wait-for graph; PostgreSQL checks after deadlock_timeout (1 s by default), InnoDB detects immediately by default, and SQL Server's lock monitor runs about every 5 seconds.
  • SQL Server escalates many row or page locks to a single table lock when one statement holds roughly 5,000 locks on an object, saving memory but increasing blocking.
  • Latches are not locks: they are short, lightweight mutexes protecting in-memory structures such as pages for microseconds, are never held across user think time and are not covered by deadlock detection.
  • InnoDB uses next-key locks (a record lock plus the gap before it) under REPEATABLE READ so other transactions cannot insert phantom rows into a scanned range.

Common mistakes & misconceptions

  • Holding a transaction open while waiting for a user or network call: locks stay held and everyone else queues behind them.
  • Treating deadlock errors as bugs to hide: they are expected under concurrency; detect the error code and retry the whole transaction.
  • Running long ALTER TABLE or reports during peak hours: one big lock can queue every later query behind it.

docs.title: Try it: Reproduce a deadlock with two psql sessions
docs.text:
-- setup
CREATE TABLE acct (id int PRIMARY KEY, bal int);
INSERT INTO acct VALUES (1, 100), (2, 100);

-- session A                         -- session B
BEGIN;                               BEGIN;
UPDATE acct SET bal=bal-50 WHERE id=1;
                                     UPDATE acct SET bal=bal-20 WHERE id=2;
UPDATE acct SET bal=bal+50 WHERE id=2;   -- waits
                                     UPDATE acct SET bal=bal+20 WHERE id=1;
-- ERROR: deadlock detected (one session is aborted)

-- who blocks whom?
SELECT pid, pg_blocking_pids(pid), wait_event_type, query FROM pg_stat_activity;

Two reports read a row under S locks together; an UPDATE needs an X lock and waits until they finish. Lock compatibility matrixConcurrency control · Concept · Current · Intermediate · General A table defining which lock modes can be held together on the same object by different transactions. S is compatible with S and IS; X conflicts with everything, including another X. Two-phase locking (2PL)Eswaran, Gray, Lorie and Traiger, IBM (1976) · Algorithm · Current · Intermediate · General Transactions acquire locks in a growing phase and release them in a shrinking phase, never acquiring after releasing. Under 2PL, a transfer cannot release its lock on account 1 and later lock account 2. Most lock-based engines, including SQL Server's default locking mode, keep write locks until commit. Lock granularityConcurrency control · Concept · Current · Intermediate · General The size of what is locked — row, page, partition or table — trading concurrency against lock-management overhead. Row locks let 500 users update different orders at once; a table lock would serialise them. Intention locksMultiple-granularity locking (Gray et al.) · Concept · Current · Advanced · Relational Table- or page-level markers (IS, IX, SIX) announcing that finer-grained locks are held inside. An UPDATE takes IX on the table and X on one row, so a LOCK TABLE request sees the conflict instantly. Lock escalationSQL Server, Db2 · Feature · Current · Advanced · Relational Converting many fine-grained locks into one coarser lock to save memory, at the cost of concurrency. A DELETE touching 20,000 rows escalates to a table lock, blocking all other writers on that table. DeadlockConcurrency control · Concept · Current · Beginner · General A cycle of transactions each waiting for a lock another holds, so none can proceed without intervention. Transfer A holds account 1 and wants 2; transfer B holds 2 and wants 1. Wait-for graphDeadlock detection · Data structure · Current · Advanced · General Graph with an edge from each waiting transaction to the one it waits on; a cycle means deadlock. The detector finds A → B → A and aborts the transaction that has done the least work. Lock timeoutPostgreSQL lock_timeout; InnoDB innodb_lock_wait_timeout · Feature · Current · Intermediate · Relational Maximum time a statement waits for a lock before failing, preventing indefinite queues. InnoDB's default innodb_lock_wait_timeout is 50 seconds; migrations often set PostgreSQL lock_timeout = '3s'. SKIP LOCKEDPostgreSQL 9.5+, MySQL 8.0, Oracle · Feature · Current · Intermediate · Relational Option that skips rows already locked by others instead of waiting, ideal for job queues. Ten workers run SELECT ... FOR UPDATE SKIP LOCKED LIMIT 1 and each grabs a different queued job. Advisory locksPostgreSQL · Feature · Current · Advanced · Relational Application-defined locks on arbitrary numbers, managed by the database but not tied to any table row. pg_try_advisory_lock(42) ensures only one instance of a nightly job runs across the cluster. Next-key (gap) locksMySQL InnoDB · Feature · Current · Advanced · Relational Locks on an index record plus the gap before it, preventing inserts into scanned ranges under REPEATABLE READ. SELECT ... WHERE price BETWEEN 10 AND 20 FOR UPDATE blocks inserting a £15 product until commit. LatchDBMS internals · Concept · Current · Advanced · General Very short-lived lock protecting an in-memory structure such as a page or hash bucket during one operation. A backend holds a buffer content latch for microseconds while adding a tuple to a page.

docs.title: 4.10 MVCC, Snapshot Isolation and Serializable Snapshot Isolation
docs.text:
Multi-version concurrency control (MVCC) keeps several versions of each row so readers never wait for writers and writers never wait for readers. Each transaction sees a consistent snapshot of the data as of a moment in time. Snapshot isolation builds on this, and serializable snapshot isolation (SSI) adds checks that abort transactions whose combination could produce a result no serial order could.

Two snapshots of the same row. Each transaction sees the version that was committed when its snapshot was taken.

Think of it like…

MVCC is like a shared document with version history: while you read Tuesday's version, a colleague edits and saves Wednesday's; you are not blocked, and you keep seeing a consistent Tuesday until you reopen it.

Real-world example

At the fictional Lumen Analytics, a 20-minute finance report runs while 2,000 orders per minute are inserted and updated. Under MVCC the report reads the snapshot taken when it started, so totals are consistent and no writer is blocked. Meanwhile each UPDATE in PostgreSQL creates a new row version; autovacuum later removes old versions once no snapshot can still see them.

docs.title: How it works
docs.text:
1. Each transaction gets an ID; each row version records which transaction created it and which (if any) deleted or replaced it.
  2. At snapshot time, the database notes which transactions had committed; only their versions are visible to this snapshot.
  3. An update writes a new version (PostgreSQL appends a new tuple; InnoDB and Oracle update in place and keep the old version in undo).
  4. If two concurrent transactions update the same row, the later one waits and then aborts (first-updater-wins) under snapshot isolation.
  5. Garbage collection (VACUUM, InnoDB purge, Oracle undo expiry) removes versions no active snapshot can see.

Who uses it

DBAs managing vacuum and undo, backend developers reasoning about concurrent behaviour, and engineers of distributed SQL databases.

Key takeaway

Know the slogan "readers don't block writers and writers don't block readers" and that MVCC needs garbage collection — long-running transactions stop it and cause bloat.

Going deeper

  • PostgreSQL stores 32-bit transaction IDs in xmin and xmax; because they wrap around after about 4 billion, VACUUM must freeze old rows, and autovacuum forces this at autovacuum_freeze_max_age (200 million by default).
  • InnoDB and Oracle keep only the newest version in the table and reconstruct older ones from undo logs; a long query that needs purged undo fails in Oracle with ORA-01555 "snapshot too old".
  • SQL Server is lock-based by default but offers row versioning through READ_COMMITTED_SNAPSHOT and SNAPSHOT isolation, keeping versions in tempdb or, with Accelerated Database Recovery, in the user database.
  • Berenson et al.'s 1995 paper "A Critique of ANSI SQL Isolation Levels" defined snapshot isolation and showed it still allows write skew, so it is not fully serializable.
  • Serializable snapshot isolation (Cahill, Röhm and Fekete, 2008) tracks read-write dependencies and aborts a transaction when a dangerous structure appears; PostgreSQL implemented it in version 9.1 (2011).
  • Distributed databases such as CockroachDB, Spanner and YugabyteDB use MVCC with timestamps from hybrid logical clocks or TrueTime, so snapshots stay consistent across many nodes.

Common mistakes & misconceptions

  • Leaving transactions idle for hours: old snapshots block vacuum and purge, so tables bloat and undo or WAL grows; set idle_in_transaction_session_timeout.
  • Believing snapshot isolation is serializable: Oracle's SERIALIZABLE and PostgreSQL's REPEATABLE READ are snapshot isolation and allow write skew.
  • Ignoring serialization failures: under SSI, transactions may abort with SQLSTATE 40001 and must be retried by the application.

docs.title: Try it: Watch row versions and snapshots in PostgreSQL
docs.text:
CREATE TABLE item (id int PRIMARY KEY, qty int);
INSERT INTO item VALUES (1, 10);
SELECT xmin, xmax, ctid, * FROM item;        -- creating txn, version address
UPDATE item SET qty = 9 WHERE id = 1;
SELECT xmin, xmax, ctid, * FROM item;        -- new xmin, new ctid

SELECT pg_current_xact_id(), pg_current_snapshot();
-- dead versions waiting for vacuum
SELECT n_live_tup, n_dead_tup FROM pg_stat_user_tables WHERE relname = 'item';

PostgreSQL, Oracle, InnoDB, CockroachDB and SQL Server's snapshot modes all use MVCC. SnapshotMVCC · Concept · Current · Intermediate · General The set of committed transactions visible to a statement or transaction, fixed when the snapshot is taken. pg_current_snapshot() returns 812:815:813, meaning transaction 813 was still running and is invisible. A row with xmin = 900 and xmax = 0 is live; after an UPDATE by 950 its xmax becomes 950. Purge lag after a big DELETE makes the History list length climb into the millions. A database with autovacuum disabled for months nears wraparound and refuses writes until VACUUM FREEZE runs. Snapshot isolation (SI)Berenson et al. (1995) · Concept · Current · Intermediate · General Each transaction reads from one snapshot and commits only if no concurrent transaction wrote the same rows. Two clerks editing different fields of the same customer: the second commit fails and must retry. First-updater-winsSnapshot isolation · Concept · Current · Advanced · Relational When two concurrent transactions update the same row, the second waits, then aborts if the first commits. PostgreSQL REPEATABLE READ raises "could not serialize access due to concurrent update". Serializable snapshot isolation (SSI)Cahill, Röhm and Fekete (2008); PostgreSQL 9.1 · Algorithm · Current · Advanced · Relational Adds tracking of read-write conflicts to snapshot isolation and aborts transactions that could break serializability. Two doctors going off call simultaneously under SERIALIZABLE: one commit fails with SQLSTATE 40001. Read view (InnoDB)MySQL InnoDB · Concept · Current · Advanced · Relational InnoDB's snapshot structure listing active transactions, used to decide which row versions a consistent read sees. Under REPEATABLE READ the read view is created at the first read and reused for the whole transaction. Read committed snapshot (RCSI)Microsoft SQL Server · Feature · Current · Intermediate · Relational Database option making READ COMMITTED use row versions instead of shared locks, so readers stop blocking writers. Turning on READ_COMMITTED_SNAPSHOT ended report-versus-checkout blocking on a busy shop database. A 3-hour export fails with ORA-01555; the DBA raises UNDO_RETENTION and enlarges the undo tablespace. Hybrid logical clock (HLC)Kulkarni et al. (2014); CockroachDB, YugabyteDB · Algorithm · Current · Advanced · Relational Timestamps combining physical time and a logical counter, giving consistent MVCC ordering across distributed nodes. CockroachDB assigns each transaction an HLC timestamp so snapshot reads are consistent across ranges.

docs.title: 4.11 Isolation Levels and Anomalies
docs.text:
Isolation levels decide how much concurrent transactions can see of each other's unfinished or recent work. Weaker levels are faster but allow anomalies — odd results such as reading uncommitted data, a value changing between two reads, rows appearing in a repeated query, two updates overwriting each other, or two transactions jointly breaking a rule. SERIALIZABLE prevents them all.

Which anomalies each level allows (SQL standard minimums)

Dirty read Non-repeatable read Phantom READ UNCOMMITTED Possible Possible Possible READ COMMITTED Prevented Possible Possible REPEATABLE READ Prevented Prevented Possible SERIALIZABLE Prevented Prevented Prevented Snapshot isolation Prevented Prevented Prevented (write skew possible)

Real engines often prevent more than the standard requires — test yours.

Think of it like…

Isolation is like exam-room rules: at the weakest level you can glance at a neighbour's unfinished answers; at the strictest, everyone sits as if alone in the room, even though they are all sitting the exam at the same time.

Real-world example

The fictional St Aidan's Hospital requires at least one doctor on call. Dr Ito and Dr Mensah both check — "2 on call" — and each takes themselves off call at the same moment. Under REPEATABLE READ (snapshot isolation) both commits succeed, leaving nobody on call: write skew. Switching the transaction to SERIALIZABLE in PostgreSQL makes one fail with a serialization error; the app retries it and sees only one doctor remains.

docs.title: How it works
docs.text:
1. Choose the isolation level per transaction or session (SET TRANSACTION ISOLATION LEVEL ...).
  2. READ UNCOMMITTED allows dirty reads; READ COMMITTED sees only committed data, but each statement may see a newer state.
  3. REPEATABLE READ keeps rows you have read stable; in MVCC engines it reads one snapshot for the whole transaction.
  4. SERIALIZABLE guarantees the result equals some one-at-a-time order, using locks (2PL) or conflict detection (SSI).
  5. Pick the weakest level that is correct for each transaction, and add retries for serialization failures.

Who uses it

Backend developers building money, booking and inventory systems, DBAs, and anyone in a system-design or database interview.

Key takeaway

Know each engine's default: PostgreSQL, SQL Server and Oracle use READ COMMITTED; MySQL InnoDB uses REPEATABLE READ; SQLite is serializable.

Going deeper

  • SQL-92 defined the four levels by three phenomena — dirty read, non-repeatable read and phantom — but Berenson et al. (1995) showed the definitions were ambiguous and missed lost updates and write skew.
  • PostgreSQL treats READ UNCOMMITTED as READ COMMITTED, and its REPEATABLE READ is snapshot isolation, which also prevents phantoms; Oracle's SERIALIZABLE is likewise snapshot isolation.
  • MySQL InnoDB's REPEATABLE READ reads from a snapshot but locking reads and updates see the latest data, so read-then-write patterns can still lose updates unless you use SELECT ... FOR UPDATE.
  • Atul Adya's 1999 MIT thesis formalised isolation levels as dependency-graph cycles, the basis of modern testing tools such as Jepsen's Elle checker and Martin Kleppmann's Hermitage test suite.
  • Lost updates can be avoided at READ COMMITTED with atomic updates (SET qty = qty - 1), explicit row locks, or optimistic concurrency using a version column checked in the WHERE clause.
  • Several distributed SQL databases, including CockroachDB and Google Spanner, default to SERIALIZABLE or stronger, while most single-node engines default to weaker levels for throughput.

Common mistakes & misconceptions

  • Assuming the level name means the same thing everywhere: REPEATABLE READ differs between MySQL and PostgreSQL; check each engine's documentation and test.
  • Read-modify-write in application code at READ COMMITTED: two requests read 10, both write 9, and one sale disappears.
  • Switching everything to SERIALIZABLE without retry logic: serialization failures become user-facing errors instead of transparent retries.

docs.title: Try it: Reproduce write skew, then fix it, in PostgreSQL
docs.text:
CREATE TABLE doctor (name text PRIMARY KEY, on_call bool);
INSERT INTO doctor VALUES ('ito', true), ('mensah', true);

-- run in two sessions at once:
BEGIN ISOLATION LEVEL REPEATABLE READ;   -- then try SERIALIZABLE
SELECT count(*) FROM doctor WHERE on_call;        -- both see 2
UPDATE doctor SET on_call = false WHERE name = 'ito';   -- other session: 'mensah'
COMMIT;
-- REPEATABLE READ: both commit (0 on call!)
-- SERIALIZABLE: one fails with SQLSTATE 40001

docs.title: Key databases, concepts, languages, tools & standards
docs.text: Name What it does Example READ UNCOMMITTEDISO SQL-92 isolation level · Standard · Current · Intermediate · Relational Weakest level: may read other transactions' uncommitted changes (dirty reads). Rarely used in practice. A SQL Server report with NOLOCK hints counts an order that is later rolled back. READ COMMITTEDISO SQL-92 isolation level · Standard · Current · Beginner · Relational Each statement sees only data committed before it began; later statements may see newer data. Default in PostgreSQL, Oracle and SQL Server; two SELECTs in one transaction can return different totals. REPEATABLE READISO SQL-92 isolation level · Standard · Current · Intermediate · Relational Rows once read cannot change for the rest of the transaction; MVCC engines implement it as one snapshot. MySQL InnoDB's default level; repeating a SELECT returns the same rows even if others commit changes. SERIALIZABLEISO SQL-92 isolation level · Standard · Current · Intermediate · Relational Strongest level: the outcome equals some serial execution of the transactions, preventing all anomalies. A booking system runs seat allocation as SERIALIZABLE and retries on SQLSTATE 40001. Dirty readIsolation anomaly (SQL-92 P1) · Concept · Current · Beginner · General Reading data written by a transaction that has not committed and might roll back. Transaction B sees a £1,000 deposit that transaction A then rolls back. Non-repeatable readIsolation anomaly (SQL-92 P2) · Concept · Current · Beginner · General Reading the same row twice in one transaction and getting different values because another transaction committed in between. A price check returns £20, then £25 a second later within the same checkout transaction. Phantom readIsolation anomaly (SQL-92 P3) · Concept · Current · Intermediate · General Re-running a range query returns new or missing rows because another transaction inserted or deleted matching rows. COUNT(*) of bookings for Friday returns 41, then 42 within one transaction. Lost updateIsolation anomaly (Berenson et al., 1995) · Concept · Current · Intermediate · General Two transactions read the same value and both write back, so one update silently overwrites the other. Two clerks read stock = 10 and each writes 9 after selling one item; stock should be 8. Write skewIsolation anomaly (Berenson et al., 1995) · Concept · Current · Advanced · General Two transactions read overlapping data, update different rows, and together break a rule neither breaks alone. Both on-call doctors go off duty simultaneously, leaving the ward uncovered. Read skewIsolation anomaly · Concept · Current · Advanced · General Reading related data at different points in time, so the values are inconsistent with each other. Transferring £100 between accounts mid-report makes the report's total £100 short. Serialization failure (SQLSTATE 40001)SQL standard error class · Concept · Current · Intermediate · Relational Error raised when the database aborts a transaction to preserve isolation; the application should retry it. A Python service wraps transfers in a retry loop that catches SerializationFailure up to three times. HermitageMartin Kleppmann (open source, 2014) · Tool · Current · Advanced · Relational Test suite documenting which anomalies each database's isolation levels actually allow. Hermitage results show MySQL REPEATABLE READ permits lost updates while PostgreSQL's does not. JepsenKyle Kingsbury (Jepsen LLC) · Tool · Current · Advanced · General Testing project and tools that check distributed databases' consistency and isolation claims under faults. Jepsen analyses have found isolation bugs in many databases, which vendors then fixed.

docs.title: 4.12 Logging and Recovery: WAL, ARIES, Checkpoints and fsync
docs.text:
To survive crashes, databases follow one golden rule: write a description of every change to an append-only log on durable storage before the changed data pages themselves. This is write-ahead logging (WAL). After a crash, the database replays the log to redo committed work and undo unfinished work. Checkpoints limit how much log must be replayed.

Committing a transaction with write-ahead logging. The client hears committed only after the log is durable; data pages follow later.

Think of it like…

WAL is like a ship's logbook: every course change is written down before the crew acts on it, so after a storm you can reconstruct exactly where the ship should be, even if some charts were lost.

Real-world example

At 14:03 the fictional Polaris Payments server loses power mid-transaction. Its PostgreSQL data files hold a mix of old and new pages, but every committed payment's WAL record was flushed with fsync before the app was told "success". On restart, PostgreSQL starts from the last checkpoint at 14:00, replays 3 minutes of WAL in 9 seconds, and opens with every committed payment present and the half-finished one gone.

docs.title: How it works
docs.text:
1. Each change generates a log record with a log sequence number (LSN) describing the change, written to the in-memory log buffer.
  2. At commit, the log is flushed to durable storage (fsync); only then is the commit acknowledged to the client.
  3. Dirty data pages are written later; before a page is written, the log up to that page's LSN must already be durable.
  4. Checkpoints periodically flush dirty pages and record a starting point so recovery need not read the whole log.
  5. After a crash, recovery analyses the log, redoes changes from the checkpoint and undoes transactions that never committed.

Who uses it

DBAs configuring durability and replication, SREs planning recovery, and engineers building storage engines or replication systems.

Key takeaway

Memorise ARIES's three phases — analysis, redo, undo — and its policy names: steal (dirty pages may be written before commit) and no-force (pages need not be written at commit).

Going deeper

  • ARIES (Mohan et al., ACM TODS 1992) introduced LSNs on every page, compensation log records for undo, and repeating history during redo; it underlies Db2, SQL Server and many teaching engines.
  • PostgreSQL writes WAL in 16 MB segment files; checkpoints run every checkpoint_timeout (5 minutes by default) or when WAL reaches max_wal_size (1 GB by default), whichever comes first.
  • Torn pages — half-written 8 KB pages after power loss — are handled by full-page images in the WAL after each checkpoint in PostgreSQL and by the doublewrite buffer in InnoDB.
  • In 2018 PostgreSQL developers discovered that Linux may clear a failed fsync error, so a retry could falsely succeed ("fsyncgate"); PostgreSQL now panics and recovers from WAL instead of retrying.
  • Group commit batches the log flushes of many concurrent transactions into one fsync, letting a single SSD handle tens of thousands of commits per second.
  • The same WAL stream drives streaming replication, point-in-time recovery and change data capture, which is why wal_level settings (replica, logical) matter far beyond crash recovery.

Common mistakes & misconceptions

  • Turning off fsync for speed in production: a power cut can corrupt the whole cluster, not just lose recent data.
  • Trusting consumer SSDs or RAID caches without power-loss protection: they may acknowledge writes that are not truly durable.
  • Confusing synchronous_commit = off with fsync = off: the first risks losing the last few transactions, the second risks corrupting everything.

docs.title: Try it: Observe the WAL in PostgreSQL
docs.text:
SELECT pg_current_wal_lsn(), pg_walfile_name(pg_current_wal_lsn());
SHOW wal_level;  SHOW synchronous_commit;  SHOW checkpoint_timeout;

CREATE TABLE w (x int);
SELECT pg_current_wal_lsn() AS before \gset
INSERT INTO w SELECT generate_series(1, 100000);
SELECT pg_size_pretty(pg_wal_lsn_diff(pg_current_wal_lsn(), :'before')) AS wal_written;

SELECT * FROM pg_stat_checkpointer;   -- PostgreSQL 17+ (older: pg_stat_bgwriter)

docs.text: Name What it does Example Write-ahead logging (WAL)Database recovery · Concept · Current · Beginner · General Log every change durably before writing the changed data pages, so any crash can be repaired from the log. PostgreSQL's pg_wal directory and InnoDB's redo log files are both write-ahead logs. Log sequence number (LSN)WAL / ARIES · Concept · Current · Intermediate · General A monotonically increasing position in the log, stored on each page to show which changes it already contains. pg_current_wal_lsn() returns 3/A1B2C3D8; replicas report how far behind that position they are. Raising innodb_redo_log_capacity cut checkpoint flushing storms during a nightly bulk load. ARIESC. CMU 15-445 students implement ARIES-style logging and recovery in the BusTub teaching database. A 2 GB transaction can exceed the buffer pool because steal allows its dirty pages to be written early. CheckpointDatabase recovery · Concept · Current · Intermediate · General A point at which dirty pages are flushed and recorded, bounding how much log crash recovery must replay. PostgreSQL's checkpointer spreads writes over 90% of the interval (checkpoint_completion_target = 0.9) to avoid I/O spikes. fsyncPOSIX system call · Command · Current · Intermediate · General Forces a file's buffered data to stable storage; databases call it at commit so acknowledged data survives power loss. pg_test_fsync measures how many fsyncs per second a disk sustains, revealing slow or lying storage. Group commitPostgreSQL, InnoDB, most engines · Feature · Current · Intermediate · General Combining many transactions' commit flushes into one fsync to raise throughput. With 200 concurrent clients, one fsync durably commits dozens of transactions at once. Full-page writes / doublewrite bufferPostgreSQL; MySQL InnoDB · Feature · Current · Advanced · Relational Protection against torn pages: logging whole page images after checkpoints, or writing pages twice before placing them. After a power cut, InnoDB restores a half-written page from its doublewrite copy. synchronous_commitPostgreSQL configuration · Feature · Current · Intermediate · Relational Controls whether commit waits for WAL flush (and replicas); off trades the last moments of commits for speed without risking corruption. A click-tracking table uses SET synchronous_commit = off; payments keep the default on. WAL archiving and PITRPostgreSQL; similar in MySQL binlogs · Feature · Current · Intermediate · Relational Copying completed WAL files to safe storage so a base backup can be rolled forward to any point in time. After a bad DELETE at 11:42, the DBA restores to 11:41 using last night's backup plus archived WAL. Rollback journal vs WAL modeSQLite · Feature · Current · Intermediate · Relational SQLite's two durability modes: copying original pages to a journal, or appending changes to a -wal file. PRAGMA journal_mode = WAL lets a mobile app's readers continue while a writer commits. fsyncgate (2018)PostgreSQL community discovery · Concept · Current · Advanced · Relational The discovery that Linux could drop fsync errors, leading PostgreSQL to panic on fsync failure rather than retry. PostgreSQL releases in early 2019 changed behaviour so a failed fsync triggers crash recovery from WAL.

docs.title: 4.13 Row vs Column Storage, Vectorized Execution and Compression
docs.text:
Row stores keep all of a row's columns together, ideal for fetching or updating whole records. Column stores keep each column together, so a query that sums one column out of 100 reads about 1% of the data, and similar values compress extremely well. Analytic engines also process data in batches of thousands of values at once (vectorized execution) to use modern CPUs efficiently.

Row store vs column store

Row store Column store Layout Whole rows together Each column together Best for OLTP: point reads, updates OLAP: scans, aggregates Reading 2 of 60 columns Reads all 60 Reads only 2 Compression Modest Often 5-10× or better Single-row insert Cheap Expensive (batched instead) Examples PostgreSQL, MySQL, Oracle ClickHouse, DuckDB, Snowflake

The same data, laid out for opposite workloads.

Think of it like…

A row store is like a filing cabinet of complete customer folders; a column store is like a set of ledgers, one per field — to total everyone's spending you open only the spending ledger.

Real-world example

The fictional Orbit Telecom has a 3-billion-row call-records table with 60 columns. In its PostgreSQL row store, "average call duration by month" scans 900 GB. In a columnar copy (DuckDB on Parquet files), the query reads only duration and call_date — about 20 GB after compression — and processes 2,048 values per operator call with SIMD instructions, finishing in 4 seconds on a laptop.

docs.title: How it works
docs.text:
1. Store each column separately, in chunks (row groups or segments) of tens of thousands to a million values.
  2. Compress each chunk with encodings suited to its data: dictionary, run-length, delta, bit-packing, frame-of-reference.
  3. Keep min/max statistics (zone maps) per chunk so whole chunks can be skipped by filters.
  4. Execute operators on vectors of values at a time, using tight loops and SIMD, or compile the query into machine code.
  5. Reassemble rows only for the final result (late materialisation), touching other columns only for rows that qualify.

Who uses it

Data engineers, analytics engineers and warehouse users; engineers working on Snowflake, BigQuery, Redshift, ClickHouse, DuckDB and Spark.

Key takeaway

Rule of thumb: row stores for OLTP (many small reads and writes of whole rows), column stores for OLAP (scans and aggregates over few columns of many rows).

Going deeper

  • C-Store (Stonebraker et al., VLDB 2005), which became Vertica, and MonetDB/X100 (Boncz et al., CIDR 2005), which became VectorWise, set the template for modern column stores and vectorized execution.
  • Vectorized engines pass batches between operators — DuckDB's standard vector holds 2,048 values — amortising interpretation overhead and letting compilers emit SIMD instructions such as AVX2 and AVX-512.
  • The alternative is query compilation: HyPer (Neumann, VLDB 2011) generated LLVM code per query; PostgreSQL has offered optional LLVM JIT for expressions since version 11.
  • Lightweight encodings dominate: dictionary for repeated strings, run-length for sorted repeats, delta and frame-of-reference for timestamps and IDs; newer schemes such as FSST for strings and ALP for floating point are used in DuckDB.
  • SQL Server columnstore indexes compress row groups of up to 1,048,576 rows into segments, and Oracle Database In-Memory keeps a columnar copy alongside the row store for mixed workloads.
  • Apache Arrow standardises the in-memory columnar layout so engines such as DuckDB, DataFusion, Polars and Velox can exchange data without converting it.

Common mistakes & misconceptions

  • Running OLTP on a column store: single-row inserts and updates are slow; batch writes or keep a row store for transactions.
  • SELECT * on columnar tables: it reads every column and throws away the main advantage; select only needed columns.
  • Assuming compression only saves disk: it also cuts I/O and memory bandwidth, which is usually the real speed gain.

docs.title: Try it: Feel columnar speed with DuckDB (pip install duckdb)
docs.text:
import duckdb
con = duckdb.connect()
con.sql("""
  CREATE TABLE calls AS
  SELECT range AS id,
         DATE '2026-01-01' + (range % 270)::int AS call_date,
         (random() * 600)::int AS duration_s,
         'note ' || range AS note
  FROM range(20000000)
""")
con.sql("SELECT date_trunc('month', call_date) m, avg(duration_s) FROM calls GROUP BY m ORDER BY m").show()
con.sql("PRAGMA storage_info('calls')").limit(8).show()   -- see per-column compression

docs.text: Name What it does Example Row-oriented storage (NSM)N-ary storage model · Concept · Current · Beginner · Relational Stores all columns of a row contiguously in a page; efficient for point lookups and whole-row writes. Fetching one customer's full profile reads a single 8 KB PostgreSQL page. Column-oriented storage (DSM)Decomposition storage model; C-Store (2005) · Concept · Current · Beginner · Analytical Stores each column contiguously, so queries read only the columns they use and compression improves. Summing revenue over 2 billion rows reads one compressed column instead of 60. PAX (hybrid layout)Ailamaki et al. (2001) · Concept · Current · Advanced · Analytical Groups rows into blocks but stores columns separately inside each block, mixing row and column benefits. Parquet row groups and ORC stripes follow a PAX-like design: rows grouped, columns separate inside. Vectorized executionMonetDB/X100 (2005); DuckDB, ClickHouse, Velox · Concept · Current · Intermediate · Analytical Operators process batches of values per call, reducing overhead and enabling SIMD instructions. A DuckDB filter checks 2,048 durations in one tight loop instead of 2,048 separate function calls. Query compilation (JIT)HyPer (2011); PostgreSQL 11+ LLVM JIT · Concept · Current · Advanced · General Generates machine code specialised for each query, removing interpretation overhead in hot loops. PostgreSQL enables JIT for queries whose estimated cost exceeds jit_above_cost (100,000 by default). SIMDCPU instruction sets (SSE, AVX2, AVX-512, ARM NEON) · Concept · Current · Intermediate · General Single Instruction, Multiple Data: one CPU instruction processes several values at once. An AVX-512 instruction compares sixteen 32-bit integers against a filter value in one step. Dictionary encodingColumnar compression · Algorithm · Current · Intermediate · Analytical Replaces repeated values with small integer codes plus a lookup dictionary. A country column with 200 distinct values across 1 billion rows stores 1-byte codes instead of strings. Run-length encoding (RLE)Columnar compression · Algorithm · Current · Intermediate · Analytical Stores a value once with a count of consecutive repeats; very effective on sorted columns. A sorted status column becomes ('delivered', 900 million), ('returned', 12 million). Delta and frame-of-reference encodingColumnar compression · Algorithm · Current · Advanced · Analytical Stores differences from the previous value or from a base value, so numbers need far fewer bits. Increasing timestamps one second apart compress to tiny deltas of 1, bit-packed into a few bits each. Zone maps (min/max indexes)Column stores; Oracle, Snowflake, ClickHouse, Parquet · Data structure · Current · Intermediate · Analytical Per-chunk minimum and maximum values that let scans skip chunks that cannot match a filter. WHERE call_date = '2026-09-01' skips 97% of row groups because their date ranges exclude it. Late materialisationColumn-store execution · Concept · Current · Advanced · Analytical Keeping data as separate columns through filters and joins, assembling full rows only for final results. Only the 3,000 rows passing all filters have their name and address columns fetched. Columnstore indexMicrosoft SQL Server (since 2012) · Feature · Current · Intermediate · Analytical Columnar storage for SQL Server tables, compressed in row groups of up to about one million rows. Adding a clustered columnstore index to a 2-billion-row fact table cut a report from minutes to seconds. Database In-MemoryOracle · Feature · Current · Advanced · Analytical Keeps a columnar in-memory copy of selected tables alongside the row store, maintained transactionally. An ERP system keeps OLTP on rows while analytic queries scan the in-memory column store. Apache ArrowApache Software Foundation · Format · Current · Intermediate · Analytical Standard in-memory columnar format and libraries for zero-copy data exchange between engines and languages. DuckDB returns query results to pandas or Polars as Arrow tables without copying. DuckDBDuckDB Foundation / DuckDB Labs (open source) · Database · Current · Beginner · Analytical Embedded in-process analytical database with columnar storage and vectorized execution, often called "SQLite for analytics". A data scientist queries 50 GB of Parquet files on a laptop with plain SQL in seconds.

docs.title: 4.14 How Vector Indexes Work: HNSW, IVF and Product Quantization
docs.text:
AI models turn text, images and audio into embeddings — lists of hundreds or thousands of numbers — where similar things sit close together. A vector index finds the nearest embeddings to a query quickly. Exact search compares against every vector; approximate nearest-neighbour (ANN) indexes such as HNSW graphs, IVF clusters and product quantization trade a little accuracy for huge speed-ups.

HNSW: a multi-layer graph search. Search starts sparse and coarse at the top and refines downward, like zooming into a map.

Think of it like…

Exact search is asking every person in a stadium how similar their taste is to yours; HNSW is asking a well-connected friend, who sends you to their friend with closer taste, and so on, until nobody nearer can be found.

Real-world example

The fictional DocuHelp support portal stores 12 million help-article chunks as 1,024-dimension embeddings in PostgreSQL with pgvector. Exact search takes about 4 seconds per question. An HNSW index with m = 16 and ef_search = 100 answers in 8 ms with 98% recall@10 measured on a test set. Storing vectors as halfvec halves memory, so the index fits in RAM.

docs.title: How it works
docs.text:
1. Choose an embedding model and a distance metric: cosine, inner product or Euclidean (L2).
  2. Pick an index: HNSW for high recall and low latency in memory, IVF for faster builds and lower memory, DiskANN-style for SSD-resident data.
  3. Build the index, tuning parameters (HNSW m and ef_construction; IVF number of lists).
  4. At query time, tune the search breadth (ef_search or probes) to balance recall against latency.
  5. Measure recall@k against exact search on a sample, and handle metadata filters so they do not starve results.

Who uses it

Engineers building semantic search, recommendations and retrieval-augmented generation (RAG), plus DBAs running pgvector or dedicated vector databases.

Key takeaway

Know the trade-off triangle — recall, latency and memory — and that HNSW's ef_search (query breadth) is the main knob for trading recall against speed.

Going deeper

  • HNSW (Malkov and Yashunin, first published 2016) builds a hierarchy of proximity graphs; search cost grows roughly logarithmically with data size, but the graph must largely sit in RAM for good latency.
  • pgvector's HNSW defaults are m = 16, ef_construction = 64 and hnsw.ef_search = 40; IVFFlat uses lists (clusters) and ivfflat.probes, which defaults to 1, so recall is low until probes is raised.
  • IVF (inverted file) clusters vectors with k-means and searches only the nearest few clusters; IVF-PQ in Meta's FAISS library (2017) combines it with product quantization to search billions of vectors.
  • Product quantization (Jégou, Douze and Schmid, 2011) splits each vector into sub-vectors and replaces each with a codebook ID, compressing a 768-float vector from 3 KB to tens of bytes at some accuracy cost.
  • DiskANN (Microsoft, NeurIPS 2019) uses the Vamana graph and keeps full vectors on SSD with compressed copies in RAM, serving billion-scale indexes on one machine; SQL Server 2025's vector index builds on it.
  • Filtered search is hard: applying WHERE category = 'billing' after an ANN search can return too few rows; pgvector 0.8 added iterative index scans, and some engines integrate filters into graph traversal.

Common mistakes & misconceptions

  • Assuming ANN results are exact: recall below 100% is the design trade-off; measure recall@k against brute-force search on your own data.
  • Mixing distance metrics: an index built with cosine operators will not be used for an L2 ORDER BY; match operator class and query operator.
  • Building IVF indexes on empty or tiny tables: the k-means centroids are meaningless, so build after loading representative data.

docs.title: Try it: HNSW and IVFFlat indexes with pgvector
docs.text:
CREATE EXTENSION IF NOT EXISTS vector;
CREATE TABLE chunk (id bigserial PRIMARY KEY, body text, emb vector(3));
INSERT INTO chunk (body, emb) VALUES
 ('reset password', '[0.9,0.1,0.0]'), ('change email', '[0.7,0.3,0.1]'),
 ('refund policy',  '[0.0,0.2,0.9]');

CREATE INDEX ON chunk USING hnsw (emb vector_cosine_ops) WITH (m = 16, ef_construction = 64);
-- alternative: CREATE INDEX ON chunk USING ivfflat (emb vector_cosine_ops) WITH (lists = 100);

SET hnsw.ef_search = 100;
SELECT body, emb <=> '[0.85,0.15,0.0]' AS cosine_distance
FROM chunk ORDER BY emb <=> '[0.85,0.15,0.0]' LIMIT 2;

docs.title: About this guide
docs.text: This guide is for students and self-learners. Product names, versions, standards and dates were checked for accuracy as of late 2026, but databases and data management changes quickly — confirm details with official documentation and standards bodies. Product names and trademarks belong to their owners.

docs.title: Chapter 6: NoSQL & Specialised Databases
docs.text: Relational databases are not the only option. This chapter explains why NoSQL appeared and what BASE means, then tours each family with its leading products: key-value stores (Redis, Valkey, DynamoDB, etcd, RocksDB), document databases (MongoDB and alternatives), wide-column stores (Cassandra, ScyllaDB, Bigtable), graph databases and their languages, time-series, search and vector databases. It also covers in-memory, multi-model, ledger and embedded or mobile databases, and finishes with how to choose the right model and combine several in one system.

docs.title: 6.1 Why NoSQL Appeared — and What BASE Means
docs.text:
In the 2000s, giant websites such as Google, Amazon and Facebook had more data and traffic than any single relational server could handle. They built new databases that spread data over thousands of cheap machines, dropped joins and fixed schemas, and sometimes relaxed instant consistency to stay fast and always available. Around 2009 these systems got the catch-all name 'NoSQL', later read as 'Not only SQL'. BASE describes their typical promise: basically available, soft state, eventually consistent.

ACID vs BASE in practice

ACID (classic relational) BASE (classic NoSQL) First priority Correctness of every transaction Availability and low latency After a write Everyone sees it immediately Replicas converge soon Scaling style Traditionally scale up Scale out from day one Schema Defined up front (on write) Flexible (on read) Joins Rich joins in the database Data pre-shaped, few joins Typical use Payments, inventory Feeds, carts, sensor data

These are ends of a spectrum; most modern databases let you mix both.

Think of it like…

A relational database is like a bank branch where every teller checks the central ledger before answering; a BASE system is like a chain of busy cafés that each take orders immediately and reconcile the shared stock list a few seconds later.

Real-world example

The fictional social app ChirpNet stores 2 billion posts. Its relational setup needed constant manual sharding, so it moved timelines to a wide-column store across 120 nodes. A new like might take a second to show for friends on another continent — acceptable for likes, so the team keeps payments and account balances in PostgreSQL, where every read must be exact.

docs.title: How it works
docs.text:
1. Data is grouped into 'aggregates' — a whole document, row of columns or value — that the app reads and writes as one unit.
  2. Aggregates are spread across many nodes by key (partitioning) and copied to several nodes (replication).
  3. Writes are accepted by one or a few replicas quickly and propagated to the others in the background.
  4. Readers may briefly see older data (soft state) until replicas converge (eventual consistency); many systems let you tune this per request.
  5. Applications avoid joins by storing data in the shape each query needs, accepting some duplication.

Who uses it

Backend and platform engineers, architects at web-scale companies, and anyone choosing a database for high-volume, flexible or globally distributed data meet NoSQL trade-offs.

Key takeaway

Explain NoSQL as a family of data models (key-value, document, wide-column, graph) chosen for scale, flexibility or access patterns — not as 'no SQL at all'; many NoSQL databases now offer SQL-like languages and ACID transactions.

Going deeper

  • The modern 'NoSQL' label dates from a June 2009 San Francisco meetup about open-source distributed non-relational databases; the hashtag stuck and was later reinterpreted as 'Not only SQL'.
  • Two papers shaped the field: Google's Bigtable (OSDI 2006) introduced the sparse wide-column model, and Amazon's Dynamo (SOSP 2007) showed consistent hashing, quorum replication and eventual consistency in production.
  • BASE was popularised by Dan Pritchett's 2008 ACM Queue article 'BASE: An ACID Alternative', which described trading immediate consistency for availability and partition tolerance at eBay scale.
  • The lines have blurred: MongoDB added multi-document ACID transactions in 4.0 (2018) and DynamoDB added transactions the same year, while PostgreSQL, MySQL and SQL Server gained strong JSON support.
  • NoSQL designs move work into the application: you model data around known queries, duplicate data instead of joining, and handle conflicts or stale reads deliberately.
  • Many NoSQL systems expose tunable consistency — for example Cassandra's ONE, QUORUM and ALL levels or DynamoDB's strongly consistent reads — so each request picks its own trade-off.

Common mistakes & misconceptions

  • Believing NoSQL means 'no schema': the schema still exists in your code and queries; changing it later still needs migrations or careful versioning.
  • Choosing NoSQL for scale you do not have: one PostgreSQL server handles many thousands of transactions per second, far beyond most new apps.
  • Assuming every NoSQL database is eventually consistent: many (MongoDB primaries, HBase, etcd, FoundationDB) are strongly consistent by default.

docs.title: Try it: Feel eventual consistency vs strong consistency (DynamoDB Local or AWS CLI)
docs.text:
# eventually consistent read (default, half the cost)
aws dynamodb get-item --table-name Posts --key '{"id":{"S":"p1"}}'

# strongly consistent read of the same item
aws dynamodb get-item --table-name Posts --key '{"id":{"S":"p1"}}' --consistent-read

docs.title: 6.2 Redis, Valkey, Memcached and the Licence Split
docs.text:
Redis is an in-memory key-value store that answers in well under a millisecond, used for caching, sessions, leaderboards, queues and rate limits. Unlike a simple cache it understands data structures such as lists, hashes, sets and sorted sets. In 2024 Redis changed to non-open-source licences, and the community forked it as Valkey under the Linux Foundation; in 2025 Redis added the open-source AGPL option back. Memcached is the older, simpler pure cache.

Redis and Valkey: a licence story. Licence changes split one community into two compatible projects.

Think of it like…

Redis is like a chef's countertop: small compared with the pantry (your main database), but everything on it is within arm's reach, already sorted into bowls, trays and stacks.

Real-world example

The fictional game studio PixelForge keeps its global leaderboard in a sorted set: ZADD after each match and ZREVRANGE to show the top 100 — 50,000 updates a second on one node. Player sessions live in hashes with a 30-minute expiry. When its cloud provider offered Valkey at a lower price, PixelForge switched without changing a line of code.

docs.title: How it works
docs.text:
1. Clients send commands over the simple text-based RESP protocol to port 6379.
  2. A main thread executes commands one at a time on data held in RAM, so each command is atomic; extra I/O threads handle networking.
  3. Keys can expire automatically (TTL), and an eviction policy such as allkeys-lru removes keys when memory fills.
  4. Optional persistence saves RDB snapshots and/or an append-only file (AOF) so data survives restarts.
  5. Replicas, Sentinel (automatic failover) or Cluster mode (16,384 hash slots across shards) add availability and scale.

Who uses it

Backend developers, SREs and cloud engineers use Redis or Valkey in almost every web stack; it appears in system-design interviews for caching, rate limiting and leaderboards.

Key takeaway

Know the licence timeline: BSD until 7.2; RSALv2/SSPL from 7.4 (March 2024); Valkey fork (March 2024, BSD); Redis 8 adds AGPLv3 as an option (May 2025).

Going deeper

  • A single Redis or Valkey node commonly serves hundreds of thousands of simple operations per second with sub-millisecond latency; the limit is usually network and memory, not CPU.
  • Cluster mode splits keys into 16,384 hash slots by CRC16 of the key; hash tags such as {user42} force related keys into the same slot so multi-key commands work.
  • Persistence options: RDB point-in-time snapshots (compact, may lose minutes of writes) and AOF with appendfsync everysec (lose at most about one second); many caches disable both.
  • Redis 8 folded the former Redis Stack modules — JSON, the Redis Query Engine with vector search, time series and probabilistic structures — into the core, and added a vector set data type.
  • Valkey is backed by AWS, Google Cloud, Oracle, Ericsson, Snap and others; AWS ElastiCache and MemoryDB, and Google Memorystore, offer Valkey at lower prices than their Redis-branded options.
  • Memcached (2003, written for LiveJournal) is multithreaded, stores only strings with a default maximum item size of 1 MB, and has no persistence or replication — simple and very fast for pure caching.

Common mistakes & misconceptions

  • Using Redis as the only copy of important data without persistence and replication: a restart can wipe everything.
  • Running KEYS * in production: it blocks the single command thread while scanning every key; use SCAN instead.
  • Forgetting maxmemory and an eviction policy: the server can run out of RAM or start rejecting writes.

docs.title: Try it: Run Valkey (or Redis) locally and build a leaderboard
docs.text:
docker run -d --name kv -p 6379:6379 valkey/valkey:latest
docker exec -it kv valkey-cli

ZADD leaderboard 3200 ana 2950 ben 4100 chen
ZREVRANGE leaderboard 0 2 WITHSCORES
SET session:ana '{"cart":3}' EX 1800
TTL session:ana

docs.title: 6.3 DynamoDB, etcd, FoundationDB and Other Key-Value Stores
docs.text:
A key-value store keeps data as pairs: a unique key and the value stored under it, like a giant dictionary. Some are huge cloud services (Amazon DynamoDB), some are small, strongly consistent stores for configuration (etcd, ZooKeeper), and some are storage engines that other databases are built on (RocksDB, LevelDB). Simplicity makes them fast and easy to scale, but you can only look things up the ways you planned for.

How DynamoDB serves a request. The partition key's hash picks a partition; each partition lives on three storage nodes in different zones.

Think of it like…

A key-value store is like a coat check: hand over ticket 417 and you get exactly that coat back instantly — but you cannot ask the attendant for 'all the blue coats'.

Real-world example

The fictional food-delivery app DashBite stores orders in DynamoDB with partition key customer_id and sort key order_time, so 'this customer's last ten orders' is one fast query. On a Friday evening traffic jumps from 2,000 to 40,000 requests per second; on-demand capacity absorbs it with single-digit-millisecond reads. Meanwhile, DashBite's Kubernetes clusters keep all their own configuration in etcd.

docs.title: How it works
docs.text:
1. Every item is addressed by a key; the store hashes or orders the key to find the partition or node that owns it.
  2. Distributed stores replicate each partition (DynamoDB keeps three copies across Availability Zones; etcd uses Raft across 3 or 5 members).
  3. Reads and writes by key are fast; range queries work only where keys are ordered (DynamoDB sort keys, RocksDB, FoundationDB).
  4. Secondary indexes or extra tables support other access patterns, at the cost of extra writes.
  5. Embedded engines such as RocksDB run inside another program and store data on local disk using LSM-trees.

Who uses it

Serverless and cloud developers (DynamoDB), Kubernetes and platform engineers (etcd), database builders (RocksDB, FoundationDB) and ad-tech or fraud teams (Aerospike) rely on key-value stores.

Key takeaway

For DynamoDB, memorise: partition key (+ optional sort key), 400 KB maximum item size, RCUs/WCUs or on-demand billing, GSIs for extra access patterns, and Streams for change events.

Going deeper

  • DynamoDB (2012) descends from ideas in the Dynamo paper but uses leader-based Multi-Paxos per partition; each partition handles up to 3,000 read units and 1,000 write units per second and about 10 GB.
  • One RCU is one strongly consistent read per second of up to 4 KB (or two eventually consistent reads); one WCU is one write per second of up to 1 KB; on-demand pricing was cut by about half in late 2024.
  • DynamoDB transactions cover up to 100 items; global tables replicate across Regions, and a multi-Region strong consistency option was added in 2025 alongside the classic last-writer-wins mode.
  • etcd stores Kubernetes' entire cluster state; it uses Raft, keeps a default 2 GB storage quota, and should run on 3 or 5 members with fast SSDs because every write is fsynced.
  • RocksDB, Meta's 2012 fork of Google's LevelDB, is an embedded LSM-tree engine underneath MyRocks, TiKV, YugabyteDB, Kafka Streams state stores and many more systems.
  • FoundationDB, bought by Apple in 2015 and open-sourced in 2018, offers an ordered key-value store with strict serializable ACID transactions and is famous for deterministic simulation testing.

Common mistakes & misconceptions

  • Choosing a low-cardinality DynamoDB partition key (such as status or country): traffic piles onto a few partitions and gets throttled.
  • Using Scan for normal queries: it reads the whole table and costs capacity for every item; design keys or indexes for each access pattern.
  • Storing large blobs in etcd or ZooKeeper: they are for small coordination data; large values slow the whole cluster.
