docs.title: 6.4 Document Databases — MongoDB and Its Alternatives
docs.text:
A document database stores each record as a self-contained document, usually JSON-like, with nested fields and lists. Documents in the same collection can have different fields, so the structure can change as the app grows. MongoDB is the best-known document database; others include Couchbase, Google Firestore, Amazon DocumentDB and PostgreSQL's JSONB column type.

A MongoDB sharded cluster. Routers consult config servers to send each query only to shards that hold the data.

Think of it like…

A document database is like a filing cabinet of complete folders: each customer's folder holds their details, addresses and past orders together, so you grab one folder instead of visiting five different drawers.

Real-world example

Elena builds the fictional recipe site CookCircle. Each recipe is one MongoDB document with a title, a list of ingredients, steps and embedded ratings. Loading a recipe page is a single read by _id. An aggregation pipeline computes 'top 10 vegan recipes this week', and a sharded cluster spreads 40 million recipes across three shards.

docs.title: How it works
docs.text:
1. The app sends JSON-like documents; the database stores them in a binary form (BSON in MongoDB) inside collections.
  2. Every document has a unique _id; secondary indexes can cover any field, including nested fields and arrays.
  3. Queries filter, project and sort documents; aggregation pipelines chain stages such as $match, $group and $lookup.
  4. A replica set keeps copies on several nodes; one primary takes writes and elects a new primary if it fails.
  5. Sharding splits a collection by a shard key across replica sets, with routers (mongos) directing each query.

Who uses it

Full-stack and mobile developers, content and catalogue platforms, gaming and IoT companies use document databases; MongoDB skills are common in job ads for JavaScript and Python developers.

Key takeaway

The core modelling question is embed or reference: embed data read together and bounded in size; reference data that is shared, large or unbounded (and remember the 16 MB document limit).

Going deeper

  • MongoDB (2009) stores BSON documents up to 16 MB, supports multi-document ACID transactions since 4.0 (2018) and across shards since 4.2; MongoDB 8.0 (October 2024) focused on performance.
  • MongoDB moved to the Server Side Public License in October 2018, so cloud providers cannot offer it as a service without open-sourcing their stack; this led to compatible alternatives such as Amazon DocumentDB.
  • MongoDB Atlas, the company's managed cloud on AWS, Azure and Google Cloud, adds Lucene-based Atlas Search and Atlas Vector Search; MongoDB bought embedding-model company Voyage AI in 2025.
  • Replica sets elect a primary using a Raft-like protocol; write concern (for example w: 'majority') and read concern control how durable and fresh each operation is.
  • Microsoft open-sourced DocumentDB in 2025 — a MongoDB-compatible engine built as PostgreSQL extensions — and it joined the Linux Foundation; FerretDB 2.0 uses it to offer a MongoDB-compatible API on Postgres.
  • PostgreSQL's JSONB (since 9.4, 2014) stores parsed binary JSON with GIN indexing and SQL/JSON path queries, often enough when you need a few flexible fields next to relational data.

Common mistakes & misconceptions

  • Embedding unbounded arrays (every comment ever in one post document): documents grow towards 16 MB and updates slow down; reference instead.
  • Choosing a monotonically increasing shard key such as a timestamp: all inserts hit one shard; use a hashed or compound key.
  • Assuming 'MongoDB-compatible' services behave identically: DocumentDB, Cosmos DB and Firestore support different subsets of operators and features.

docs.title: 6.5 Wide-Column Stores — Cassandra 5, ScyllaDB, HBase and Bigtable
docs.text:
Wide-column databases store data in tables of rows, but each row can have many columns grouped by a partition key and sorted by clustering columns, and the data is spread across many machines. They are built for huge volumes of fast writes — billions of events, messages or sensor readings — across data centres, with no single point of failure. You design tables around the exact queries you will run.

A Cassandra write at QUORUM. With three replicas, the client succeeds after two acknowledgements; the third catches up.

Think of it like…

A wide-column store is like a postal sorting centre: every letter is routed by postcode (partition key) to one sorting bay, where it is kept in date order (clustering column), so 'all letters for postcode 1012 this week' is one quick grab.

Real-world example

The fictional smart-meter company GridPulse collects a reading every 15 minutes from 5 million homes — about 480 million rows a day. It stores them in Apache Cassandra 5 with partition key (meter_id, day) and clustering column reading_time. A six-node cluster in each of two data centres absorbs the writes, and fetching one home's day of readings is a single-partition query that takes a few milliseconds.

docs.title: How it works
docs.text:
1. Nodes form a ring; each owns token ranges, and the partition key's hash decides which nodes store a row.
  2. A client sends a write to any node, which acts as coordinator and forwards it to the replicas (often 3 per data centre).
  3. Each replica appends to a commit log and an in-memory memtable, later flushed to immutable SSTables on disk.
  4. The consistency level (ONE, QUORUM, LOCAL_QUORUM, ALL) decides how many replicas must answer before success.
  5. Background compaction merges SSTables, drops overwritten data and expired tombstones; repair keeps replicas in sync.

Who uses it

Platform and data engineers at messaging, IoT, streaming, finance and e-commerce companies run wide-column stores; Apple, Netflix and Discord are well-known large users of Cassandra or ScyllaDB.

Key takeaway

Remember 'query-first design': in Cassandra you typically create one table per query pattern, duplicating data, because there are no joins and only limited secondary indexing.

Going deeper

  • Cassandra was built at Facebook in 2008, combining Dynamo-style partitioning and replication with a Bigtable-style storage model, and became an Apache top-level project in 2010.
  • Cassandra 5.0 (September 2024) added Storage-Attached Indexes (SAI), a vector type with approximate nearest-neighbour search, trie-based memtables and SSTables, the Unified Compaction Strategy and dynamic data masking.
  • ScyllaDB rewrote Cassandra in C++ on the Seastar framework with a shard-per-core design; in late 2024 it stopped releasing an open-source edition and moved to a single source-available release.
  • Deletes write tombstones, markers that hide data until compaction removes them after gc_grace_seconds (10 days by default); millions of tombstones in one partition make reads slow or fail.
  • Google Bigtable (paper 2006, cloud service 2015) supports the HBase API and has added GoogleSQL queries; Apache HBase runs a similar model on Hadoop's HDFS with ZooKeeper coordination.
  • IBM acquired DataStax, the main commercial Cassandra company behind Astra DB, in 2025; AWS offers Amazon Keyspaces, a serverless Cassandra-compatible service.

Common mistakes & misconceptions

  • Creating huge partitions (for example all readings for a meter forever): keep partitions to tens of megabytes by adding a time bucket such as day to the key.
  • Using Cassandra like a relational database with ALLOW FILTERING everywhere: queries then scan the cluster; model tables for each query instead.
  • Skipping regular repair: replicas drift apart and deleted data can reappear ('zombie' data) after tombstones expire.

docker exec -it cass cqlsh

CREATE KEYSPACE grid WITH replication = {'class':'SimpleStrategy','replication_factor':1};
CREATE TABLE grid.readings (meter_id text, day date, ts timestamp, kwh double,
  PRIMARY KEY ((meter_id, day), ts)) WITH CLUSTERING ORDER BY (ts DESC);

docs.title: 6.6 Graph Databases and Graph Query Languages
docs.text:
A graph database stores things (nodes) and the relationships between them (edges) as first-class data. Questions like 'friends of friends', 'shortest route' or 'which accounts share a device with a known fraudster' become quick walks along edges instead of many expensive joins. There are two main styles: property graphs (Neo4j and most products) and RDF triple stores used for linked data and knowledge graphs.

A small fraud graph. Alice and Bob never transact directly, but sharing a device links Bob to a flagged card.

Think of it like…

A graph database is like a detective's pinboard with photos joined by red string: to find connections you follow the strings directly instead of re-reading every file in the cabinet.

Real-world example

Investigators at the fictional bank Westmoor use Neo4j to model customers, cards, phones and devices. A Cypher query finds every account within three hops of a confirmed fraudster that shares a device or phone number — a question that needed a 12-table SQL join and 40 seconds before, and now returns in under 100 ms. Twenty-three linked accounts are frozen the same afternoon.

docs.title: How it works
docs.text:
1. Model the domain as nodes with labels (Person, Card, Device) and relationships with types (OWNS, USES), each holding properties.
  2. Load data and create indexes on the properties used to find starting nodes, such as account number.
  3. Write a pattern query: find start nodes by index, then traverse relationships hop by hop.
  4. Use graph algorithms (shortest path, PageRank, community detection) for analytics across the whole graph.
  5. For RDF, data is stored as subject-predicate-object triples identified by URIs and queried with SPARQL.

Who uses it

Fraud and anti-money-laundering analysts, recommendation and network engineers, knowledge-graph and semantic-web specialists, and AI teams building GraphRAG use graph databases.

Key takeaway

Know the standard: ISO/IEC 39075 GQL (April 2024) is the first new ISO database query language since SQL, and it is heavily based on Cypher's pattern style.

Going deeper

  • Native graph stores like Neo4j use 'index-free adjacency': each node record points directly to its relationships, so a hop costs roughly the same whatever the total graph size.
  • GQL (ISO/IEC 39075:2024) standardises property-graph queries; SQL/PGQ (part 16 of SQL:2023) lets relational databases query tables as graphs with the same pattern syntax.
  • RDF 1.1 (2014) models facts as triples; SPARQL 1.1 (2013) queries them and supports federation across endpoints; OWL ontologies add reasoning; RDF 1.2 work adds statements about statements.
  • Neo4j moved to calendar versioning in 2025 (2025.x releases) and introduced Cypher 25, aligning Cypher with GQL; the Community Edition is GPLv3 and AuraDB is its managed cloud service.
  • Amazon Neptune supports Gremlin, openCypher and SPARQL; Neptune Analytics (2023) is an in-memory engine for graph algorithms and vector search over large graphs.
  • GraphRAG approaches build a knowledge graph from documents with an LLM, then retrieve connected entities and summaries to answer questions better than plain vector search for some tasks.

Common mistakes & misconceptions

  • Using a graph database for simple tabular data: lists of orders or invoices are better in a relational database; graphs shine when relationships are the question.
  • Unbounded variable-length traversals like -[*]-: they can explode across 'supernodes' with millions of edges; always cap hop counts.
  • Confusing property graphs and RDF: they use different models, languages and tools, so pick based on whether you need linked-data standards.

MATCH (p:Person {name:'Alice'})-[:USES]->(:Device)<-[:USES]-(other) RETURN other.name;

docs.title: 6.7 Time-Series Databases — InfluxDB 3, TimescaleDB, Prometheus, QuestDB
docs.text:
Time-series data is a stream of measurements stamped with a time: CPU usage every 10 seconds, a sensor reading every minute, a stock price every millisecond. Time-series databases are built to ingest these points very fast, compress them heavily, and answer questions like 'average per 5 minutes over the last day'. They also delete or summarise old data automatically.

The life of a time-series point. Data gets cheaper to store, and coarser, as it ages.

Think of it like…

A time-series database is like a ship's logbook: you only ever add new lines at the bottom, you read it by date ranges, and after a while old pages are summarised and archived.

Real-world example

The fictional wind-farm operator Breezeway has 300 turbines, each sending 50 sensor values every second — 15,000 points per second. InfluxDB 3 stores them as Parquet files on object storage, and engineers query 'average blade vibration per minute for turbine 112 this week' in SQL. Raw data is kept 30 days; per-minute averages are kept for ten years.

docs.title: How it works
docs.text:
1. Devices or agents send points: a measurement name, tags (such as turbine_id), field values and a timestamp.
  2. The database buffers recent points in memory and a write-ahead log, then writes them to time-partitioned chunks or files.
  3. Older chunks are compressed with delta-of-delta timestamps and XOR or columnar encodings, often 10x or more.
  4. Queries scan only the time ranges needed and aggregate into time buckets (per minute, per hour).
  5. Retention policies drop raw data after a set age, and downsampling jobs keep cheaper summaries.

Who uses it

SREs and DevOps engineers (monitoring), IoT and industrial engineers, energy and finance teams (tick data) and observability platforms all run time-series databases.

Key takeaway

Watch cardinality: the number of unique tag combinations (series), not the number of points, is what usually breaks a time-series database.

Going deeper

  • InfluxDB 3 Core (open source) and Enterprise reached general availability in April 2025; the engine is written in Rust on Apache Arrow, DataFusion and Parquet and supports SQL and InfluxQL but not InfluxDB 2's Flux language.
  • Facebook's Gorilla paper (VLDB 2015) compressed timestamps with delta-of-delta encoding and values with XOR, averaging about 1.37 bytes per point; Prometheus and many others use similar schemes.
  • Prometheus (CNCF graduated) pulls metrics over HTTP, keeps recent data in an in-memory head block with a WAL, writes two-hour blocks to disk and keeps 15 days by default; Prometheus 3.0 shipped in November 2024.
  • TimescaleDB hypertables split a table into time-based chunks and convert old chunks to compressed columnar form; the company behind it renamed itself TigerData in 2025.
  • QuestDB uses a column-oriented, time-partitioned storage model with SQL extensions such as SAMPLE BY and LATEST ON, and accepts InfluxDB line protocol for high-speed ingestion.
  • Long-term Prometheus storage at scale usually means Thanos, Grafana Mimir or VictoriaMetrics, which accept remote write and store blocks in object storage.

Common mistakes & misconceptions

  • Using unbounded values (user IDs, request IDs) as tags or labels: each creates a new series and can exhaust memory — keep them as fields or in logs.
  • Keeping raw high-frequency data forever: set retention and downsampling from day one so storage costs stay predictable.
  • Treating Prometheus as long-term storage: its local TSDB is meant for weeks, not years; use remote write to a long-term store.

docs.title: Try it: Time-bucket queries in TimescaleDB and PromQL
docs.text:
-- TimescaleDB (PostgreSQL extension)
SELECT time_bucket('5 minutes', ts) AS bucket, avg(vibration)
FROM turbine_readings WHERE turbine_id = 112 AND ts > now() - interval '1 day'
GROUP BY bucket ORDER BY bucket;

# Prometheus PromQL: per-second request rate over 5 minutes
rate(http_requests_total{job="api"}[5m])

docs.title: 6.8 Search Engines — Elasticsearch, OpenSearch, Solr, Meilisearch, Typesense
docs.text:
Search engines are databases specialised in finding the most relevant text, not just exact matches. They break text into words, normalise them (lower-case, remove endings), and build an inverted index that lists, for every word, the documents containing it. Results are ranked by relevance. Many are also used for logs and analytics, and most now combine keyword search with AI vector search.

From text to ranked results. Indexing and querying use the same analyzer so words match consistently.

Think of it like…

A search engine is like the index at the back of a textbook: instead of reading every page to find 'photosynthesis', you look it up once and jump straight to pages 12, 48 and 203 — with the most important page listed first.

Real-world example

The fictional online bookshop PageTurn has 3 million titles. A customer types 'harry poter spells'. OpenSearch's analyzer lower-cases the words, fuzzy matching fixes the typo, BM25 ranks books where 'spells' appears in the title above those mentioning it once in a review, and a vector query adds magic-themed books that never use the word. Results return in 40 ms.

docs.title: How it works
docs.text:
1. Documents are sent as JSON and passed through an analyzer: a tokenizer splits text, filters lower-case, remove stop words and stem.
  2. Each resulting term is added to an inverted index pointing to the documents (and positions) where it appears.
  3. The index is split into shards (each a Lucene index) replicated across nodes; new data becomes searchable after a refresh, about every second.
  4. A query is analysed the same way, matching documents are scored (BM25 by default) and the top results returned.
  5. Aggregations count and group results for filters and dashboards; vector fields enable semantic and hybrid search.

Who uses it

Search and relevance engineers, e-commerce and content teams, SREs and security analysts (log search and SIEM) and AI engineers building retrieval systems use search engines.

Key takeaway

Name the engine under most of them: Apache Lucene powers Elasticsearch, OpenSearch and Solr, so concepts like analyzers, segments and BM25 transfer between them.

Going deeper

  • Apache Lucene (Doug Cutting, 1999) stores immutable segments that are merged in the background; BM25 has been Lucene's default similarity since version 6 (2016) and Lucene 10 arrived in 2024.
  • Elastic changed Elasticsearch from Apache 2.0 to SSPL and the Elastic License in 2021, then added AGPLv3 as an option in 2024; Elasticsearch 9.0 (April 2025) moved to Lucene 10.
  • AWS forked Elasticsearch 7.10.2 as OpenSearch in 2021; in September 2024 the project moved to the OpenSearch Software Foundation under the Linux Foundation, and OpenSearch 3.0 shipped in 2025.
  • Near-real-time search: new documents become visible after a refresh (default about one second) creates a new searchable segment; the translog keeps them durable before that.
  • Hybrid search runs a keyword query and a vector query and merges the lists, often with Reciprocal Rank Fusion (score = sum of 1/(k + rank), commonly with k = 60).
  • Smaller engines trade features for simplicity: Meilisearch (Rust) and Typesense (C++) give typo-tolerant instant search with tiny setup, while Vespa targets large-scale ranking and recommendation.

Common mistakes & misconceptions

  • Using a search engine as the system of record: indexes can need rebuilding; keep the source of truth in a database and re-index from it.
  • Too many small shards: each has memory overhead; aim for shards of roughly 10-50 GB rather than thousands of tiny ones.
  • Ignoring analyzers per language: English stemming on German or Hindi text gives poor matches; choose language-specific analyzers.

curl 'localhost:9200/books/_search?pretty' -H 'Content-Type: application/json' \
  -d '{"query":{"match":{"title":{"query":"harry poter","fuzziness":"AUTO"}}}}'

docs.title: 6.9 Vector Databases — pgvector, Pinecone, Milvus, Weaviate, Qdrant, Chroma
docs.text:
AI models can turn text, images or audio into embeddings: lists of hundreds or thousands of numbers where similar meanings end up close together. A vector database stores these embeddings and quickly finds the nearest ones to a query, which powers semantic search, recommendations and retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) for chatbots. You can use a dedicated vector database or add vector search to a database you already run.

Dedicated vector DB or vectors in your existing DB?

Dedicated vector database Vector search in existing DB Examples Pinecone, Milvus, Qdrant, Weaviate pgvector, OpenSearch, Atlas, Oracle Extra system to run Yes No Keeping data in sync Pipeline needed Same transaction Very large scale Billions of vectors, tuned Millions to low billions Joins & SQL filters Metadata filters only Full SQL or native queries Best for Vector-heavy AI products Apps adding AI features

Most teams start on the right-hand side and move left only when needed.

Think of it like…

Embeddings place every item on a giant map of meaning; a vector database is the map's 'what's near me?' button, finding the closest cafés to where you are standing even though their names share no words with your search.

Real-world example

The fictional help-desk company SupportSphere has 200,000 support articles. Each is split into chunks and embedded into 1,024-number vectors stored in Qdrant with metadata such as product and language. When a customer asks 'my invoice shows the wrong VAT', the system embeds the question, finds the 8 nearest chunks filtered to the billing product, and an LLM writes an answer citing them — in under a second.

docs.title: How it works
docs.text:
1. An embedding model converts each item (text chunk, image) into a vector with a fixed number of dimensions, such as 768 or 1,536.
  2. Vectors are stored with an ID and metadata (source, date, permissions) in the vector store.
  3. An approximate nearest-neighbour (ANN) index such as HNSW or IVF is built so searches avoid comparing against every vector.
  4. A query is embedded with the same model, and the k closest vectors by cosine, dot-product or Euclidean distance are returned, often with metadata filters.
  5. Results feed search pages, recommendations or an LLM prompt (RAG); recall is checked against exact search to tune the index.

Who uses it

AI and ML engineers, search engineers, backend developers building chatbots and recommendation systems, and data platform teams evaluating AI infrastructure use vector databases.

Key takeaway

A strong interview answer: 'Start with vector search in the database you already have (pgvector, your search engine, your document DB); move to a dedicated vector database when scale, latency or filtering needs demand it.'

Going deeper

  • Raw float32 vectors are large: one million 1,536-dimension embeddings take about 6 GB before index overhead, so products offer scalar, binary or product quantization to shrink memory several-fold.
  • Approximate search trades accuracy for speed; recall@10 of 0.95 means 95 % of the true ten nearest neighbours were found, and parameters such as HNSW's ef_search tune that balance.
  • Filtering is hard: post-filtering after ANN can return too few results, so engines like Qdrant, Weaviate and pgvector 0.8+ (iterative scans) integrate filters into the search.
  • Mainstream databases added vectors: PostgreSQL (pgvector), MySQL HeatWave, Oracle 23ai/26ai, SQL Server 2025, MongoDB Atlas, Redis 8, Elasticsearch/OpenSearch and Cassandra 5.
  • Milvus graduated in the LF AI & Data Foundation and is offered as Zilliz Cloud; Qdrant is written in Rust; Weaviate in Go; Chroma (Apache 2.0) targets developer simplicity and offers Chroma Cloud.
  • Object-storage-based vector stores emerged for cheap, large collections: Amazon S3 Vectors (2025) stores vectors directly in S3 buckets, trading some latency for much lower cost.

Common mistakes & misconceptions

  • Mixing embeddings from different models or versions in one index: their spaces are incompatible; re-embed everything when you change models.
  • Ignoring access control: a RAG system must filter by the user's permissions, or it can leak documents they are not allowed to see.
  • Judging only by benchmark speed: real quality depends on chunking, the embedding model and filters; measure recall and answer quality on your own data.

CREATE EXTENSION IF NOT EXISTS vector;
CREATE TABLE docs (id bigserial PRIMARY KEY, body text, embedding vector(3));
INSERT INTO docs (body, embedding) VALUES ('invoice VAT', '[0.9,0.1,0.0]'), ('reset password', '[0.0,0.2,0.9]');
CREATE INDEX ON docs USING hnsw (embedding vector_cosine_ops);

docs.title: 6.10 In-Memory Databases and Data Grids
docs.text:
An in-memory database keeps its working data in RAM instead of reading it from disk, which makes reads and writes thousands of times faster. Because RAM is lost when power fails, these systems protect data with snapshots, logs and replicas. Some are full relational databases (SAP HANA, VoltDB), some are features inside bigger databases, and some are distributed 'data grids' that spread data across many servers' memory.

Why memory is fast: typical access latency. Log scale: each step down the storage hierarchy is roughly ten to a hundred times slower.

Think of it like…

Working from RAM versus disk is like cooking with ingredients already chopped on the counter instead of fetching each one from a basement storeroom — but you still keep a written recipe log in case someone knocks the counter over.

Real-world example

The fictional mobile operator TeleNova must check a caller's balance and authorise each call in under 5 milliseconds for 30 million subscribers. It runs Volt Active Data, which keeps all balances in memory across 12 nodes, logs every transaction to disk and replicates to a second site. Disk-based tests had peaked at 8,000 authorisations a second; the in-memory cluster handles over 150,000.

docs.title: How it works
docs.text:
1. All active data and indexes are loaded into RAM, often in structures designed for memory rather than disk pages.
  2. Transactions run against memory with lightweight concurrency control, sometimes on single-threaded partitions to avoid locks.
  3. For durability, changes go to a sequential command or redo log on fast disk, and periodic snapshots capture full state.
  4. Replicas on other nodes or sites take over if a node fails; after a restart, the snapshot plus log rebuild memory.
  5. Data that outgrows memory is spilled, tiered to SSD or offloaded to cheaper storage.

Who uses it

Telecom, trading, gaming, ad-tech and ERP teams (SAP HANA) use in-memory databases; Java architects use data grids such as Hazelcast and Apache Ignite.

Key takeaway

Remember 'in-memory does not mean volatile': good in-memory databases are durable through logs, snapshots and replication — the difference is where the working set lives.

Going deeper

  • SAP HANA (2010) is an in-memory, column-oriented relational database; SAP S/4HANA runs only on HANA, which makes HANA skills important for SAP consultants.
  • VoltDB grew from the H-Store research project (Michael Stonebraker and colleagues); it partitions data and runs each partition's transactions serially on one thread, avoiding locks entirely.
  • SQL Server In-Memory OLTP (project Hekaton, 2014) and the Oracle Database In-Memory option (dual row and column formats, 2014) bring in-memory techniques inside traditional databases.
  • Data grids such as Hazelcast and Apache Ignite partition key-value data across a cluster's RAM with backups on other nodes and can run computations next to the data.
  • Durability usually combines a write-ahead or command log fsynced in batches (group commit) with periodic snapshots; recovery time grows with memory size, so snapshots matter.
  • Intel's Optane persistent memory promised byte-addressable durable memory but was discontinued in 2022; CXL memory expansion is the newer route to larger memory pools.

Common mistakes & misconceptions

  • Underestimating RAM cost and growth: memory costs far more per gigabyte than SSD; plan sizing for indexes, replicas and growth headroom.
  • Turning off logging for speed in a system of record: a crash then loses data since the last snapshot.
  • Ignoring restart time: reloading hundreds of gigabytes into memory can take many minutes, so keep replicas ready to take over.

docs.title: Try it: See the memory-vs-disk gap yourself (Linux)
docs.text:
# write 1 GB to RAM-backed tmpfs vs disk and compare speed
dd if=/dev/zero of=/dev/shm/test bs=1M count=1024 conv=fdatasync
dd if=/dev/zero of=./test bs=1M count=1024 conv=fdatasync
rm /dev/shm/test ./test

docs.title: 6.11 Multi-Model Databases — Cosmos DB, ArangoDB, SurrealDB and More
docs.text:
A multi-model database supports several data models — for example documents, graphs, key-value and sometimes relational tables or vectors — in one engine with one query language or API. The aim is to avoid running and synchronising several separate databases. The trade-off is that one engine may not match the best specialist at every model.

One engine, many models. Multi-model databases expose several data models over shared storage, indexes and replication.

Think of it like…

A multi-model database is like a multi-tool: knife, screwdriver and scissors in one pocket. Handy and lighter than a toolbox, though a dedicated screwdriver may still be better for a big job.

Real-world example

The fictional travel start-up TripWeave stores user profiles as documents, a graph of cities and flight connections, and session data as key-value — all in ArangoDB. One AQL query finds users' saved destinations, then walks the flight graph for routes with at most one stop. Running one database instead of three cut their on-call load, though they later added a separate search engine for free-text hotel search.

docs.title: How it works
docs.text:
1. Data is stored once in a common internal format, often JSON documents in collections.
  2. Different models are views over that storage: edges are documents with _from and _to; key-value is lookup by key.
  3. A single query language or several APIs access the models, sometimes combining them in one query.
  4. Indexes, transactions and replication are shared across all the models.
  5. You decide which features to use and whether some workloads still need a specialist system.

Who uses it

Start-ups wanting fewer moving parts, enterprise architects consolidating systems, and Azure developers using Cosmos DB's multiple APIs encounter multi-model databases.

Key takeaway

For Cosmos DB, memorise the five consistency levels from strongest to weakest: Strong, Bounded Staleness, Session (the default), Consistent Prefix and Eventual.

Going deeper

  • Azure Cosmos DB (2017) offers several APIs — NoSQL, MongoDB, Apache Cassandra, Apache Gremlin and Table — plus a PostgreSQL option based on Citus, with turnkey multi-region replication.
  • Cosmos DB bills throughput in Request Units: a point read of a 1 KB item costs 1 RU, and writes and queries cost more; capacity can be provisioned, autoscaled or serverless.
  • ArangoDB (2011) combines documents, graphs and key-value with the AQL language; from version 3.12 (2024) it moved from Apache 2.0 to a source-available licence.
  • SurrealDB (Rust, Business Source License) combines document, graph, relational-style, time-series and vector features behind its SurrealQL language, and can run embedded, in the browser or as a cluster.
  • Fauna, a serverless multi-model document-relational database, shut down its service in May 2025 — a reminder to weigh vendor viability and keep export paths.
  • Mainstream engines have become multi-model too: PostgreSQL (JSONB, PostGIS, pgvector, Apache AGE) and Oracle's 'converged database' cover many models through extensions and built-in types.

Common mistakes & misconceptions

  • Expecting best-in-class performance for every model: benchmark your heaviest workload; a specialist may still be needed.
  • Ignoring Cosmos DB RU costs: unindexed queries or cross-partition scans can burn thousands of RUs; check the request charge of each query.
  • Overlooking licence changes: ArangoDB and SurrealDB use source-available terms — check them before embedding or reselling.

// in the web UI at http://localhost:8529, AQL:
FOR city IN cities FILTER city.name == 'Lisbon'
  FOR v, e IN 1..2 OUTBOUND city flights
    RETURN DISTINCT v.name

docs.title: 6.12 Ledger, Immutable and Versioned Databases
docs.text:
Some data must never be secretly changed: financial records, audit trails, medical consents, supply-chain events. Ledger databases make tampering detectable by chaining every change with cryptographic hashes, so altering an old record breaks the chain. Related ideas include immutable databases that only ever add facts, temporal tables that keep every past version, and 'Git for data' systems that version whole databases.

How a ledger proves nothing changed. Changing any old row changes its hash and breaks every later link.

Think of it like…

A ledger database is like a bound, numbered notebook where each page carries a fingerprint of the page before it: tear out or rewrite a page and every later fingerprint stops matching.

Real-world example

The fictional pharmacy chain MediTrust must prove to auditors that no prescription record was edited after dispensing. It stores dispensing events in SQL Server ledger tables. Every night the database digest — a single hash summarising all history — is saved to immutable cloud storage. When an auditor checks a 2025 record, the verification procedure recomputes the hashes and confirms nothing has changed.

docs.title: How it works
docs.text:
1. Each committed transaction's rows are hashed, and transactions are grouped into blocks.
  2. Each block's hash includes the previous block's hash, forming a chain (often organised as a Merkle tree).
  3. A small digest of the latest block is published or stored somewhere the database administrators cannot alter.
  4. Updates and deletes keep the old versions in history tables instead of destroying them.
  5. Verification recomputes hashes from the data and compares them with the saved digests; any mismatch reveals tampering.

Who uses it

Auditors, compliance and security engineers, fintech, healthcare and supply-chain developers, and teams needing provable history use ledger and immutable databases.

Key takeaway

Distinguish ledger databases from blockchains: a ledger database is run by one trusted organisation and makes tampering detectable; a blockchain spreads trust across many parties with consensus.

Going deeper

  • Amazon QLDB, AWS's managed ledger database launched in 2019, reached end of support on 31 July 2025; AWS pointed customers to Aurora PostgreSQL with audit and history patterns instead.
  • SQL Server 2022 and Azure SQL offer updatable and append-only ledger tables; digests can be stored automatically in immutable Azure Blob Storage or Azure Confidential Ledger.
  • Oracle offers immutable tables (insert-only) and blockchain tables (insert-only with each row chained by hash and optionally signed) in 19c release updates and later versions.
  • SQL:2011 introduced system-versioned temporal tables that keep every row version with validity periods; SQL Server, MariaDB and Db2 support them, and PostgreSQL relies on extensions or triggers.
  • Datomic stores immutable facts (datoms) and lets you query the database 'as of' any past time; its binaries became free under Apache 2.0 in 2023 under Nubank's ownership.
  • Dolt is a MySQL-compatible database with Git-style branch, diff and merge for data; immudb is an open-source database that uses Merkle trees to provide cryptographic proofs of inclusion.

Common mistakes & misconceptions

  • Thinking a ledger stops tampering: it detects tampering; you still need access control and digests stored outside the administrators' reach.
  • Forgetting privacy laws: immutable records clash with the right to erasure, so keep personal data separable (for example encrypted with deletable keys).
  • Using a blockchain when one organisation controls all the data: a ledger table or audit log is simpler, faster and cheaper.

docs.title: Try it: Create an append-only ledger table (SQL Server 2022+)
docs.text:
CREATE TABLE dbo.Dispensing (
  Id INT NOT NULL, Patient NVARCHAR(50), Drug NVARCHAR(50), At DATETIME2
) WITH (LEDGER = ON (APPEND_ONLY = ON));

INSERT INTO dbo.Dispensing VALUES (1, 'P-881', 'Amoxicillin', SYSUTCDATETIME());
EXECUTE sp_generate_database_ledger_digest;   -- save this JSON somewhere immutable

docs.title: 6.13 Embedded, Mobile and In-Browser Databases
docs.text:
Many apps keep data on the device itself so they work offline and feel instant. Phones use SQLite underneath higher-level libraries such as Android's Room and Apple's Core Data or SwiftData. Web browsers offer IndexedDB, and can now even run SQLite or Postgres compiled to WebAssembly. Sync engines then copy changes between the device and a server database when a connection is available.

Offline-first data flow. Apps read and write locally; sync moves changes to the server when a connection exists.

Think of it like…

An embedded database is like a field notebook a park ranger carries: they write observations all day without signal, then copy them to the central office records when they get back to base.

Real-world example

The fictional vet-clinic app PawChart runs on tablets in rural farms with no signal. Visits are written to a local SQLite database through Room on Android and SwiftData on iPads. When a vet drives back into coverage, a sync engine uploads new visits to the clinic's PostgreSQL and downloads updated vaccine schedules, resolving conflicts by last edit per field.

docs.title: How it works
docs.text:
1. Pick a local store: SQLite (directly or via Room, Core Data, SwiftData), an object store (ObjectBox, Realm) or, on the web, IndexedDB or SQLite-Wasm on OPFS.
  2. Define models; the library maps objects to tables or documents and handles schema migrations between app versions.
  3. The UI reads from and writes to the local database, so it works offline and responds instantly.
  4. A sync layer records changes and exchanges them with a server when online, handling conflicts.
  5. Server-side, the canonical data lives in a cloud database, with per-user permissions on what syncs.

Who uses it

Android and iOS developers, front-end and full-stack web developers, desktop and embedded/IoT engineers, and teams building offline-first or 'local-first' apps use these databases.

Key takeaway

Remember that localStorage is not a database: it is a tiny (about 5 MB), synchronous string store — use IndexedDB or SQLite-Wasm for real data in the browser.

Going deeper

  • Android ships SQLite in the OS and Google recommends the Room library (Jetpack), which checks SQL at compile time and manages migrations; Apple's Core Data (2005) and SwiftData (2023) also store data in SQLite by default.
  • MongoDB deprecated Atlas Device Sync and the Realm SDKs in September 2024 and ended them on 30 September 2025; the Realm database remains open source but apps needed new sync solutions.
  • IndexedDB is the W3C browser API for transactional, indexed storage of structured objects; quotas are usually a share of free disk space, managed per origin by the browser.
  • The Origin Private File System (OPFS) gives web apps fast private file access, which lets the official SQLite WebAssembly build and DuckDB-Wasm persist real databases inside browsers.
  • PGlite (by ElectricSQL) compiles PostgreSQL to WebAssembly in a few megabytes, so a real Postgres can run in a browser tab or Node.js process for local-first apps and tests.
  • Local-first sync engines such as ElectricSQL, PowerSync and Zero replicate subsets of a server database (often Postgres) to device storage and stream changes both ways.

Common mistakes & misconceptions

  • Shipping an app update that changes the schema without a migration: users' existing local databases fail to open or crash on start.
  • Relying on browser storage as permanent: browsers can evict data under storage pressure; request persistent storage and keep a server copy.
  • Ignoring sync conflicts: two offline edits to the same record must be resolved by clear rules or CRDTs, not silently overwritten.

docs.title: Try it: Store and read data with IndexedDB in a browser console
docs.text:
const req = indexedDB.open('pawchart', 1);
req.onupgradeneeded = () => req.result.createObjectStore('visits', { keyPath: 'id' });
req.onsuccess = () => {
  const tx = req.result.transaction('visits', 'readwrite');
  tx.objectStore('visits').put({ id: 1, pet: 'Bella', note: 'vaccinated' });
  tx.oncomplete = () => console.log('saved');
};

docs.title: 6.14 Choosing the Right Data Model — Polyglot Persistence
docs.text:
Polyglot persistence means using different databases for different jobs inside one system — for example PostgreSQL for orders, Redis for sessions, a search engine for product search and a graph for recommendations. Each piece fits its job well, but every extra database adds cost, operations work and the challenge of keeping data in sync. Good architects start simple and add specialist stores only when a clear need appears.

A typical polyglot e-commerce system. One system of record; every other store is derived from it and can be rebuilt.

Think of it like…

It is like a kitchen: you could cook everything in one big pot, or use a wok, an oven and a kettle for different dishes. More tools give better results — but also more washing up and more things that can break.

Real-world example

The fictional marketplace CraftHub began with only PostgreSQL. At 2 million products, keyword search became slow, so they added OpenSearch fed by change data capture. Then a Valkey cache cut page loads from 300 ms to 40 ms. They considered a graph database for 'people who bought this also bought', but pgvector and a nightly job in Postgres were good enough — one fewer system to run.

docs.title: How it works
docs.text:
1. List the access patterns: lookups by key, rich ad-hoc queries, full-text search, relationship traversals, time ranges, similarity.
  2. Note the requirements: consistency, latency, write volume, data size, retention and compliance.
  3. Start with one strong general-purpose database (usually relational) and measure where it struggles.
  4. Add a specialist store only for a proven need, fed from the system of record by change data capture or events.
  5. Budget for the operations: monitoring, backups, upgrades, security and on-call skills for every database you add.

Who uses it

Solution and software architects, tech leads, platform teams and system-design interview candidates make these choices.

Key takeaway

In system-design interviews, name one system of record and explain how each secondary store (cache, search, analytics) is derived from it and what happens if it is stale.

Going deeper

  • Martin Fowler popularised the term polyglot persistence around 2011, by analogy with polyglot programming; the risk he highlighted was operational complexity, not technical capability.
  • Writing to two stores from application code (the dual-write problem) leaves them inconsistent when one write fails; deriving secondary stores from the primary's log via CDC or an outbox avoids this.
  • Model-to-workload rules of thumb: key-value for lookups by ID, document for self-contained aggregates, wide-column for massive write streams, graph for multi-hop relationships, search for relevance, time-series for metrics.
  • YCSB (Yahoo! Cloud Serving Benchmark, 2010) provides standard workloads A-F for comparing key-value and NoSQL stores, while TPC-C and TPC-H remain the classic relational benchmarks.
  • Jepsen, Kyle Kingsbury's testing project, has found consistency bugs in many distributed databases by injecting network partitions and clock faults — read its reports before trusting marketing claims.
  • Vendor viability and licence risk matter: Fauna's 2025 shutdown, QLDB's retirement and licence changes at Redis, Elastic, MongoDB and others all forced customers to react.

Common mistakes & misconceptions

  • Adding a new database for every feature: each one needs backups, monitoring, upgrades, security reviews and on-call knowledge.
  • Letting the application dual-write to several stores: failures leave silent inconsistencies; derive copies from one source via CDC or an outbox.
  • Choosing on hype or benchmarks alone: test your own access patterns and failure modes, and check the vendor's track record.

docs.title: Chapter 9: Operations, Security, AI, Careers & Learning
docs.text: This final chapter is about running databases in the real world and building a career around them. It covers the DBA's job, performance tuning and monitoring, securing data and staying compliant, how applications talk to databases through ORMs, and how AI and databases now work together. It finishes with the practical side: jobs, current certifications, learning resources, hands-on labs, a 16-week study plan and interview questions with model answers.

docs.title: 9.1 The DBA's Job: Provisioning, Upgrades, Patching & Capacity
docs.text:
A database administrator (DBA) keeps an organisation's databases running, safe, fast and recoverable. Day to day that means creating new databases (provisioning), applying security fixes (patching), moving to new versions (upgrades), making sure there will be enough disk, memory and CPU next year (capacity planning) and fixing slow queries. In the cloud many chores are automated, but someone still has to decide, check and own them.

The DBA's operating loop. None of these is a one-off project: each step feeds the next, and restore tests close the loop.

Think of it like…

A DBA is like the facilities manager of a busy hospital: patients never see them, but they keep the power on, schedule repairs for 3 a.m., and make sure there are enough beds before flu season.

Real-world example

Priya is the only DBA at fictional Harbour Freight Logistics, which runs 14 PostgreSQL clusters. Each quarter she applies the latest minor release during a Sunday maintenance window after testing it on staging. In spring she noticed the orders database growing 40 GB a month on a 1 TB volume and requested more storage months before it would fill. In autumn she planned the jump from PostgreSQL 13, which lost community support in November 2025, to a current version using pg_upgrade, rehearsed first on a restored copy.

docs.title: How it works
docs.text:
1. Provision: create the instance or cluster from code (Terraform, Ansible, a Kubernetes operator) with standard settings, users, backups and monitoring built in.
  2. Patch: apply minor releases and security fixes on a regular cadence — staging first, then production in a maintenance window.
  3. Upgrade: plan major-version moves with pg_upgrade, logical replication or a blue/green switchover, rehearsed on a restored copy.
  4. Plan capacity: track growth of data, connections, CPU and I/O, and forecast when each limit will be hit.
  5. Maintain: statistics, vacuum or index maintenance, restore drills, access reviews and runbooks.
  6. Respond: be on call for incidents, then write blameless post-mortems and automate the fix.

Who uses it

DBAs, database reliability engineers, platform and cloud engineers, and backend teams that own their own managed databases.

Key takeaway

In interviews, describe the DBA job as 'availability, recoverability, security, performance and capacity' — and stress that an untested backup is not a backup.

Going deeper

  • PostgreSQL supports each major version for five years and ships minor releases at least quarterly (usually February, May, August and November); minor upgrades only swap binaries, while major upgrades need pg_upgrade, dump/restore or logical replication.
  • pg_upgrade --link can upgrade a multi-terabyte cluster in minutes by hard-linking data files instead of copying them, but the old cluster cannot safely be started afterwards — take a verified backup first.
  • Vendor lifecycles drive upgrades: MySQL 8.0 reached end of life in April 2026 (8.4 is the LTS line), SQL Server 2016 extended support ended on 14 July 2026, and Amazon RDS charges for Extended Support on expired versions.
  • Capacity planning uses trends, not snapshots: track monthly data growth, peak connections, CPU, IOPS and storage latency, forecast the date each limit is reached, and act at roughly 70-80% utilisation.
  • Managed services (RDS, Cloud SQL, Azure SQL) take over hardware, OS patching and automated backups; the customer still owns schema, queries, users, parameter choices, cost and restore testing.
  • Kubernetes operators such as CloudNativePG, Crunchy PGO and Percona's operators encode DBA tasks — failover, backups, rolling minor upgrades — as controllers that continuously reconcile a declared cluster spec.

Common mistakes & misconceptions

  • Assuming 'managed' means no DBA work: the provider patches the server, but nobody else will fix your slow queries, bad schema or untested restores.
  • Upgrading a major version without testing the application: planner changes and removed features can break queries; rehearse on a production-sized copy.
  • Treating backups as done because the job is green: only a regular, timed restore proves you can meet your recovery objectives.

docs.title: Try it: Check version, uptime and database sizes in PostgreSQL
docs.text:
SELECT version();
SELECT now() - pg_postmaster_start_time() AS uptime;
SELECT datname, pg_size_pretty(pg_database_size(datname)) AS size
FROM pg_database
ORDER BY pg_database_size(datname) DESC;

docs.title: 9.2 Performance Tuning Workflow: From Slow Query to Fix
docs.text:
Performance tuning means finding what makes a database slow and fixing the biggest cause first. You measure (which queries use the most total time?), look at how the database runs them (the execution plan), then fix with a better index, a rewritten query, a configuration change or a change in how the application calls the database. Then you measure again.

A repeatable tuning workflow. Measure before and after every change, and change one thing at a time.

Think of it like…

It is like speeding up a supermarket: first you time the queues to find the slowest till, then decide whether to open a lane (hardware), train the cashier (configuration) or stop customers paying in coins (a query rewrite).

Real-world example

At fictional Fernwood Books the product page took 2.4 seconds. pg_stat_statements showed one query consumed 38% of all database time: it filtered orders by customer_id with no index, scanning 9 million rows. Adding an index cut it from 410 ms to 0.6 ms. A second fix replaced 51 separate author lookups (an N+1 pattern) with one join, and the page dropped to 180 ms.

docs.title: How it works
docs.text:
1. Define the goal: which user action is slow, and what is the target (for example p95 under 200 ms)?
  2. Find the top offenders by total time (calls × mean time) using pg_stat_statements, the slow-query log or Query Store.
  3. Read the plan with EXPLAIN (ANALYZE, BUFFERS): look for big row-estimate errors, sequential scans of large tables and sorts spilling to disk.
  4. Apply the cheapest effective lever: index, query rewrite, application pattern (N+1, pagination), then configuration, then hardware.
  5. Verify with the same measurement under realistic load, and watch for regressions in writes or other queries.
  6. Record the change and add an alert or test so the problem cannot quietly return.

Who uses it

DBAs, backend engineers, database reliability engineers and performance engineers — tuning questions appear in nearly every database interview.

Key takeaway

Rank queries by total time (calls × average), not by the single slowest run: a 5 ms query called 2 million times an hour matters more than one 30-second report.

Going deeper

  • PostgreSQL's log_min_duration_statement logs slow statements, auto_explain adds their plans and pgBadger turns the logs into reports; MySQL's slow_query_log uses long_query_time, which defaults to 10 seconds — far too high for web applications.
  • pg_stat_statements normalises queries (constants become $1, $2) and tracks calls, time, rows and buffer hits; SQL Server's Query Store, on by default for new databases since 2022, also keeps plan history for forcing good plans.
  • Common rewrites: make predicates sargable (created_at >= '2026-01-01' instead of year(created_at) = 2026), replace large OFFSETs with keyset pagination, and select only the columns you need so covering indexes can work.
  • Memory starting points: PostgreSQL shared_buffers around 25% of RAM, with work_mem sized per sort or hash step (one query may use it several times); InnoDB's buffer pool commonly 50-75% of RAM on a dedicated server.
  • Every index speeds some reads but slows each INSERT, UPDATE and DELETE and consumes disk and cache; check pg_stat_user_indexes and drop indexes with idx_scan = 0 after a full business cycle.
  • The N+1 problem shows up as thousands of identical fast queries per request; it is invisible in slow-query logs, so look at call counts in pg_stat_statements or application traces.

Common mistakes & misconceptions

  • Tuning by guesswork: changing five settings at once makes it impossible to know what helped; measure, change one thing, measure again.
  • Testing on a tiny development database: plans differ between 1,000 rows and 50 million; use production-like volumes and fresh statistics.
  • Adding an index for every slow query: overlapping indexes slow writes and waste memory; prefer one well-designed composite index.
  • Blaming the database for application patterns: chatty N+1 calls and missing connection pooling often cost more than any single query.

docs.title: Try it: Top 5 queries by total time in PostgreSQL (needs pg_stat_statements)
docs.text:
-- postgresql.conf: shared_preload_libraries = 'pg_stat_statements'
CREATE EXTENSION IF NOT EXISTS pg_stat_statements;
SELECT calls,
       round(total_exec_time::numeric, 1) AS total_ms,
       round(mean_exec_time::numeric, 2)  AS mean_ms,
       left(query, 80) AS query
FROM pg_stat_statements
ORDER BY total_exec_time DESC
LIMIT 5;

Average latency is 40 ms but p99 is 2.1 seconds, revealing a lock wait that hits one request in a hundred.

docs.title: 9.3 Monitoring & Observability for Databases
docs.text:
Monitoring means continuously collecting numbers (metrics), messages (logs) and traces from your database so you notice problems before users do. Observability is the wider goal: having enough data to answer new questions like 'why was checkout slow at 14:03?' without shipping new code. Good database monitoring watches load, errors, latency and saturation, plus internals such as locks, replication lag and cache hit rate.

Where database telemetry comes from. No single source explains an incident; correlating them is what makes a system observable.

Think of it like…

A database dashboard is like a car's instrument panel: speed, fuel and engine temperature at a glance, with warning lights that come on before the engine seizes.

Real-world example

Tomás runs the platform team at fictional Kestrel Tickets. Prometheus scrapes postgres_exporter every 15 seconds, Grafana shows connections, transactions per second, replication lag and disk use, and an alert fires when lag exceeds 30 seconds. On a big concert's sale day the dashboard showed connections at 495 of 500 and lock waits climbing; traces linked them to a seat-reservation UPDATE that held locks too long.

docs.title: How it works
docs.text:
1. Decide what 'healthy' means: SLOs such as 99.9% of queries under 100 ms and replication lag under 10 seconds.
  2. Collect metrics from the database's statistics views (pg_stat_*, performance_schema, DMVs) with an exporter or agent.
  3. Collect logs (errors, slow queries, deadlocks, checkpoints) and, ideally, query-level samples and plans.
  4. Correlate with application traces so a slow web request links to the exact SQL statement.
  5. Alert on symptoms users feel and on fast-approaching limits (disk 85% full, connections near max), not on every blip.
  6. Review dashboards after incidents and fix alerts that were noisy or missing.

Who uses it

Site reliability engineers, DBAs, platform teams and on-call developers; monitoring is also a large vendor market (Datadog, Grafana Labs, SolarWinds, Redgate, Percona).

Key takeaway

Learn the four golden signals — latency, traffic, errors, saturation — and be ready to name a database-specific example of each.

Going deeper

  • Google's SRE book popularised the four golden signals; Brendan Gregg's USE method (utilisation, saturation, errors) suits resources such as disks and CPUs, while RED (rate, errors, duration) suits request flows.
  • Wait-event analysis asks what sessions are waiting on — CPU, I/O, locks, network. PostgreSQL exposes wait_event in pg_stat_activity, SQL Server aggregates sys.dm_os_wait_stats and Oracle samples Active Session History every second.
  • Key database metrics: active and idle-in-transaction connections, transactions per second, buffer cache hit ratio (often above 99% for OLTP), deadlocks, temporary-file spills, checkpoint frequency, replication lag, transaction-ID age and table bloat.
  • Prometheus scrapes exporters such as postgres_exporter and mysqld_exporter over HTTP, Grafana visualises the series and Alertmanager routes alerts; commercial suites (Datadog, pganalyze, SolarWinds DPA, Redgate Monitor) add query samples and plan history.
  • OpenTelemetry semantic conventions define standard attributes for database spans (database system, operation, query text), so a trace can show that a 1.8-second request spent 1.6 seconds in one SQL statement.
  • Alert fatigue is real: page humans only for urgent, actionable symptoms, and send slow-burn warnings (disk 75% full and rising) as tickets instead.

Common mistakes & misconceptions

  • Alerting on averages: a fine average CPU can hide one saturated core or a terrible p99; use percentiles and per-resource views.
  • Monitoring only the database host: watch the connection pool, application latency and replicas too — many incidents start there.
  • Logging every statement in production: full statement logging can cut throughput and fill disks; use thresholds and sampling.

docs.title: Try it: What is my PostgreSQL server doing right now?
docs.text:
SELECT pid, usename, state, wait_event_type, wait_event,
       now() - query_start AS running_for,
       left(query, 60) AS query
FROM pg_stat_activity
WHERE state <> 'idle'
ORDER BY running_for DESC NULLS LAST;

docs.title: 9.4 Database Security I: Authentication, Least Privilege, RLS & Auditing
docs.text:
Database security starts with three questions: who are you (authentication), what may you do (authorisation), and what did you do (auditing). Good practice gives every person and application its own login with only the permissions it needs (least privilege), and keeps a tamper-resistant record of sensitive actions. Row-level security goes further and filters which rows each user can see.

Defence in depth for a database. An attacker must beat every layer; a single misconfigured layer should not expose the data.

Think of it like…

It is like a hotel: the front desk checks ID (authentication), your key card opens only your room and the gym (least privilege), some floors are restricted to certain guests (row-level security), and the door system logs every swipe (auditing).

Real-world example

Fictional clinic chain MediNorth had one shared 'app' login with full rights. After an audit they created separate roles: the web app can read and write appointments but not drop tables, analysts read a masked reporting view, and DBAs log in personally with MFA through a bastion host. PostgreSQL row-level security makes each clinic's staff see only their own clinic's patients, and pgaudit logs every read of the diagnoses table.

docs.title: How it works
docs.text:
1. Shrink the attack surface: no public IP, firewall rules allowing only application subnets, TLS required.
  2. Authenticate strongly: individual accounts, SCRAM or cloud IAM/Kerberos/SSO instead of shared passwords, MFA for humans.
  3. Authorise with roles: group permissions into roles (app_read, app_write, analyst) and grant roles to users; never run applications as superuser.
  4. Restrict data inside tables with views, column privileges and row-level security policies.
  5. Audit: log logins, privilege changes, DDL and access to sensitive tables into a separate system.
  6. Review regularly: remove leavers, rotate credentials and re-check grants every quarter.

Who uses it

DBAs, security engineers, auditors, backend developers and anyone designing multi-tenant SaaS applications.

Key takeaway

A strong interview answer: 'Each application has its own least-privilege role, secrets come from a vault, humans use SSO with MFA, and access to sensitive data is audited.'

Going deeper

  • PostgreSQL has defaulted to SCRAM-SHA-256 since version 14, and PostgreSQL 18 deprecated MD5 passwords and added OAuth authentication; MySQL 8.4 disables mysql_native_password by default and MySQL 9.0 removed it in favour of caching_sha2_password.
  • Cloud identity replaces stored passwords: Amazon RDS IAM authentication issues 15-minute tokens, Azure SQL accepts Microsoft Entra ID, and Cloud SQL supports IAM database authentication — so disabling a leaver's identity removes their database access too.
  • Row-level security exists in PostgreSQL (since 9.5), SQL Server (since 2016) and Oracle (Virtual Private Database); in PostgreSQL, table owners and superusers bypass policies unless FORCE ROW LEVEL SECURITY is set and the app uses a non-owner role.
  • Audit options include pgaudit for PostgreSQL, SQL Server Audit, Oracle Unified Auditing (traditional auditing was desupported in 23ai), MySQL Enterprise Audit and the MariaDB audit plugin; ship audit logs to a SIEM that DBAs cannot edit.
  • CIS Benchmarks give free, scored hardening checklists — for example restricting superuser use, disabling unused extensions and enabling connection and DDL logging — that auditors often use as the baseline.
  • In 2024 attackers used passwords stolen by infostealer malware to access about 165 Snowflake customer accounts that lacked MFA; Snowflake then announced it would phase out single-factor password sign-ins — MFA and network policies matter for cloud data platforms too.

Common mistakes & misconceptions

  • One shared application login for everything: you lose accountability and cannot revoke one service without breaking all of them; give each service its own role.
  • Granting ALL or superuser 'to make it work': an injection bug then becomes full data theft or DROP TABLE; grant only the needed actions on the needed objects.
  • Assuming RLS restricts the table owner: owners and superusers bypass policies unless FORCE ROW LEVEL SECURITY is set and the app uses a separate role.
  • Leaving a database reachable from the internet: thousands of exposed MongoDB and Elasticsearch servers have been wiped and held to ransom; keep databases on private networks.

docs.title: Try it: Least-privilege roles and a row-level security policy in PostgreSQL
docs.text:
CREATE ROLE app_rw NOLOGIN;
GRANT SELECT, INSERT, UPDATE ON appointments TO app_rw;
CREATE ROLE web_app LOGIN PASSWORD 'change-me' IN ROLE app_rw;

ALTER TABLE appointments ENABLE ROW LEVEL SECURITY;
CREATE POLICY clinic_only ON appointments
  USING (clinic_id = current_setting('app.clinic_id')::int);

docs.title: 9.5 Database Security II: Encryption, Key Management & Secrets
docs.text:
Encryption scrambles data so that only someone with the key can read it. Databases need it in two places: in transit (between the application and the database, using TLS) and at rest (on disks, backups and snapshots). The keys must be stored separately — in a key management service — and the passwords applications use to connect (secrets) belong in a vault, not in source code.

Envelope encryption key hierarchy. Rotating a master key only re-wraps the small data keys; revoking it makes everything below unreadable.

Think of it like…

Encryption at rest is a locked safe, encryption in transit is an armoured van, and key management is the bank that keeps the safe keys in a different building.

Real-world example

Fictional fintech PayLark runs PostgreSQL on AWS. Storage and snapshots are encrypted with a customer-managed AWS KMS key, the app connects with sslmode=verify-full, and national ID numbers are encrypted in the application before they are saved. Database passwords come from AWS Secrets Manager and rotate every 30 days. When a laptop holding an old database export was stolen, the export was encrypted — so it was a non-event.

docs.title: How it works
docs.text:
1. Encrypt in transit: require TLS 1.2 or newer on the server and make clients verify the server certificate.
  2. Encrypt at rest: enable storage encryption or transparent data encryption (TDE) for data files, logs and backups.
  3. Protect the keys: keep master keys in a KMS or HSM, use envelope encryption and rotate keys on a schedule.
  4. Add field-level encryption for the most sensitive columns so DBAs, logs and backups see only ciphertext.
  5. Manage secrets: store connection credentials in a vault, inject them at runtime and rotate them automatically.
  6. Log and alert on key use, and test that encrypted backups restore with the right keys.

Who uses it

Security engineers, DBAs, cloud architects and developers in regulated industries such as payments, health and government.

Key takeaway

Remember what each layer protects against: TDE protects stolen disks and backups, not a logged-in attacker or SQL injection — the database decrypts for anyone it lets in.

Going deeper

  • PostgreSQL's sslmode=require encrypts the connection but does not check the server's identity; verify-full checks the certificate chain and host name, defeating man-in-the-middle attacks. Since PostgreSQL 12 the server's minimum protocol defaults to TLS 1.2.
  • TDE encrypts data files and logs below the SQL layer with AES: SQL Server since 2008 (Standard edition since 2019), Oracle via Advanced Security, MySQL via keyring-based InnoDB encryption; community PostgreSQL relies on disk encryption or extensions like pg_tde.
  • Envelope encryption: a data-encryption key encrypts the data and is itself encrypted by a key-encryption key held in a cloud KMS or an HSM (often FIPS 140-validated); rotating the master key only re-wraps the data keys.
  • Client-side schemes keep keys away from the server entirely: SQL Server Always Encrypted (deterministic or randomised, with secure enclaves for richer queries) and MongoDB Queryable Encryption, whose range queries became generally available in MongoDB 8.0.
  • Dynamic secrets: Vault's database secrets engine creates a unique, short-lived database user per application instance and drops it when the lease expires. IBM completed its HashiCorp acquisition in 2025; OpenBao is a Linux Foundation fork.
  • Your application's user passwords must be hashed, not encrypted, with slow salted algorithms such as Argon2id, scrypt or bcrypt, so a stolen table cannot simply be reversed.

Common mistakes & misconceptions

  • Believing TDE stops attackers who can log in: TDE decrypts transparently for any authorised session, so access control and injection defences still matter.
  • Using sslmode=require and assuming you are safe from interception: without certificate verification a man-in-the-middle can impersonate the server.
  • Storing the key beside the data: a key in the same backup bucket or Git repository as the encrypted dump gives no protection.
  • Hard-coding database passwords in source code or container images: they leak through Git history; load them from a vault at runtime.

A leaked users table holds Argon2id hashes, so attackers cannot decrypt passwords and each guess costs real computing time.

docs.title: 9.6 SQL Injection & Parameterised Queries
docs.text:
SQL injection happens when an application builds a SQL statement by gluing user input into the text, so an attacker can type SQL instead of data and change what the query does. The fix is to send the query and the data separately — parameterised queries (also called prepared statements or bind variables) — so input is always treated as a value, never as code.

How injection rewrites a login query. Same input, two outcomes: concatenation lets it become SQL, a bound parameter keeps it as data.

Think of it like…

It is like a form letter where someone fills the 'name' blank with 'Bob. Also, pay all invoices to me' — if the clerk reads the whole letter as instructions, the attacker has written part of the order.

Real-world example

Fictional bookshop Inkwell built its login query by pasting the typed email straight into the SQL text. A tester typed ' OR 1=1 -- as the email and was logged in as the first user in the table. The fix was one line: cursor.execute("SELECT id FROM users WHERE email = %s", (email,)). The same input is now just a strange email address that matches nobody.

docs.title: How it works
docs.text:
1. The application takes input: a form field, URL parameter, header or JSON value.
  2. Vulnerable code concatenates it into SQL text, e.g. "... WHERE id = " + id.
  3. An attacker supplies SQL syntax (quotes, OR 1=1, UNION SELECT, stacked statements) that changes the query's logic.
  4. The database cannot tell intended SQL from injected SQL and runs it with the application's privileges.
  5. Defence: parameterised queries keep data separate; allow-lists handle identifiers; least privilege limits damage; testing finds leftovers.

Who uses it

Every backend developer, application security engineer, penetration tester and DBA — it is one of the most common security interview topics.

Key takeaway

Know the rankings: SQL injection (CWE-89) was #2 in the 2025 CWE Top 25, and Injection is A05 in the OWASP Top 10:2025. The primary defence is parameterised queries, not escaping.

Going deeper

  • Main variants: in-band (error-based and UNION-based, where results appear on the page), blind (boolean or time-based, inferring data bit by bit) and out-of-band (data exfiltrated through DNS or HTTP requests made by the database).
  • With parameterised queries the SQL text is parsed with placeholders ($1, ?, :name, @p1) and values are bound afterwards, so they cannot change the statement's structure; PostgreSQL's extended query protocol even sends them in separate messages.
  • Placeholders cannot stand in for identifiers such as table names, column names or ORDER BY direction; map user choices through an allow-list or use quoting functions such as PostgreSQL's quote_ident() or format('%I').
  • Stored procedures are only safe if they avoid building dynamic SQL from their arguments: EXEC('...' + @input) inside a procedure is just as injectable. Use sp_executesql with parameters (SQL Server) or EXECUTE ... USING (PL/pgSQL).
  • The 2025 CWE Top 25, based on over 39,000 CVE records, ranks SQL injection #2; OWASP's Top 10:2025 moved Injection from third to fifth place, yet it still accounts for one of the largest numbers of CVEs of any category.
  • NoSQL is not immune: passing a raw JSON object such as {"$ne": null} into a MongoDB filter can bypass a password check; validate types with schema-validation libraries and cast inputs to expected types.

Common mistakes & misconceptions

  • Escaping quotes by hand instead of parameterising: encoding tricks and edge cases defeat home-made escaping; use the driver's placeholders.
  • Thinking an ORM makes you immune: raw-SQL escape hatches (text(), FromSqlRaw, .raw()) combined with string formatting are injectable.
  • Relying on a WAF alone: firewalls catch common payloads but can be bypassed; fix the code and keep the WAF as an extra layer.
  • Giving the application's database user DDL or superuser rights: least privilege turns a potential full takeover into a limited read.

docs.title: Try it: Vulnerable vs safe query with Python's built-in sqlite3
docs.text:
import sqlite3
db = sqlite3.connect(':memory:')
db.execute("CREATE TABLE users(id INTEGER, email TEXT)")
db.executemany("INSERT INTO users VALUES (?, ?)", [(1, 'ana@x.io'), (2, 'bo@x.io')])
evil = "' OR 1=1 --"

# UNSAFE: input becomes part of the SQL text
print(db.execute("SELECT id FROM users WHERE email = '" + evil + "'").fetchall())  # [(1,), (2,)]

# SAFE: input is sent as a bound parameter
print(db.execute("SELECT id FROM users WHERE email = ?", (evil,)).fetchall())  # []

docs.text: Name What it does Example SQL injection (CWE-89)MITRE CWE · Concept · Current · Beginner · Relational Attack in which untrusted input changes a SQL statement's meaning because it was concatenated into the query text. A search box accepting ' UNION SELECT email, password_hash FROM users -- leaks the users table into the search results. A security team maps its code-review checklist to A05:2025, requiring parameterised queries in every pull request. A team's CI linter rejects any cursor.execute() call built with an f-string, forcing developers to pass values as parameters. Bind variables and placeholders$1 PostgreSQL, ? Oracle reuses one plan for SELECT * FROM emp WHERE id = :id across a million calls instead of hard-parsing each one. Allow-listing identifiersSecure coding practice · Pattern · Current · Intermediate · Relational Mapping user choices to a fixed set of known column or table names, because placeholders cannot replace identifiers. sort=price maps to the price column; any other value falls back to created_at, so 'id; DROP TABLE' never reaches SQL. A page that responds five seconds slower when the admin hash starts with 'a' leaks the hash one character at a time. Second-order injectionAttack technique · Concept · Current · Advanced · Relational Malicious input stored safely at first, then later concatenated into another query by different code. A username saved as admin'-- is harmless at signup but breaks a password-reset query that concatenates stored names. Safe dynamic SQLsp_executesql (SQL Server), EXECUTE ... NoSQL injectionAttack technique (MongoDB and other document stores) · Concept · Current · Intermediate · Document Injecting query operators into document-database filters, for example a JSON {"$ne": null} where a plain string was expected. A login API passing the request body straight into find() lets {"$ne": ""} match any password; forcing a string type blocks it. sqlmapOpen-source project · Tool · Current · Advanced · Relational Open-source tool that detects and exploits SQL injection automatically; use it only on systems you are authorised to test. A penetration tester with written permission runs sqlmap against a staging URL and confirms a time-based blind injection. The OWASP Core Rule Set blocks requests containing UNION SELECT while developers patch the vulnerable endpoint.
