Universities, airlines and government agencies were hit within weeks, showing why both secure coding and fast patching matter.

docs.title: 9.7 Compliance & Privacy: GDPR, HIPAA, PCI DSS, Residency & Retention
docs.text:
Laws and industry rules decide how personal and payment data may be collected, stored, protected, moved and deleted. For database people this becomes practical work: knowing where personal data lives, encrypting and restricting it, keeping it only as long as needed, deleting it on request, keeping it in the right country, and proving all of this to auditors.

Three rulebooks database teams meet most

GDPR (EU) HIPAA (US health) PCI DSS v4.0.1 Protects Personal data of people in the EU Protected health information Cardholder and authentication data Applies to Controllers and processors Covered entities, business associates Anyone storing or processing cards Enforced by National data protection authorities HHS Office for Civil Rights Card brands via acquiring banks Encryption Risk-based (Art. 32) Addressable safeguard today Required for stored card numbers Breach notice 72 hours to regulator Up to 60 days to individuals Per card-brand rules Penalties Up to €20M or 4% turnover Tiered civil penalties Fines, loss of card acceptance

Different scopes, same database controls: know your data, restrict it, encrypt it, log it, delete it on time.

Think of it like…

Compliance is like food-safety rules in a restaurant kitchen: labelled containers, use-by dates, separate boards for raw meat, and an inspector who checks your records — not just your cooking.

Real-world example

Fictional Berlin start-up FitTrail stores EU customers' workout and heart-rate data. Under GDPR they keep it in an EU cloud region, delete inactive accounts after 24 months with a nightly job, and answer erasure requests within one month. Card payments go to a payment provider, so card numbers never touch their database — which shrinks their PCI DSS scope to a short self-assessment.

docs.title: How it works
docs.text:
1. Map the data: inventory which tables and columns hold personal, health or card data (a data catalogue or classification scan).
  2. Minimise: collect only what you need, and tokenise or avoid storing the riskiest fields, such as full card numbers.
  3. Protect: encryption, least privilege, masking in non-production copies, audit logs.
  4. Locate: keep data and backups in permitted regions and document any cross-border transfers.
  5. Retain and delete: set a retention period per data type and automate deletion, including replicas, backups and logs.
  6. Prove it: keep evidence — policies, access reviews, audit trails — for auditors and regulators.

Who uses it

DBAs, data engineers, privacy engineers, security and compliance teams, and anyone handling data in health, finance, retail or the public sector.

Key takeaway

Know the headline numbers: GDPR fines up to €20 million or 4% of global annual turnover, 72 hours to notify a regulator of a breach, and PCI DSS v4.0.1 as the current card standard.

Going deeper

  • GDPR (Regulation 2016/679, applying since 25 May 2018) maps directly onto database design: data minimisation, storage limitation, integrity and confidentiality (Article 32 security) and data protection by design and by default (Article 25).
  • The right to erasure is hard in practice because data hides in replicas, caches, search indexes, warehouse copies, logs and backups; common answers are prompt deletion from live systems, documented backup expiry and crypto-shredding of per-user keys.
  • HIPAA's Security Rule currently treats encryption as an 'addressable' safeguard; HHS proposed in January 2025 to make encryption at rest and in transit and MFA mandatory, but as of October 2026 the final rule had not been issued.
  • PCI DSS v4.0.1 (June 2024) is the current card standard; its future-dated requirements became mandatory on 31 March 2025. Requirement 3 bans storing CVV, PIN or full-track data after authorisation and requires stored card numbers to be unreadable.
  • Residency pressure comes from GDPR transfer rules (the EU-US Data Privacy Framework dates from July 2023), India's DPDP Act 2023, China's PIPL and sector rules, so teams pin databases, replicas and backups to specific regions.
  • Pseudonymised data, where a separate key can re-identify people, is still personal data under GDPR; only genuinely anonymised data falls outside it, and true anonymisation is much harder than removing names.

Common mistakes & misconceptions

  • Copying production personal data into test and developer databases: use masked or synthetic data instead.
  • Deleting a user only from the main table: forgotten replicas, search indexes, warehouse copies and logs leave erasure incomplete.
  • Storing CVV codes 'temporarily' for payment retries: PCI DSS forbids keeping sensitive authentication data after authorisation.
  • Assuming 'our cloud provider is certified, so we are compliant': certifications cover the provider's layer, not your schema, access or retention.

docs.title: Try it: Find likely personal-data columns by name in PostgreSQL

FROM information_schema.columns
WHERE column_name ~* '(email|phone|birth|ssn|passport|address|iban|card)'
  AND table_schema NOT IN ('pg_catalog', 'information_schema')
ORDER BY 1, 2;

docs.title: 9.8 ORMs & Application Integration: SQLAlchemy, Hibernate, EF Core, Prisma, Django
docs.text:
An ORM (object-relational mapper) lets programmers work with database rows as ordinary objects in their programming language — a Customer class instead of a customers table — and writes the SQL for them. ORMs save a lot of repetitive code and help prevent SQL injection, but they can also hide slow, chatty or surprising SQL, so you still need to understand what they generate.

From object to disk: the application data stack. Every layer can add latency or surprises; good engineers can see through all of them.

Think of it like…

An ORM is like an interpreter at a business meeting: the conversation flows easily, but if you never check what is being said, you may agree to things you did not mean.

Real-world example

At fictional Pebble Tutors a Django page listed 200 lessons with each teacher's name. It ran 201 queries and took 900 ms. Query logging showed one SELECT per teacher; adding select_related('teacher') produced a single JOIN and the page fell to 40 ms. Later, a nightly report that loaded 3 million ORM objects into memory was rewritten as one SQL aggregate that finished in seconds.

docs.title: How it works
docs.text:
1. Map classes to tables (models or entities) with fields, keys and relationships.
  2. Open a session or context that tracks loaded objects and pending changes (the unit of work).
  3. Build queries in code (filter(), Where(), findMany()); the ORM translates them to SQL with bound parameters.
  4. Load related data lazily (on first access) or eagerly (joins or batched IN queries) — a key performance decision.
  5. Commit: the ORM sends INSERT, UPDATE and DELETE statements inside a transaction.
  6. Inspect the generated SQL in logs, and drop to raw (still parameterised) SQL for complex reports.

Who uses it

Backend and full-stack developers in Python, Java, C#, TypeScript and Ruby, and the DBAs who review the SQL those applications generate.

Key takeaway

In interviews, say you like ORMs for everyday CRUD and safety, always log and review the generated SQL, prevent N+1 with eager loading, and use plain SQL for heavy reporting.

Going deeper

  • Current lines: SQLAlchemy 2.0 (2023) unified on a select() style; Hibernate ORM 7 (2025) implements Jakarta Persistence 3.2; EF Core 10 shipped with .NET 10 in November 2025; Prisma ORM 7 (late 2025) replaced its Rust engine.
  • Eager-loading options to beat N+1: Django select_related (JOIN) and prefetch_related (second IN query), SQLAlchemy joinedload and selectinload, EF Core Include(), Hibernate JOIN FETCH or entity graphs, Prisma include, Rails includes.
  • The unit-of-work and identity-map patterns mean a session tracks each loaded row once and flushes all changes at commit; long-lived sessions therefore grow in memory and can hold stale data.
  • Object-relational impedance mismatch: objects have inheritance, identity and graphs; tables have rows, keys and joins. ORMs offer inheritance strategies (single table, joined tables, table per class), each with different query costs.
  • Between raw SQL and full ORMs sit query builders and SQL-first tools: jOOQ (Java), Kysely and Drizzle (TypeScript), sqlc (generates typed code from SQL files) and Dapper (.NET micro-ORM).
  • Connection handling matters: frameworks should use a short transaction per request and return connections to a pool such as HikariCP (Spring Boot's default) or an external pooler, never holding them across slow network calls.

Common mistakes & misconceptions

  • Never looking at generated SQL: enable SQL logging in development and review it for N+1 patterns, SELECT * and missing filters.
  • Loading millions of objects to compute a total: let the database aggregate with GROUP BY or a raw query instead.
  • Using string formatting inside raw-SQL escape hatches: FromSqlRaw, text() and .raw() with f-strings are injectable; pass parameters.
  • Holding a transaction open across slow external calls: it keeps locks and connections busy; make external calls outside the transaction.

docs.title: Try it: SQLAlchemy 2.0: eager-load to avoid N+1 (models Lesson and Teacher assumed)
docs.text:
from sqlalchemy import select
from sqlalchemy.orm import selectinload
# create_engine(url, echo=True) prints every SQL statement
stmt = (select(Lesson)
        .options(selectinload(Lesson.teacher))
        .where(Lesson.day == 'Mon'))
for lesson in session.scalars(stmt):
    print(lesson.title, lesson.teacher.name)  # 2 queries total, not 1 + N

docs.title: 9.9 Databases & AI: Vector Search, RAG, Text-to-SQL & MCP
docs.text:
AI and databases now work together in both directions. Databases help AI: they store embeddings (lists of numbers that capture meaning) and run vector search so chatbots can look up relevant facts — retrieval-augmented generation, or RAG. AI helps databases: models turn questions into SQL (text-to-SQL), explain query plans and, through the Model Context Protocol (MCP), let AI agents use databases as tools — which needs careful security.

An AI assistant querying a database through MCP. The model never holds credentials: the MCP server runs SQL with a read-only role and returns the SQL for review.

Think of it like…

Vector search is a librarian who finds books by what they are about rather than by exact title words; text-to-SQL is an interpreter who turns your question into the library's catalogue language.

Real-world example

Fictional insurer Larkspur builds a claims assistant. Policy documents are split into chunks, embedded and stored with pgvector in their existing PostgreSQL database, filtered by product and country. A question retrieves the eight most relevant chunks, which the LLM uses to answer with citations. Analysts also ask 'How many water-damage claims did we pay in Q2?' — an MCP server gives the model a read-only role on a curated reporting schema, and every generated SQL statement is logged.

docs.title: How it works
docs.text:
1. Embed: an embedding model turns text, images or rows into vectors (for example 768 or 1,536 numbers).
  2. Store and index: save vectors beside the source data and build an approximate nearest-neighbour index (HNSW or IVF).
  3. Retrieve: embed the user's question, find the nearest vectors, and combine them with keyword search and metadata filters.
  4. Generate: pass the retrieved chunks to the LLM as context and ask it to answer and cite sources (RAG).
  5. For text-to-SQL: give the model schema descriptions and examples, generate SQL, validate it, run it with a read-only role and show the SQL.
  6. Evaluate and guard: measure retrieval quality and SQL accuracy, log everything, and keep humans in the loop for any writes.

Who uses it

AI engineers, backend developers, data engineers, analytics teams and DBAs who now support vector workloads and AI agents.

Key takeaway

Explain RAG in one sentence: 'retrieve relevant facts from your own data at question time and give them to the model, instead of retraining it' — and add that retrieval quality usually matters more than the choice of model.

Going deeper

  • Mainstream engines now ship vector search — pgvector (HNSW, IVFFlat), SQL Server 2025's VECTOR type, Oracle AI Database 26ai's AI Vector Search, MongoDB Atlas Vector Search, cloud warehouses — often removing the need for a separate vector store.
  • Hybrid retrieval combines keyword (BM25) and vector results, commonly merged with reciprocal rank fusion, and applies metadata filters (tenant, language, date); a reranking model then reorders the top 50-100 candidates before they reach the LLM.
  • Text-to-SQL is measured on benchmarks such as Spider (2018), BIRD (2023) and Spider 2.0 (2024), whose enterprise-style tasks remain much harder than classic Spider; real deployments improve accuracy with curated views, column descriptions, example queries and semantic layers.
  • In-database AI functions call models from SQL: Oracle Select AI generates SQL from natural language, SQL Server 2025 generates embeddings with AI_GENERATE_EMBEDDINGS from external models, and Snowflake Cortex and Databricks offer SQL AI functions and natural-language analytics.
  • The Model Context Protocol, introduced by Anthropic in November 2024 and since moved to the Linux Foundation's Agentic AI Foundation, standardises how AI apps call tools; database servers include Google's MCP Toolbox for Databases and the MongoDB MCP Server.
  • Agent risks: prompt injection hidden in retrieved data can steer an agent into harmful queries. Mitigations are dedicated read-only roles, row limits and statement timeouts, allow-listed tools, full query logging and human approval before any write or DDL.

Common mistakes & misconceptions

  • Giving an AI agent the application's admin credentials: use a dedicated read-only role on a curated schema with statement timeouts.
  • Assuming generated SQL is correct because it runs: plausible SQL can join wrongly or double-count; validate against known answers.
  • Skipping metadata and permission filters in RAG: vector search can otherwise surface another customer's documents.
  • Mixing embeddings from different models: vectors from different models are not comparable; re-embed and re-index together when you switch.

docs.title: Try it: Tiny semantic search with pgvector (3-dimensional toy vectors)
docs.text:
CREATE EXTENSION IF NOT EXISTS vector;
CREATE TABLE docs (id int PRIMARY KEY, body text, embedding vector(3));
INSERT INTO docs VALUES
  (1, 'flooded kitchen claim', '[0.9,0.1,0.0]'),
  (2, 'car windscreen crack',  '[0.0,0.2,0.9]');
SELECT id, body, embedding <=> '[0.8,0.2,0.1]' AS cosine_distance
FROM docs
ORDER BY cosine_distance
LIMIT 1;

docs.title: 9.10 Careers in Databases: DBA, Data Engineer, DRE & More
docs.text:
Many jobs revolve around databases. Some keep databases healthy (DBA, database reliability engineer), some build the pipelines that move data (data engineer), some model data for analysis (analytics engineer), some write the applications that use databases (backend engineer), and some design whole data landscapes (data architect). They all share SQL, data modelling and a habit of careful, reversible change.

Common career paths around databases. There is no single ladder: people move between operations, engineering and analytics as their interests grow.

Think of it like…

Think of a city's water system: some people run the treatment plant (DBAs), some lay the pipes (data engineers), some fit the taps in homes (backend engineers) and some plan the whole network (architects).

Real-world example

Sam starts as a data analyst at fictional retailer Northgate, writing SQL reports. He learns dbt and becomes an analytics engineer after 18 months. His colleague Leah begins as a backend developer, becomes the team's go-to person for PostgreSQL performance, joins the platform team as a database reliability engineer, and three years later becomes the company's data architect.

docs.title: How it works
docs.text:
1. Learn the shared core: SQL, relational modelling, one database in depth (PostgreSQL is a great default), Linux and Git.
  2. Pick a direction: operations (DBA/DRE), pipelines (data engineering), modelling and metrics (analytics engineering) or applications (backend).
  3. Add the matching toolset: cloud and automation; Python, Spark and orchestration; dbt and BI tools; or a web framework and ORM.
  4. Build public evidence: a portfolio repository, a blog post about a tuning win, a certification if your target employers value it.
  5. Get a foot in the door through junior, intern, support or analyst roles, then specialise.

Who uses it

Students, career changers, developers and analysts deciding where database skills fit into their careers.

Key takeaway

Job titles vary wildly between companies — read the responsibilities, not the title; one company's 'data engineer' is another's DBA or analytics engineer.

Going deeper

  • US Bureau of Labor Statistics (May 2024): median pay $104,620 for database administrators and $135,980 for database architects; employment for the combined group is projected to grow 4% from 2024 to 2034, about average for all occupations.
  • Database reliability engineering applies SRE practice — automation, SLOs, infrastructure as code, blameless post-mortems — to data stores; the term was popularised by the 2017 O'Reilly book Database Reliability Engineering by Laine Campbell and Charity Majors.
  • Analytics engineering grew up around dbt in the late 2010s: analytics engineers write tested, version-controlled SQL transformations and metric definitions that sit between raw data and dashboards.
  • Few employers now hire 'junior DBAs'; common entry routes are backend development, data analysis, IT support or sysadmin roles, and graduate data-engineering programmes.
  • Specialist niches pay well: database kernel engineers at vendors, performance consultants, database security specialists and migration experts (for example Oracle to PostgreSQL, or on-premises to cloud).
  • AI is changing tasks rather than removing the need: assistants draft SQL and suggest indexes, but employers still need people who understand data models, correctness, security and cost to review and own the results.

Common mistakes & misconceptions

  • Collecting certificates without hands-on proof: employers trust a GitHub project or a written tuning case study at least as much as a badge.
  • Learning five databases shallowly: master SQL and one relational engine deeply first; the concepts transfer.
  • Ignoring soft skills: DBAs and data engineers spend much of their time explaining risk, negotiating maintenance windows and writing documentation.

docs.title: 9.11 Database Certifications in 2026: Which Are Current
docs.text:
Certifications are vendor exams that show you know a particular product. They can help you get past HR filters and give your learning a structure, especially for Microsoft, Oracle, AWS, Google, MongoDB, Snowflake and Databricks roles. Exams change often — several popular ones were retired in 2024-2025 and new ones appeared in 2026 — so always check the vendor's page before you start studying.

A typical database certification ladder (2026). Climb only as far as your target role needs; hands-on projects matter at every level.

Think of it like…

A certification is like a driving licence for one make of lorry: it proves you passed a test, but employers still want to see you drive.

Real-world example

Aisha, a final-year student, takes Microsoft DP-900 (Azure Data Fundamentals) to learn the vocabulary, then spends three months building PostgreSQL projects. Her first job is at a company running Azure SQL, so after six months she passes DP-300 (Azure Database Administrator Associate), which her employer pays for. A friend aiming at analytics instead takes SnowPro Core and builds a dbt portfolio project.

docs.title: How it works
docs.text:
1. Choose by target employer and platform: read 20 job adverts and count which clouds and databases appear.
  2. Start with a fundamentals exam only if you are new to the field (DP-900 or a cloud foundational exam).
  3. Study from the official exam guide (skills measured) plus hands-on labs on a free tier or local Docker.
  4. Use reputable practice tests — never 'dumps', which breach exam agreements.
  5. Book it, pass it, then keep current: many certifications expire after one to three years and need renewal.

Who uses it

Students, career changers and working DBAs or data engineers whose employers or clients value vendor credentials.

Key takeaway

Check status before studying: AWS retired its Database Specialty exam in April 2024 and Microsoft retired DP-203 in March 2025, yet prep material for both still circulates.

Going deeper

  • Microsoft in 2026: DP-900, DP-300 (Azure DBA), DP-700 (Fabric Data Engineer, replacing DP-203), DP-600 (Fabric Analytics Engineer), plus new DP-800 (SQL AI Developer) and DP-750 (Azure Databricks Data Engineer). Associate certifications renew free yearly online.
  • Oracle renamed its flagship Oracle AI Database 26ai in October 2025; the current DBA track is 1Z0-182 (Administration Associate) and 1Z0-183 (Administration Professional), while 1Z0-082 and 1Z0-083 belong to the older 19c path.
  • AWS retired the Database Specialty and Data Analytics Specialty exams in April 2024; AWS Certified Data Engineer – Associate (DEA-C01) is now its data credential, with 65 questions in 130 minutes, a 720/1000 pass mark and three-year validity.
  • Snowflake's SnowPro Core moved to exam version COF-C03 in February 2026; SnowPro Advanced exams cover architect, data engineer, administrator, data analyst and data scientist roles.
  • Databricks offers Data Engineer Associate and Professional, Data Analyst Associate, Machine Learning Associate and Professional, Generative AI Engineer Associate and an Apache Spark Developer Associate; most cost about US$200 and are valid for two years.
  • Google Cloud's Professional Cloud Database Engineer expects years of database experience and covers Cloud SQL, AlloyDB, Spanner, Bigtable, Firestore and migrations; MongoDB University offers the Associate Developer and Associate DBA exams.

Common mistakes & misconceptions

  • Studying for a retired exam because a course or book still sells it: confirm the exam code on the vendor's own site first.
  • Using brain-dump sites: they breach candidate agreements, can get certifications revoked and teach nothing useful.
  • Expecting a certificate alone to land a job: pair it with hands-on projects you can explain in an interview.

A candidate finds an old DBS-C01 course for sale and checks AWS's site before wasting money on it.

docs.title: 9.12 Learning Resources: Courses, Books & Practice Sites
docs.text:
You can learn databases to a professional level for free or nearly free. A good mix is an interactive SQL practice site to build fluency, a university course on how databases really work, a few classic books, and the official documentation of the database you use. The best learners also read query plans and engineering blogs from companies that run databases at scale.

A practical learning path. Each stage builds on the previous one; keep typing queries throughout.

Think of it like…

Learning databases is like learning to cook: practice sites are knife drills, courses are cookery school, books are the great cookbooks, and documentation is the label on every ingredient.

Real-world example

Jonas, a self-taught developer, spends four weeks on SQLBolt and PostgreSQL Exercises, then watches the CMU 15-445 lectures on YouTube at two a week. He reads Use The Index, Luke while tuning his own side project, and the second edition of Designing Data-Intensive Applications over the summer. In interviews he explains B+trees, MVCC and replication with real examples from his project.

docs.title: How it works
docs.text:
1. Build fluency first: write SQL every day for a month on interactive sites.
  2. Learn indexing and query plans with Use The Index, Luke and your own EXPLAIN experiments.
  3. Understand internals with CMU 15-445 (or Berkeley CS186) and a book such as Database Internals.
  4. Understand distributed systems and trade-offs with Designing Data-Intensive Applications.
  5. Go deep on one engine with its official documentation and an internals book.
  6. Stay current with release notes, conference talks and engineering blogs.

Who uses it

Students, self-learners, bootcamp graduates and working developers filling gaps before an interview or a new role.

Key takeaway

If you read one book, read Designing Data-Intensive Applications (2nd edition, 2026); if you take one course, take CMU 15-445 — both are mentioned by name in senior interviews.

Going deeper

  • CMU 15-445/645 (Andy Pavlo, with Jignesh Patel co-teaching recent editions) publishes full lecture videos and slides free; its BusTub C++ projects have you build a buffer pool, B+tree index, query executor and concurrency control.
  • Designing Data-Intensive Applications by Martin Kleppmann, with Chris Riccomini joining for the second edition (O'Reilly, early 2026), covers storage engines, replication, partitioning, transactions, consistency and stream processing with updated cloud-era examples.
  • Use The Index, Luke (use-the-index-luke.com) by Markus Winand is a free web book on SQL indexing across Oracle, PostgreSQL, MySQL, SQL Server and Db2; its sister site modern-sql.com explains newer standard SQL features and which databases support them.
  • Deeper books: Database Internals (Alex Petrov, 2019) on storage engines and distributed algorithms; PostgreSQL 14 Internals (Egor Rogov, free PDF); Database System Concepts as the standard textbook; SQL Antipatterns (Bill Karwin) for design mistakes.
  • Practice sites: SQLBolt and Select Star SQL (beginner tutorials), PostgreSQL Exercises, SQL Murder Mystery, DataLemur, HackerRank and LeetCode (interview problems), and db<>fiddle for sharing runnable examples.
  • Staying current: official release notes (PostgreSQL ships one major release a year), Andy Pavlo's annual 'Databases in 20XX' retrospective, talks from PGConf, VLDB and SIGMOD, and engineering blogs of companies that run databases at scale.

Common mistakes & misconceptions

  • Watching courses without typing: you learn SQL and tuning by running queries and reading plans yourself.
  • Starting with internals before SQL fluency: build everyday SQL skill first, and the internals will make far more sense.
  • Learning from outdated tutorials: check versions — advice written for MySQL 5.x or PostgreSQL 9.x often no longer applies.

docs.title: 9.13 Hands-On Labs & a 16-Week Study Plan
docs.text:
Reading only gets you so far — you become job-ready by running databases yourself. With Docker you can start PostgreSQL, MySQL, MongoDB or Redis on a laptop in seconds, load realistic sample databases, break things and fix them. A structured study plan turns this into steady progress, from your first SELECT to a portfolio project you can talk about in interviews.

A 16-week study plan. About 8-10 hours a week; every phase ends with something you can show.

Think of it like…

It is like learning to fly: ground school matters, but the hours in the flight simulator — including practising engine failures — are what make you a pilot.

Real-world example

Over 16 weeks, student Maya runs PostgreSQL 18 in Docker, loads the Pagila DVD-rental sample and writes 150 queries. She benchmarks with pgbench, adds indexes and records before-and-after timings, sets up a streaming replica and practises point-in-time recovery after 'accidentally' dropping a table. Her final project — a small booking API with tests, migrations and a monitoring dashboard — is on GitHub with a README explaining every design choice.

docs.title: How it works
docs.text:
1. Weeks 1-3: SQL foundations — SELECT, joins, GROUP BY and window functions on a sample database, ten queries a day.
  2. Weeks 4-5: modelling — design a schema for a real-world idea, normalise it and write migrations.
  3. Weeks 6-8: internals and performance — indexes, EXPLAIN ANALYZE, transactions and isolation, pgbench experiments.
  4. Weeks 9-10: operations — backups and restores, replication, monitoring, users and security.
  5. Weeks 11-13: breadth — a NoSQL store (MongoDB or Redis), DuckDB analytics on Parquet, a managed cloud database.
  6. Weeks 14-16: portfolio project, write-up, mock interviews and (optionally) a certification.

Who uses it

Students and career changers who want a structured route to a first data, backend or DBA role.

Key takeaway

Keep a learning log: for every experiment write down the command, the result and what surprised you — it becomes interview stories and blog posts.

Going deeper

  • Sample databases worth knowing: Pagila (PostgreSQL port of MySQL's Sakila), Chinook (music store, many engines), Northwind (trading company), Microsoft's AdventureWorks and WideWorldImporters, MySQL's employees database (about 4 million rows) and the Stack Overflow data dump for large-scale tuning.
  • Benchmark tools: pgbench ships with PostgreSQL (TPC-B-like; each scale unit adds 100,000 account rows), sysbench is common for MySQL, and HammerDB runs TPC-C- and TPC-H-derived workloads; use a quiet machine and repeat runs.
  • DuckDB queries Parquet or CSV files directly with SQL — for example the public NYC taxi trip data — giving you analytical-engine experience on a laptop with no server.
  • Practise failure on purpose: kill the primary and promote a replica, restore to a point in time just before a DROP TABLE, fill the disk, provoke a deadlock — and write down what happened and how you recovered.
  • Cloud practice without big bills: use free tiers and free plans, set budget alerts on day one, tag resources and delete them (including snapshots) after each lab.
  • A strong portfolio project shows the schema (ER diagram), migrations, tests, indexes with EXPLAIN evidence, a backup-and-restore script and a short write-up of trade-offs — more convincing than a dozen tutorial clones.

Common mistakes & misconceptions

  • Only following tutorials step by step: change something, break it and debug it — that is where real learning happens.
  • Leaving cloud labs running: forgotten instances and snapshots create surprise bills; set budgets and alerts.
  • Exposing lab databases with weak passwords on public ports: bots find them within hours; bind to localhost or a private network.

docs.title: 9.14 Interview Questions with Model Answers
docs.text:
Database interviews test three things: can you write correct SQL, do you understand how databases behave (indexes, transactions, scaling), and can you make sensible trade-offs and explain them clearly. Below are common questions with short model answers to adapt — the best answers add a concrete example from something you have actually done.

Answering a troubleshooting question. Interviewers score the method as much as the final fix.

Think of it like…

An interview is like a driving test: knowing the highway code helps, but the examiner mostly wants to see you drive calmly, check your mirrors and explain what you are doing.

Real-world example

Asked 'A query got slow overnight — what do you do?', candidate Rahul answers in steps: check whether data volume, plan or load changed; find the query in pg_stat_statements; run EXPLAIN ANALYZE. In his example a bulk load left statistics stale, causing a sequential scan; running ANALYZE brought back the index scan, and he added monitoring for plan changes. The interviewer later said the structure mattered more than the exact fix.

docs.title: How it works
docs.text:
1. Clarify the question: data size, read/write mix, latency targets and constraints.
  2. State your approach out loud before diving into details.
  3. Give the core answer with correct terms, then one concrete example or number.
  4. Name the trade-offs and alternatives — every database choice costs something.
  5. Finish with how you would verify or monitor the result.

Who uses it

Candidates for data analyst, backend, data engineering, DBA and DRE roles — and interviewers designing fair questions.

Key takeaway

Use STAR (situation, task, action, result) for experience questions, and 'measure, hypothesise, change one thing, verify' for troubleshooting questions.

Going deeper

  • Behavioural questions matter for DBA and DRE roles: expect 'tell me about an outage you handled' or 'a change that went wrong'; good answers show calm diagnosis, clear communication with stakeholders and a blameless follow-up that prevented a repeat.
  • System-design rounds usually include a data layer: choose a primary store and justify it, estimate size (10 million users × 2 KB = 20 GB), derive indexes from access patterns, then discuss caching, replication, sharding only if needed, and backups.
  • Practical tasks commonly include writing SQL with joins and window functions, reading an EXPLAIN plan, designing a schema from requirements, or fixing an N+1 problem in ORM code.
  • Numbers worth knowing: main-memory access about 100 ns, SSD random read in the tens to hundreds of microseconds, same-region network round trip around 0.5 ms, cross-continent round trip roughly 70-150 ms, PostgreSQL page 8 KB, InnoDB page 16 KB.
  • Honesty wins: 'I haven't used Spanner, but I'd expect its TrueTime commit wait to add write latency' shows reasoning, whereas invented experience is quickly exposed by follow-up questions.

Common mistakes & misconceptions

  • Jumping to sharding or NoSQL for modest data: first say that one well-indexed PostgreSQL server can handle terabytes and thousands of queries per second.
  • Reciting definitions without examples: anchor every answer in a concrete scenario or number.
  • Ignoring correctness while optimising: mention transactions, constraints and how you would prove that results did not change.

docs.title: Key databases, concepts, languages, tools & standards
docs.text: Name What it does Example Q: What does ACID mean?Model answer · Concept · Beginner · Relational Atomicity (all or nothing), Consistency (rules always hold), Isolation (concurrent transactions don't interfere), Durability (committed data survives crashes). A transfer debits and credits in one transaction; a crash midway rolls both back, and a committed transfer survives a restart. Q: Clustered vs non-clustered index?Model answer · Concept · Intermediate · Relational A clustered index stores the table's rows in key order (one per table); non-clustered indexes are separate structures pointing to rows. SQL Server and InnoDB cluster tables by primary key; PostgreSQL stores rows in a heap, so all its indexes are secondary. Q: Why not index every column?Model answer · Concept · Beginner · Relational Each index costs disk, memory and time on every INSERT, UPDATE and DELETE, and the optimiser may never use many of them. Dropping six unused indexes from a 14-index table noticeably cut insert latency without slowing any important query. Q: WHERE vs HAVING?Model answer · Concept · Beginner · Relational WHERE filters rows before grouping; HAVING filters groups after aggregation, so it can test COUNT, SUM and similar. WHERE status = 'paid' ... GROUP BY customer_id HAVING SUM(total) > 1000 finds the big paying customers. Q: DELETE vs TRUNCATE vs DROP?Model answer · Concept · Beginner · Relational DELETE removes chosen rows and logs each one; TRUNCATE empties a whole table quickly; DROP removes the table and its definition. Clearing a 50-million-row staging table nightly with TRUNCATE takes moments, while DELETE generates gigabytes of log. Q: Explain isolation levels.Model answer · Concept · Intermediate · Relational Read uncommitted, read committed, repeatable read and serializable; stronger levels prevent more anomalies at the cost of concurrency or retries. PostgreSQL defaults to read committed; a seat-booking check-then-insert needs serializable or a unique constraint. Q: A query became slow overnight — what do you do?Model answer · Concept · Intermediate · Relational Check what changed (data, plan, load, locks), find it in query statistics, read EXPLAIN ANALYZE, fix the cause, verify and monitor. Stale statistics after a bulk load caused a bad plan; ANALYZE restored the index scan, from 12 seconds to 15 ms. Q: What is the N+1 problem?Model answer · Concept · Intermediate · Relational One query for a list plus one per item; fix it with joins, batched IN queries or the ORM's eager loading. select_related('author') turned 101 queries into one for a 100-post page. Q: How do you prevent SQL injection?Model answer · Concept · Beginner · Relational Parameterised queries everywhere, allow-lists for identifiers, least-privilege accounts, code review and security testing. Sorting by a user-chosen column uses a dictionary of allowed columns, while every value goes through placeholders. Q: Replication vs sharding?Model answer · Concept · Intermediate · General Replication copies the same data to more servers for availability and read scaling; sharding splits data so each server holds a part. Read replicas fix a read-heavy blog; a 40 TB multi-tenant SaaS shards by tenant_id to scale writes. Q: What are RPO and RTO?Model answer · Concept · Intermediate · General Recovery point objective is acceptable data loss; recovery time objective is acceptable downtime. Together they drive backup and HA design. An RPO of 5 minutes and an RTO of 1 hour suggest continuous WAL archiving plus rehearsed point-in-time restores. Q: When would you choose NoSQL?Model answer · Concept · Intermediate · General When access patterns, scale or data shape suit a specialised model better; relational remains the safe default for most applications. Session lookups at 200,000 operations per second suit Redis; orders needing joins and constraints stay in PostgreSQL. Q: How do you change a big table without downtime?Model answer · Concept · Advanced · Relational Use backward-compatible steps (expand and contract): add the new column, backfill in batches, dual-write, switch reads, then drop the old one. Renaming email to email_address took four deployments over a week with zero downtime on a 300-million-row table. Q: How would you secure a production database?Model answer · Concept · Intermediate · General Private network, TLS, individual accounts with MFA, least-privilege roles, encryption at rest, a secrets vault, auditing and patching. The candidate walks through each defence layer from firewall to audit log, naming one concrete tool for each.

docs.title: Chapter 5: Relational & Distributed SQL Databases
docs.text: This chapter tours the real relational products you will meet at work. It opens up PostgreSQL in depth — processes, versions, MVCC and VACUUM, extensions — then covers MySQL and MariaDB, Oracle, SQL Server and Azure SQL, SQLite, Db2 and other engines, and DuckDB for embedded analytics. It ends with distributed SQL (Spanner, CockroachDB, YugabyteDB, TiDB, Aurora DSQL), cloud-managed and serverless Postgres services, and how to choose a database with its licence and business landscape in mind.

docs.title: 5.1 PostgreSQL In Depth — Architecture, Versions and Community
docs.text:
PostgreSQL (often just 'Postgres') is a free, open-source relational database that grew out of the POSTGRES research project at UC Berkeley in 1986 and has been developed by a worldwide volunteer and company community ever since. It is famous for being correct, standards-friendly and easy to extend. Inside, one supervisor process starts a separate worker process for every connection, and they all share a block of memory that caches data pages.

PostgreSQL's process family. One supervisor forks a backend per client and a set of background helpers that all share memory.

Think of it like…

A Postgres server is like a busy restaurant: the host at the door (the postmaster) gives every guest their own waiter (a backend process), while kitchen staff work quietly in the background washing dishes, writing the order book and restocking shelves.

Real-world example

Maya runs the fictional online shop Lumen Books on PostgreSQL 18, using one 4-vCPU virtual machine with 16 GB of RAM. She sets shared_buffers to 4 GB, keeps the write-ahead log on fast SSD, and lets autovacuum tidy tables overnight. When Black Friday arrives, 300 web workers share 40 real database connections through a pooler, and the shop handles 2,000 orders an hour without trouble.

docs.title: How it works
docs.text:
1. The postmaster process listens on TCP port 5432 and checks pg_hba.conf to decide who may connect and how they must authenticate.
  2. For each accepted connection it forks a dedicated backend process that parses, plans and executes that client's SQL.
  3. Backends read and change 8 KB data pages in shared buffers, the shared memory cache, and record every change in the write-ahead log (WAL) first.
  4. Background processes — checkpointer, background writer, WAL writer, autovacuum and others — flush pages to disk and clean up old row versions.
  5. On a crash, Postgres replays the WAL from the last checkpoint so every committed transaction survives.

Who uses it

Backend developers, DBAs, data engineers, start-ups and governments alike run PostgreSQL; it powers everything from small SaaS apps to some of the largest internet services, and most clouds sell Postgres-compatible services.

Key takeaway

Interviewers love the process-per-connection model: say that each connection is a full OS process, so thousands of idle connections waste memory — which is why Postgres shops put a connection pooler in front.

Going deeper

  • Every connection is a separate operating-system process costing several megabytes; max_connections defaults to 100, so busy applications use a pooler instead of raising it to thousands.
  • shared_buffers defaults to just 128 MB; a common starting point is about 25 % of RAM, because Postgres also relies on the operating system's page cache (so data is often cached twice).
  • Tables and indexes live as files under the data directory (PGDATA) split into 1 GB segments of 8 KB pages; values larger than about 2 KB are compressed or moved to a side table called TOAST.
  • The project ships one major version a year (usually September), quarterly minor releases, and supports each major for five years; PostgreSQL 13 reached end of life in November 2025 and 14 does so in November 2026.
  • PostgreSQL 18 (September 2025) added an asynchronous I/O subsystem, a built-in uuidv7() function, virtual generated columns, OAuth 2.0 login, B-tree skip scans and keeping planner statistics across pg_upgrade.
  • PostgreSQL 19 was in beta through summer 2026; the project said in late September that a release candidate was due in early October and general availability could follow in October 2026.
  • No company owns Postgres: the PostgreSQL Global Development Group, a small core team and hundreds of contributors employed by firms such as EDB, Microsoft, AWS, Google and Snowflake build it.

Common mistakes & misconceptions

  • Opening thousands of direct connections: each is a whole process, so memory and context switching explode — put PgBouncer or your cloud's proxy in front instead.
  • Treating a major upgrade like a minor one: 18.1 to 18.2 is a simple binary swap, but 17 to 18 needs pg_upgrade, dump/restore or logical replication.
  • Running an end-of-life major version for years: it stops getting security fixes, so plan an upgrade at least every few years.

docs.text: Name What it does Example PostgreSQLPostgreSQL Global Development Group · Database · Current · Beginner · Relational Open-source object-relational database known for correctness, rich SQL, extensibility and a permissive licence; one of the most used databases worldwide. Lumen Books keeps customers, orders and stock in one PostgreSQL 18 server, using foreign keys and transactions so no order ever references a missing book. postmasterPostgreSQL core · Feature · Current · Intermediate · Relational The parent supervisor process that listens for connections, forks a backend per client and restarts helpers if they crash. When a backend crashes from a bug, the postmaster resets shared memory, restarts all processes and runs crash recovery automatically. Backend processPostgreSQL core · Feature · Current · Intermediate · Relational The dedicated operating-system process serving one client connection: it parses, plans and executes that session's SQL. SELECT pg_backend_pid(); shows your own backend's process ID, which you can also see in top or Task Manager. shared_buffersPostgreSQL configuration · Feature · Current · Intermediate · Relational The shared memory cache of 8 KB data pages used by all backends; the single most important memory setting. On a 16 GB server Maya raises shared_buffers from the 128 MB default to 4 GB and her cache hit ratio climbs above 99 %. PGDATA (data directory)PostgreSQL core · Concept · Current · Beginner · Relational The folder holding one 'database cluster': all databases, the WAL in pg_wal, and configuration files such as postgresql.conf. SHOW data_directory; on Ubuntu typically returns /var/lib/postgresql/18/main. postgresql.conf and pg_hba.confPostgreSQL configuration · Feature · Current · Beginner · Relational The main settings file and the host-based authentication file that controls which users, databases and addresses may connect, and how. A line 'hostssl shop app 10.0.0.0/16 scram-sha-256' lets the app connect only over TLS from the private network. System catalogs (pg_catalog)PostgreSQL core · Feature · Current · Intermediate · Relational Internal tables describing every table, column, index, function and type; Postgres stores its own metadata as ordinary relations. SELECT relname, reltuples FROM pg_class WHERE relkind = 'r' ORDER BY reltuples DESC LIMIT 5; lists the five largest tables by estimated rows. psqlPostgreSQL project · Tool · Current · Beginner · Relational PostgreSQL's interactive command-line client, with handy backslash commands for describing objects and timing queries. psql -h localhost -U maya shop, then \dt lists tables, \d orders describes one, and \timing shows query durations. pg_dump and pg_restorePostgreSQL project · Tool · Current · Beginner · Relational Tools that export a database to a consistent logical dump file and load it back, even into a newer major version. pg_dump -Fc shop > shop.dump at midnight, then pg_restore -d shop_test shop.dump builds a fresh test copy. pg_upgradePostgreSQL project · Tool · Current · Intermediate · Relational Upgrades a cluster to a new major version in place by reusing data files; --link mode finishes in minutes even for terabytes. The DBA stops Postgres 16, runs pg_upgrade --link to version 18, and the 2 TB database is back online in under ten minutes. PostgreSQL 18PostgreSQL Global Development Group, Sept 2025 · Database · Current · Intermediate · Relational Current major release adding asynchronous I/O, uuidv7(), virtual generated columns, OAuth authentication and B-tree skip scans. After upgrading to 18 with io_method = worker, a reporting team sees large sequential scans finish noticeably faster on cloud disks. PostgreSQL 19PostgreSQL Global Development Group, 2026 · Database · Emerging · Advanced · Relational Next major version, in beta during 2026 with general availability expected around October 2026; some planned features were pulled late in beta. A DBA team tests their application against the PostgreSQL 19 release candidate in staging before planning a 2027 upgrade. Major and minor releasesPostgreSQL versioning policy · Concept · Current · Beginner · Relational Major versions (17, 18) add features yearly and are supported five years; minor versions (18.1, 18.2) only fix bugs and security issues. Lumen Books applies every quarterly minor release within a week, but schedules the jump from 16 to 18 as a planned project. PostgreSQL Global Development GroupCommunity, core team and contributors · Organisation · Current · Beginner · Relational The community that develops PostgreSQL; no single company controls it, which reduces the risk of sudden licence changes. Engineers from several competing cloud vendors review each other's patches on the pgsql-hackers mailing list. PostgreSQL LicencePostgreSQL Global Development Group · Standard · Current · Beginner · Relational A short permissive licence similar to BSD/MIT: anyone may use, modify and sell Postgres, including inside closed-source products. Because of this licence, AWS, Google, Microsoft and start-ups like Neon could build commercial services on Postgres without paying royalties.

docs.title: 5.2 PostgreSQL MVCC, VACUUM and Bloat in Practice
docs.text:
PostgreSQL never overwrites a row in place. An UPDATE writes a brand-new version of the row and marks the old one as expired, so readers can keep seeing the old version until they finish. The leftover dead versions must later be cleaned up by a process called VACUUM; if nobody cleans, tables swell up ('bloat') and, in the worst case, the database protects itself by refusing writes.

The life of a row version. Space from dead versions is reused only after VACUUM proves no transaction still needs them.

Think of it like…

It is like a whiteboard where you never erase — you cross out the old line and write the new one underneath, so anyone mid-read can still follow the old line. Every so often a cleaner (VACUUM) wipes the crossed-out lines so the board does not fill up.

Real-world example

Ravi's fictional ride-sharing app RideNest updates each driver's location row every 5 seconds — 20,000 drivers means about 17 million updates a day. Because autovacuum was left at default settings, the 'driver_locations' table grew from 50 MB to 9 GB of mostly dead rows. Tuning autovacuum for that table and lowering its fillfactor so updates stay on the same page brought it back to under 100 MB.

docs.title: How it works
docs.text:
1. Every row version (tuple) carries xmin, the ID of the transaction that created it, and xmax, the ID of the one that deleted or replaced it.
  2. A query takes a snapshot and only sees versions whose xmin committed before the snapshot and whose xmax did not.
  3. UPDATE inserts a new version and sets xmax on the old one; DELETE only sets xmax — the space is not freed yet.
  4. Autovacuum notices tables with many dead tuples, removes versions no running transaction can see, and records the free space for reuse.
  5. VACUUM also 'freezes' very old rows so 32-bit transaction IDs can wrap around safely, and ANALYZE refreshes planner statistics.

Who uses it

PostgreSQL DBAs, site reliability engineers and backend developers with update-heavy tables meet VACUUM tuning sooner or later; it is a classic Postgres interview topic.

Key takeaway

Remember the three jobs of VACUUM: reclaim dead tuples, update the visibility map (enabling index-only scans), and freeze old transaction IDs to prevent wraparound.

Going deeper

  • Autovacuum triggers when dead tuples exceed autovacuum_vacuum_threshold (50) plus autovacuum_vacuum_scale_factor (20 %) of the table, so a 100-million-row table waits for 20 million dead rows unless you tune it per table.
  • Transaction IDs are 32-bit, giving about 2 billion usable IDs before wraparound; freezing marks old rows as visible-to-all, and if freezing falls far behind Postgres stops accepting writes to protect data.
  • Heap-only tuple (HOT) updates put the new version on the same page and skip index updates when no indexed column changes; a fillfactor of 70-90 leaves room to make this likely.
  • A long-running or 'idle in transaction' session holds back the oldest visible snapshot, so VACUUM cannot remove anything newer than it, and bloat builds across the whole database.
  • VACUUM FULL rewrites the table compactly but takes an ACCESS EXCLUSIVE lock; the pg_repack extension rebuilds tables online with only brief locks.
  • The visibility map stores two bits per page (all-visible, all-frozen); all-visible pages let index-only scans skip the heap and let VACUUM skip work.

Common mistakes & misconceptions

  • Disabling autovacuum because it 'uses I/O': bloat and wraparound risk follow; tune cost limits and per-table thresholds instead.
  • Running VACUUM FULL on a busy production table: it blocks all reads and writes until done — use pg_repack or plain VACUUM.
  • Leaving application sessions 'idle in transaction': set idle_in_transaction_session_timeout so forgotten transactions do not block cleanup.

docs.title: Try it: See dead tuples and autovacuum activity
docs.text:
SELECT relname, n_live_tup, n_dead_tup, last_autovacuum, last_autoanalyze
FROM pg_stat_user_tables
ORDER BY n_dead_tup DESC LIMIT 10;

-- hidden system columns on any table
SELECT xmin, xmax, * FROM orders LIMIT 3;

docs.title: 5.3 PostgreSQL Extensions — PostGIS, pgvector, TimescaleDB, Citus and More
docs.text:
An extension is an add-on package that teaches PostgreSQL new tricks — new data types, functions, index types or even background jobs — without forking the database. You install the files and run CREATE EXTENSION. This is a big reason Postgres can act as a map database, a vector database, a time-series database or a sharded cluster.

What extensions plug into. The same core engine gains new data types, indexes and workers from extensions.

Think of it like…

Extensions are like apps on a smartphone: the phone (Postgres) stays the same, but installing a maps app or a camera app gives it whole new abilities.

Real-world example

Tomás builds the fictional delivery service QuickCrate. PostGIS answers 'which couriers are within 2 km of this shop?', pgvector finds products similar to a customer's last purchase, and pg_cron deletes expired carts every night — all inside one PostgreSQL database instead of four separate systems.

docs.title: How it works
docs.text:
1. Install the extension's files on the server (an OS package, a build from source, or tick a box on a managed service).
  2. Some extensions must also be preloaded via shared_preload_libraries and need a restart (for example pg_cron, TimescaleDB, Citus).
  3. Run CREATE EXTENSION name; inside the database to register its types, functions and operators.
  4. Use the new features in ordinary SQL; ALTER EXTENSION name UPDATE; upgrades it later.
  5. On managed clouds, check the provider's list of allowed extensions and versions before you design around one.

Who uses it

GIS analysts, AI/ML engineers, IoT and observability teams, and SaaS platforms that need to scale out all lean on Postgres extensions.

Key takeaway

In interviews, 'Postgres is extensible' means more than plugins: extensions can add data types, operators, index access methods, foreign data wrappers and background workers.

Going deeper

  • An extension bundles a control file, SQL scripts and usually a shared library written in C (or Rust via the pgrx framework); CREATE EXTENSION runs its scripts inside one database.
  • PostGIS (first released 2001) adds geometry and geography types, hundreds of ST_ functions and GiST-indexed spatial queries; it is widely considered the most capable open-source spatial database.
  • pgvector adds a vector type with HNSW and IVFFlat indexes and distance operators such as <-> (L2) and <=> (cosine); it is offered by every major managed Postgres service.
  • Citus, owned by Microsoft since 2019 and open source, turns Postgres into a sharded cluster with distributed tables; it powers Azure's elastic clusters offering.
  • TimescaleDB adds hypertables that auto-partition by time, plus compression and continuous aggregates; its company renamed itself TigerData in 2025, and some features use the Timescale Licence rather than Apache 2.0.
  • Managed services restrict extensions for safety: AWS, Google and Azure each publish allow-lists, so an extension that needs superuser or custom C code may simply be unavailable.

Common mistakes & misconceptions

  • Assuming every extension works on your cloud: check the provider's supported-extension list and version before committing a design.
  • Forgetting extensions during major upgrades: pg_upgrade needs the same extensions installed for the new version, often at compatible versions.
  • Treating an extension as free of licence questions: TimescaleDB community features and some others use source-available licences.

docs.title: Try it: List and enable extensions
docs.text:
SELECT name, default_version, installed_version
FROM pg_available_extensions ORDER BY name;

CREATE EXTENSION IF NOT EXISTS pg_trgm;   -- fuzzy text matching
SELECT similarity('postgres', 'postgress');

docs.title: 5.4 MySQL, InnoDB, HeatWave and MariaDB
docs.text:
MySQL is the open-source relational database that powered the early web — the 'M' in the LAMP stack — and it is still one of the most deployed databases in the world. Oracle has owned it since 2010. Its default storage engine, InnoDB, provides transactions and crash safety. MariaDB is a community-driven fork created in 2009 by MySQL's original author, and the two have slowly drifted apart.

From MySQL AB to two families. Ownership changes explain why MariaDB exists and why MySQL versions changed shape.

Think of it like…

MySQL and MariaDB are like two siblings raised in the same house who moved to different cities: they share a family resemblance and many habits, but each has picked up new ones the other does not understand.

Real-world example

Hannah's fictional blog network InkWell runs 300 WordPress sites on MySQL 8.4 LTS. Each page view runs a handful of simple primary-key lookups that InnoDB answers from memory in under a millisecond. When the 8.0 line reached end of life in April 2026, she had already moved to 8.4 and plans to test 9.7 LTS next.

docs.title: How it works
docs.text:
1. A client connects to mysqld on port 3306; MySQL uses one thread (not one process) per connection.
  2. The server layer parses and optimises SQL, then calls a pluggable storage engine — almost always InnoDB.
  3. InnoDB stores each table as a B+tree clustered on the primary key; secondary indexes point to primary key values.
  4. Changes go to the redo log and buffer pool first; an undo log keeps old versions for MVCC and rollback.
  5. The binary log (binlog) records committed changes for replication to replicas and for point-in-time recovery.

Who uses it

Web developers, WordPress/Drupal/Magento hosts, SaaS companies and large internet firms run MySQL; MariaDB ships as the default 'MySQL' in many Linux distributions.

Key takeaway

Know the difference between InnoDB's clustered primary key and Postgres's heap tables: in InnoDB a random UUIDv4 primary key scatters inserts across the tree, so sequential keys are much faster.

Going deeper

  • Since 2023 MySQL uses two tracks: Long-Term Support lines (8.4 in 2024, 9.7 in April 2026) that get only fixes, and frequent Innovation releases with new features; Oracle has announced calendar-style numbers for later Innovation releases.
  • InnoDB clusters rows by primary key in 16 KB pages; the buffer pool (innodb_buffer_pool_size, often 50-75 % of RAM on a dedicated server) caches pages, and the redo log makes commits durable.
  • MySQL's default isolation level is REPEATABLE READ (PostgreSQL's is READ COMMITTED), and InnoDB uses gap and next-key locks to prevent phantoms for locking reads.
  • MySQL HeatWave is Oracle's cloud service adding an in-memory, massively parallel columnar engine for analytics, plus Lakehouse queries on object storage, AutoML and GenAI vector features; it runs on OCI, AWS and Azure.
  • MariaDB has diverged: it has its own optimiser, system-versioned tables, sequences, Aria and ColumnStore engines and a native VECTOR type (11.7+); its LTS lines include 10.11, 11.4, 11.8 and 12.3 (2026).
  • MariaDB plc was taken private by K1 Investment Management in 2024, while the separate non-profit MariaDB Foundation looks after the open-source server and its community.

Common mistakes & misconceptions

  • Assuming MariaDB is a drop-in MySQL replacement: since roughly MySQL 5.7 / MariaDB 10.x the JSON storage, replication GTIDs and many features differ — test before switching.
  • Using utf8 in MySQL: it means the old 3-byte utf8mb3 that cannot store emoji; use utf8mb4 (the default since 8.0).
  • Running an Innovation release in production without a plan: each is supported only until the next one, so most teams stay on LTS.

docs.title: Try it: Check your MySQL or MariaDB server
docs.text:
SELECT VERSION();
SHOW ENGINES;                         -- InnoDB should be DEFAULT
SHOW VARIABLES LIKE 'innodb_buffer_pool_size';
SELECT @@transaction_isolation;       -- REPEATABLE-READ by default

docs.title: 5.5 Oracle Database — 19c, 23ai, 26ai, RAC and Exadata
docs.text:
Oracle Database is the commercial relational database that has dominated large enterprises — banks, telecoms, governments, airlines — since the 1980s. It is expensive and complex, but packed with features for very high availability, security and performance. Its newest long-term release, Oracle AI Database 26ai (October 2025), builds AI vector search and other AI features directly into the database.

Oracle RAC on Exadata. Several database servers share one database; storage cells filter data before sending it up.

Think of it like…

Oracle is like a fully staffed luxury hotel: everything you could want is on site — concierge, spa, security, backup generators — but you pay for every service and need trained staff to run it.

Real-world example

The fictional bank Northgate Savings runs its core ledger on a two-node Oracle RAC cluster on Exadata, with an Active Data Guard standby 300 km away. When one RAC node fails at 2 a.m., sessions move to the surviving node within seconds. In 2026 the bank applies the 26ai release update and starts using AI Vector Search to find similar fraud cases in the same database.

docs.title: How it works
docs.text:
1. An Oracle instance (memory structures such as the SGA plus background processes) opens a database made of data files, control files and redo logs.
  2. Since 21c, every database is a container database (CDB) holding one or more pluggable databases (PDBs) that applications connect to.
  3. Real Application Clusters (RAC) let several servers open the same database at once, sharing blocks over a fast interconnect (Cache Fusion).
  4. Data Guard ships redo to standby databases in another site for disaster recovery; Active Data Guard lets the standby serve read-only queries.
  5. Exadata hardware and the Autonomous Database cloud service add storage offload, automated tuning and patching on top.

Who uses it

Oracle DBAs, enterprise architects, ERP teams (Oracle E-Business Suite, many SAP and banking systems) and consultants in finance, telecom and government work with Oracle daily.

Key takeaway

Know the release types: 19c and 23ai/26ai are long-term releases; 26ai replaced 23ai through a release update rather than a full upgrade, so '23.26' version numbers appear in 2026.

Going deeper

  • Oracle Database 23ai (May 2024, previously called 23c) added AI Vector Search, JSON Relational Duality views, SQL domains, a BOOLEAN type and SQL Firewall; Oracle AI Database 26ai (October 2025) is the long-term successor delivered as a release update.
  • On-premises 26ai for Linux x86-64 arrived with the January 2026 release update (version 23.26.1); Oracle says AI Vector Search is included at no extra cost.
  • Exadata Smart Scan pushes WHERE filtering and column projection to the storage servers, so only matching rows cross the network — often a large cut in data moved for analytic scans.
  • Oracle licences Enterprise Edition per processor (cores multiplied by a core factor, 0.5 for most Intel/AMD chips) or per named user; options such as RAC, Partitioning and Active Data Guard cost extra.
  • Oracle Database@Azure, @AWS and @Google Cloud place Oracle-run Exadata infrastructure inside those clouds' data centres, so applications on the hyperscaler reach Oracle with low latency.
  • The Multitenant architecture's non-CDB style is desupported from 21c onward, so 19c-to-23ai/26ai upgrades usually also convert databases into pluggable databases.

Common mistakes & misconceptions

  • Running Oracle in a cloud VM without reading the licensing rules: virtualisation and option usage can trigger large audit bills — check with licensing experts.
  • Thinking RAC alone is disaster recovery: RAC protects against a server failure in one site; you still need Data Guard or backups for site loss.
  • Assuming 'AI database' means an LLM inside: 26ai mainly adds vector search, model calls and agent tooling around your data — the SQL engine is still the core.

docs.title: 5.6 Microsoft SQL Server 2025 and Azure SQL
docs.text:
SQL Server is Microsoft's commercial relational database, very common in businesses that use Windows, .NET and Microsoft 365 — and it also runs on Linux and in containers. SQL Server 2025, released in November 2025, adds AI-era features such as a vector data type, regular expressions and a native JSON type. In Azure, Microsoft sells the same engine as managed services called Azure SQL.

Three ways to run the SQL Server engine

SQL Server (VM or on-prem) Azure SQL Managed Instance Azure SQL Database You manage OS Yes No No Patching & backups You Microsoft Microsoft SQL Agent, cross-DB queries Yes Yes No (use elastic jobs) Scale model Bigger server vCores per instance vCores, serverless, Hyperscale Best for Full control, any feature Lift-and-shift apps New cloud apps

Moving right, you manage less but give up some instance-level control.

Think of it like…

SQL Server and Azure SQL are like the same car model sold three ways: buy it and maintain it yourself (SQL Server), lease it with servicing included (Managed Instance), or simply book rides and never see the engine (Azure SQL Database).

Real-world example

The fictional logistics company Brightline Freight runs its warehouse system on SQL Server 2022 in its own data centre. In 2026 it upgrades to SQL Server 2025 to use optimized locking, which cuts blocking between pickers' updates, and mirrors operational tables into Microsoft Fabric for Power BI reports. A new customer portal is built on Azure SQL Database serverless, which pauses when idle overnight.

docs.title: How it works
docs.text:
1. Clients connect over the TDS protocol (port 1433) and send T-SQL, Microsoft's SQL dialect.
  2. The relational engine parses and optimises each query, caching execution plans for reuse; Query Store records plans and runtimes over time.
  3. The storage engine keeps 8 KB pages in a buffer pool and writes a transaction log before data files.
  4. Choose where it runs: SQL Server on Windows, Linux or containers; Azure SQL Managed Instance; or Azure SQL Database (including serverless and Hyperscale).
  5. Pick an edition (Enterprise, Standard, Express, Developer) and licence by cores or by server plus client access licences.

Who uses it

Microsoft-stack developers (.NET, C#), business-intelligence teams, DBAs in finance, healthcare, retail and government, and Azure cloud engineers use SQL Server and Azure SQL.

Key takeaway

Be ready to compare Azure SQL Database (single managed database, no instance-level features) with Managed Instance (near-full SQL Server compatibility, including SQL Agent and cross-database queries).

Going deeper

  • SQL Server 2025 (version 17.x) became generally available at Microsoft Ignite in November 2025, adding a native vector type with DiskANN-based vector indexes, T-SQL AI functions and calls to model endpoints.
  • SQL Server 2025 also brought regular-expression functions such as REGEXP_LIKE, a native JSON data type, optimized locking (transaction ID locking plus lock-after-qualification) and mirroring of data into Microsoft Fabric.
  • Editions: Enterprise (all features), Standard (capped CPU and memory), free Express (small databases; Microsoft raised its size cap to 50 GB in 2025) and free Developer edition for non-production use.
  • Licensing is per core, sold in two-core packs with a minimum of four cores per server or VM, or Server + CAL for Standard; Azure Hybrid Benefit reuses on-premises licences in Azure.
  • Azure SQL Database Hyperscale separates compute from page servers and log service, supporting databases of over 100 TB with fast backups and quick read-replica creation.
  • SQL Server has run on Linux since 2017; Azure Data Studio was retired in 2026, and Microsoft points users to SSMS and the MSSQL extension for Visual Studio Code.

Common mistakes & misconceptions

  • Using Express in production for a growing app: it caps CPU, memory and database size, so plan the move to Standard early.
  • Using Developer edition in production: it is licensed only for development and testing even though it has every Enterprise feature.
  • Assuming Azure SQL Database supports everything SQL Server does: features like SQL Agent, CLR and cross-database queries need Managed Instance or a VM.

-- then in SSMS or sqlcmd

docs.title: 5.7 SQLite — The Database Embedded Everywhere
docs.text:
SQLite is a small relational database engine that lives inside your application as a library — there is no server to install. A whole database is a single ordinary file. It is almost certainly the most widely deployed database in the world: every Android and iOS phone, every major web browser and countless desktop apps contain it.

Inside the SQLite library. The whole stack runs inside your application's process — no network, no server.

Think of it like…

If PostgreSQL is a public library with staff and opening hours, SQLite is a notebook in your backpack: always with you, needs no staff, and perfect for one person writing at a time.

Real-world example

Aisha builds the fictional note-taking app PocketNotes. Each user's notes live in one SQLite file on their phone, so the app works offline on a plane. She turns on WAL mode so the interface can read notes while a background sync writes changes, and uses the FTS5 full-text extension so searching 5,000 notes takes milliseconds.

docs.title: How it works
docs.text:
1. Your program links the SQLite library (a single C file) and opens a database file — or creates it if missing.
  2. SQL is compiled into bytecode and run by SQLite's virtual machine, which reads and writes B-tree pages in the file.
  3. Writes are protected by locks on the file: many readers may read, but only one writer at a time.
  4. In rollback-journal mode a copy of original pages is saved before changes; in WAL mode new pages are appended to a -wal file and later checkpointed.
  5. Copying the file (safely, with the backup API or VACUUM INTO) copies the entire database.

Who uses it

Mobile, desktop, embedded and IoT developers use SQLite constantly; data scientists use it for small datasets; it also runs edge and serverless databases such as Cloudflare D1 and Turso.

Key takeaway

Remember SQLite's sweet spot in one line: low-concurrency, local data with one writer at a time — and that it is in the public domain, so there is no licence at all.

Going deeper

  • SQLite was created by D. Richard Hipp in 2000, is in the public domain, and the developers promise to support the stable file format (unchanged since 2004) through the year 2050.
  • The US Library of Congress lists SQLite as a recommended storage format for datasets, partly because the file format is documented and stable.
  • WAL mode (since 2010) lets readers continue while one writer appends to the write-ahead log; checkpoints copy pages back to the main file, by default at about 1,000 pages.
  • SQLite uses flexible typing by default (a column's type is only an 'affinity'); STRICT tables (3.37, 2021) enforce declared types, and JSONB storage arrived in 3.45 (2024).
  • The project tests extremely thoroughly — aiming for 100 % branch coverage — and in 2026 the current line is 3.53.x after 3.52.0 was withdrawn for a bug.
  • Turso maintains libSQL, an open fork adding replication and network access, and is building Turso Database, a Rust rewrite with concurrent writes that was still in beta in mid-2026.

Common mistakes & misconceptions

  • Putting a SQLite file on a network file share (NFS/SMB): file locking can fail and corrupt data — keep the file on local disk.
  • Using SQLite for a busy multi-writer web app without care: only one writer at a time, so heavy concurrent writes queue up; use WAL and short transactions or a server database.
  • Copying the .db file while it is being written: use the .backup command, the backup API or VACUUM INTO for a consistent copy.

docs.title: Try it: Create a SQLite database from the command line
docs.text:
sqlite3 notes.db
PRAGMA journal_mode = WAL;
CREATE TABLE note (id INTEGER PRIMARY KEY, title TEXT NOT NULL, body TEXT) STRICT;
INSERT INTO note (title, body) VALUES ('Shopping', 'milk, eggs');
SELECT * FROM note;
.quit

docs.title: 5.8 IBM Db2 and Other Relational Engines You Will Meet
docs.text:
Beyond PostgreSQL, MySQL, Oracle and SQL Server there are other relational databases you may meet at work. IBM Db2 descends from IBM's original System R research and still runs much of the world's banking and insurance on mainframes. Others — Informix, SAP ASE, Firebird, Java-embedded engines like H2 and Microsoft Access — are found in particular niches or older systems.

The relational family tree. Most products descend from a few research projects and business deals.

Think of it like…

These engines are like regional languages: not everyone speaks them, but if you work in a certain town (a bank, an old factory system, a Java test suite) you will hear them every day.

Real-world example

Leon joins the fictional insurer Harbour Mutual as a junior developer. Policies live in Db2 for z/OS on an IBM mainframe, processing millions of COBOL transactions a night, while a newer claims portal uses PostgreSQL. His team's Java tests spin up an in-memory H2 database so they run in seconds without a real server.

docs.title: How it works
docs.text:
1. Identify the platform: mainframe (Db2 for z/OS), IBM i (Db2 for i), or Linux/Unix/Windows (Db2 LUW).
  2. Learn the vendor's SQL dialect and tools — most follow ISO SQL closely, so your core skills transfer.
  3. Check support status and licensing: some engines are actively developed, others only maintained.
  4. For legacy systems, plan migrations carefully: test SQL dialect differences, stored procedures and data types.
  5. For test-only engines (H2, HSQLDB), remember results can differ from production — prefer containers of the real database.

Who uses it

Mainframe developers and DBAs in banks and insurers, ERP consultants, Java developers and anyone maintaining long-lived business systems meet these engines.

Key takeaway

Mainframe Db2 skills are scarce and well paid; even a basic understanding of Db2 for z/OS, COBOL-SQL and JCL can set a graduate apart in finance.

Going deeper

  • Db2 comes in three main families: Db2 for z/OS on IBM Z mainframes (version 13), Db2 for i built into IBM i, and Db2 for Linux, UNIX and Windows (version 12.1 released in late 2024).
  • Db2 BLU Acceleration (2013) added in-memory columnar tables with compression and SIMD processing; Db2 Warehouse packages it for analytics, and Amazon RDS for Db2 has existed since 2023.
  • IBM Z mainframes still process a large share of the world's card and banking transactions; Db2 for z/OS with CICS or IMS and COBOL programs form the classic stack.
  • Firebird descends from Borland's InterBase, open-sourced in 2000; it remains popular in small business software in Brazil, Russia and Europe, with Firebird 5 released in 2024.
  • H2, HSQLDB and Apache Derby are pure-Java engines that can run inside a JVM; they are handy for tests and demos but differ from production databases in SQL details.
  • SAP ASE (formerly Sybase ASE) and IBM Informix are mature engines kept for existing customers; Microsoft Access uses the ACE/Jet engine for single-user desktop databases.

Common mistakes & misconceptions

  • Testing against H2 but running on PostgreSQL: dialect and behaviour differences cause bugs that only appear in production; use Testcontainers with the real database.
  • Writing off mainframe Db2 as obsolete: it is actively developed and runs critical systems; migrations off it are long, risky projects.
  • Letting a shared Access file become a multi-user business system: it was never designed for many concurrent users or large data.
